findings.description: The krbtgt account password has not been changed in an extended period (typically 180+ days). The krbtgt account is used to encrypt all Kerberos Ticket Granting Tickets (TGTs) in the domain. If its key material is compromised, an attacker can forge Golden Tickets.
findings.impact: A compromised krbtgt key enables Golden Ticket attacks, granting the attacker unrestricted access to any resource in the domain for the lifetime of the key. Kerberos maintains two most-recent krbtgt key versions — rotating the password invalidates the oldest one. Microsoft recommends rotating the krbtgt password at least every 180 days, and immediately after any suspected domain compromise.

findings.title: Stale Domain Accounts
findings.remediation_brief: Implement a regular account review process (at least quarterly). Disable accounts inactive for 90+ days. Delete accounts inactive for 180+ days after confirming they are no longer needed. Automate with PowerShell: Search-ADAccount -AccountInactive -TimeSpan 90.00:00:00 | Disable-ADAccount. Audit disabled accounts for sensitive group memberships before deletion.
findings.description: Domain user accounts were found that have not logged in for an extended period (90+ days) and are still enabled. Stale accounts represent dormant attack surface that attackers can target without triggering alerts tied to active users.
findings.impact: Stale accounts are attractive targets for attackers because their compromise is less likely to be noticed — no legitimate user will report unexpected activity. These accounts may retain their original (potentially weak) passwords, group memberships, and access permissions. If any stale account has privileged access, it presents an unmonitored path to escalation.

findings.title: SID History Abuse Risk
findings.remediation_brief: Audit all accounts with SID History: Get-ADUser -Filter 'SIDHistory -like "*"' -Properties SIDHistory | Select Name,SIDHistory. Remove SID History entries after domain migration is complete and verified: Set-ADUser -Identity <user> -Remove @{SIDHistory=<SID>}. Enable SID filtering on all trusts to prevent cross-domain SID History abuse. Monitor Event ID 4765 (SID History added) and Event ID 4766 (SID History add attempt failed).
findings.description: User or group accounts with non-empty SID History attributes were found. SID History is a legitimate migration feature that preserves access to resources in a source domain after migration. However, SID History can be abused to inject arbitrary SIDs (including Domain Admins) into a user's token.
findings.impact: An attacker who can modify the SID History attribute can inject the SID of a privileged group (e.g., Domain Admins, Enterprise Admins) into their own or another account's SID History. The injected SID is included in the user's Kerberos tickets and PAC, granting access to all resources the injected SID has permission to. This is a stealthy persistence technique because the user's group memberships appear normal.

findings.title: ESC1 - Misconfigured Certificate Template
findings.remediation_brief: Disable 'Supply in the request' option on the Subject Name tab of vulnerable certificate templates. Instead, configure 'Build from Active Directory information'. Restrict enrollment permissions to only the users/groups that require the template. Remove unnecessary EKUs (especially 'Any Purpose'). Consider removing the template entirely if not operationally required. Audit with: certutil -v -template | findstr /i 'CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT'.
findings.description: A certificate template allows enrollees to specify a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in the certificate request, AND low-privileged users can enroll, AND the template has an EKU that permits authentication (Client Authentication, PKINIT, Smart Card Logon, or any purpose). This is the ESC1 attack vector identified by SpecterOps.
findings.impact: Any low-privileged domain user can request a certificate with an arbitrary SAN (e.g., specifying a Domain Admin UPN). This certificate can then be used for Kerberos authentication as the impersonated user, achieving complete domain compromise without needing to know the target user's password. This is the most commonly exploited ADCS vulnerability.

findings.title: ESC2 - Overly Permissive Template
findings.remediation_brief: Replace 'Any Purpose' EKU with specific, required EKUs only (e.g., Client Authentication only if that is the purpose). Remove templates with no EKU unless operationally justified. Restrict enrollment permissions to the minimum required groups. Audit all templates for overly broad EKU settings using certipy or Certutil.
findings.description: A certificate template has an Extended Key Usage (EKU) of 'Any Purpose' (OID 2.5.29.37.0) or no EKU at all (which is equivalent to any purpose), AND low-privileged users can enroll. Certificates with Any Purpose or no EKU restrictions can be used for any purpose including client authentication, code signing, and subordinate CA issuance.
findings.impact: A certificate with 'Any Purpose' or no EKU can be used for client authentication (impersonating any user), code signing (creating trusted malicious software), or even as a subordinate CA certificate (issuing arbitrary certificates). The combination of unrestricted EKU and broad enrollment permissions creates a powerful attack vector for domain compromise.

findings.title: ESC3 - Enrollment Agent Template
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict enrollment permissions on Enrollment Agent templates to only authorized Certificate Enrollment administrators. Configure enrollment restrictions on the CA: right-click CA > Properties > Enrollment Agents tab to restrict which enrollment agents can enroll for which templates and users. Consider disabling the Enrollment Agent template if not operationally required.
findings.description: A certificate template with the Certificate Request Agent EKU (OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.311.20.2.1) allows low-privileged users to enroll. An Enrollment Agent certificate enables the holder to request certificates on behalf of other users, including privileged accounts.
findings.impact: An attacker can first obtain an Enrollment Agent certificate, then use it to request certificates for any other user in the domain (e.g., Domain Admins) using a second template that allows enrollment by enrollment agents. This two-step attack achieves domain compromise by impersonating any user via certificate-based authentication.

findings.title: ESC4 - Vulnerable Template ACL
findings.remediation_brief: Audit all certificate template ACLs and remove write permissions for non-administrative groups. Only Enterprise Admins, Domain Admins, and designated PKI administrators should have write access to templates. Use: certutil -v -template | Select-String 'Allow.*Write'. Review and tighten ACLs via certtmpl.msc. Enable ADCS auditing to detect template modifications.
findings.description: A certificate template's access control list (ACL) grants write permissions (WriteDACL, WriteOwner, WriteProperty, or GenericWrite) to low-privileged users or groups. This allows an attacker to modify the template configuration to introduce ESC1-ESC3 conditions.
findings.impact: An attacker with write access to a certificate template can modify it to enable ESC1 (add CT_FLAG_ENROLLEE_SUPPLIES_SUBJECT), change EKUs to 'Any Purpose', or enable enrollment for their own account. After modification, they exploit the newly created ESC1/ESC2/ESC3 condition for domain compromise. The template modification itself may go unnoticed without specific ADCS auditing.

findings.title: ESC6 - EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 Flag Set
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag on the CA: certutil -config "CA\CAName" -setreg policy\EditFlags -EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. Restart the CA service: net stop certsvc && net start certsvc. Verify: certutil -config "CA\CAName" -getreg policy\EditFlags — the output should NOT include EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2. After disabling, audit all recently issued certificates for suspicious SAN values.
findings.description: The Certificate Authority has the EDITF_ATTRIBUTESUBJECTALTNAME2 flag enabled. This CA-level configuration allows ANY certificate requester to specify an arbitrary Subject Alternative Name (SAN) in their request, regardless of template settings. This effectively makes every authentication template on this CA vulnerable to ESC1.
findings.impact: With this flag enabled, any domain user who can enroll in any template with an authentication EKU can specify an arbitrary SAN, impersonating any user in the domain including Domain Admins. This is a CA-wide misconfiguration that bypasses per-template SAN controls — fixing individual templates does not mitigate this issue. A single CA with this flag compromises the entire domain.

findings.title: ESC8 - NTLM Relay to HTTP Enrollment
findings.remediation_brief: Enable HTTPS on all ADCS web enrollment endpoints and disable HTTP. Enable Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA) in IIS: IIS Manager > Authentication > Windows Authentication > Advanced Settings > Extended Protection = Required. Alternatively, disable the web enrollment role entirely if not required and use certreq or autoenrollment instead. Install patches for PetitPotam (CVE-2021-36942). Enable NTLM relay mitigations: enable SMB signing, LDAP signing, and channel binding.
findings.description: The AD Certificate Services web enrollment endpoint is accessible over HTTP (not HTTPS) and/or does not enforce Extended Protection for Authentication (EPA). This allows NTLM relay attacks where a coerced machine account authentication (e.g., via PetitPotam, PrinterBug) can be relayed to the enrollment endpoint to request a certificate as the machine.
findings.impact: An attacker can coerce a domain controller to authenticate to their machine (using PetitPotam, PrinterBug, or similar), then relay that authentication to the ADCS HTTP enrollment endpoint to obtain a certificate as the DC's machine account. This certificate allows the attacker to authenticate as the DC, enabling DCSync to extract all domain credentials. This is a full domain compromise path.

findings.title: Malicious Browser Extension Detected ({browser})
findings.remediation_brief: Remove the malicious extension(s) immediately. Check other browsers on the system for the same extensions. Review browsing history for credential exposure. Force password resets for any accounts accessed while the extension was installed. Deploy browser extension whitelisting via Group Policy.
findings.description: One or more browser extensions match known malicious extensions in the threat intelligence database. These extensions may be stealing credentials, injecting ads, or exfiltrating browsing data.
findings.impact: Malicious browser extensions can intercept all web traffic including passwords, session tokens, banking credentials, and form data. They can inject content into pages, redirect searches, cryptomine, and exfiltrate browsing history. They persist across browser restarts and are often difficult for users to identify.

findings.title: Browser Proxy Configured ({browser})
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the proxy configuration is authorized and expected. Compare with system proxy settings. If a browser-specific proxy is not required, remove it. Investigate whether malware or a malicious extension configured the proxy.
findings.description: A browser-level proxy configuration was detected, separate from system proxy settings. This proxy intercepts all browser traffic and may route it through an unintended intermediary.
findings.impact: A browser-level proxy can intercept all HTTP/HTTPS traffic from the browser, including login credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data. Browser-level proxies may bypass system proxy settings, making them harder to detect. If the proxy is malicious, it enables credential theft and traffic manipulation.

findings.title: Suspicious Bookmark Detected ({browser})
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate each suspicious bookmark. Check if the user intentionally saved it or if it was created by malware. Review browser history for visits to the bookmarked URLs. Remove the bookmarks and block the domains at the DNS/proxy level. Scan the system for malware.
findings.description: One or more browser bookmarks link to domains or IPs associated with known malicious infrastructure in the threat intelligence database.
findings.impact: Bookmarks to malicious domains may indicate the user regularly visits compromised or phishing sites. This could be a watering hole attack vector, a phishing landing page saved by a targeted user, or a bookmark planted by malware for persistence or redirection.

findings.title: Expired Certificate
findings.remediation_brief: Renew or replace all expired certificates. Remove expired certificates that are no longer needed. Implement certificate lifecycle management with automated renewal alerts at 30, 14, and 7 days before expiry.
findings.description: One or more certificates in the local machine or current user certificate store have expired.
findings.impact: Expired certificates cause service disruptions, authentication failures, and trust warnings. They may also indicate neglected systems or processes. Expired certificates used for code signing or SSL/TLS expose users to man-in-the-middle and substitution attacks.

findings.title: Certificate Expiring Soon
findings.remediation_brief: Renew expiring certificates before their expiry date. Use automated certificate management tools (ACME, internal CA auto-enrollment) where possible. Verify new certificates are properly installed and tested before the old ones expire.
findings.description: One or more certificates will expire within the next 30 days.
findings.impact: Certificates expiring soon risk service disruptions if not renewed in time. SSL/TLS certificate expiry causes browser warnings and connection failures. Authentication certificate expiry can lock out users.

findings.title: Self-Signed Certificate in Trust Store
findings.remediation_brief: Replace weak certificates with ones using SHA-256 or stronger signature algorithms and RSA 2048-bit or longer keys (or ECDSA P-256+). Update internal CA templates to enforce modern cryptographic standards.
findings.description: Certificates using deprecated signature algorithms (SHA1) or insufficient key lengths (RSA < 2048 bits) were detected.
findings.impact: SHA1 signatures are vulnerable to collision attacks, enabling certificate forgery. RSA keys shorter than 2048 bits can be factored with sufficient computational resources, compromising the certificate's security.

findings.title: Weak Certificate Signature Algorithm
findings.remediation_brief: Review all non-standard root certificates. Verify each against the organization's internal CA infrastructure. Remove any certificates that cannot be accounted for. If a rogue root is found, investigate how it was installed and treat the system as potentially compromised.
findings.description: A self-signed certificate that is not from a well-known Certificate Authority was found in the Trusted Root Certification Authorities store.
findings.impact: Unknown root certificates in the trusted store could enable man-in-the-middle attacks by allowing an attacker's CA to issue trusted certificates for any domain. This could be from legitimate enterprise CA deployment or from malware installing rogue roots.

findings.title: Weak Certificate Key Size
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one using at least a 2048-bit RSA key (3072-bit or 4096-bit recommended for long-lived certificates). For new deployments, consider ECDSA P-256 or P-384 keys which provide equivalent security at smaller sizes. Update the certificate on all services and endpoints.
findings.description: A certificate using a key size shorter than 2048 bits was detected. Keys shorter than 2048 bits are considered weak and can be factored with modern computing resources, compromising all protections the certificate provides.
findings.impact: A weak key can be factored using distributed computing or cloud resources. 1024-bit RSA keys have been publicly factored, and NIST deprecated keys shorter than 2048 bits since 2013. An attacker who factors the key can forge signatures, decrypt traffic, and impersonate the certificate holder.

findings.title: Firewall Profile Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Develop a system hardening plan based on the CIS Benchmark for the specific Windows version. Prioritize Level 1 controls first as they have minimal operational impact. Implement changes through Group Policy for consistent deployment across endpoints.
findings.description: The endpoint's configuration passes fewer than 50% of applicable CIS Benchmark controls, indicating severe hardening deficiencies.
findings.impact: Below 50% CIS compliance represents a fundamentally unhardened system with numerous security weaknesses. The system is significantly more vulnerable to common attack techniques than a properly hardened baseline.

findings.title: Screen Lock Timeout Not Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Address the specific failing CIS controls, prioritizing those related to authentication, access control, and network security. Focus on Level 1 controls that have not been implemented. Use Group Policy to enforce configurations across the organization.
findings.description: The endpoint passes between 50% and 80% of applicable CIS Benchmark controls, indicating room for improvement in system hardening.
findings.impact: While partially hardened, the system has notable security gaps that could be exploited. Each unaddressed CIS control represents a specific attack vector that an adversary could leverage.

findings.title: NetBIOS over TCP/IP Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Remediate all DISA STIG Category I findings immediately. These represent the highest priority security issues. Apply STIG fixes via Group Policy or SCAP compliance tools. Document any findings requiring a Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) if immediate remediation is not possible.
findings.description: Category I DISA STIG findings (high severity) are present, representing vulnerabilities that could directly lead to system compromise.
findings.impact: STIG CAT I findings represent the most critical security weaknesses. They typically allow unauthorized access, denial of service, or information disclosure with high impact. DoD and many other organizations require zero CAT I findings for system accreditation.

findings.title: IPv6 Transition Technologies Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Plan remediation of DISA STIG Category II findings within 90 days. Prioritize those related to authentication and access control. Apply STIG fixes via Group Policy where possible for consistent deployment.
findings.description: Category II DISA STIG findings (medium severity) are present, representing security weaknesses that could contribute to system compromise.
findings.impact: STIG CAT II findings are significant security weaknesses that, while not immediately critical, contribute to an insecure posture and may be combined with other findings to achieve compromise. Organizations typically require CAT II remediation within 90 days.

findings.title: Remote Registry Service Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Use the hardening score as a baseline measurement and track improvements over time. Prioritize remediation of findings that contribute most to the score deficit. Establish a target hardening score and implement a continuous improvement program.
findings.description: An aggregate endpoint hardening score was calculated based on all security checks performed, providing an overall security posture assessment.
findings.impact: The hardening score provides a quantitative measure of the endpoint's security configuration. A low score indicates multiple security weaknesses that collectively increase the risk of compromise, while a high score indicates a well-hardened system.

findings.title: WiFi Passwords Stored in Cleartext
findings.remediation_brief: Configure WiFi profiles to not store passwords locally where possible. Use 802.1X/EAP certificate-based authentication instead of PSK. For WPA2-Personal/WPA3-Personal networks, limit local admin access and implement endpoint detection for credential harvesting tools. Remove saved profiles for networks no longer in use.
findings.description: Wireless network profiles on this system store passwords in cleartext. The 'netsh wlan show profiles key=clear' command can extract these credentials without elevated privileges on some Windows versions, or with local admin on others.
findings.impact: An attacker with local access can extract stored WiFi passwords for all previously connected networks. These credentials may grant access to corporate wireless networks, enabling lateral movement or unauthorized network access from outside the physical premises.

findings.title: Saved Remote Sessions Found
findings.remediation_brief: Remove saved credentials from remote access tools. Configure PuTTY and WinSCP to use SSH key authentication instead of passwords. Delete FileZilla sitemanager.xml entries that contain passwords. Remove .rdp files with embedded credentials. Use a secrets manager or enterprise password vault for remote access credentials.
findings.description: Saved remote access session configurations were found on this system, potentially containing stored credentials. This includes PuTTY sessions (registry), WinSCP sessions (registry/ini), FileZilla sitemanager.xml entries, and/or saved .rdp files with password hashes.
findings.impact: Stored remote session credentials provide an attacker with ready-made access paths to other systems. PuTTY and WinSCP may store passwords in reversible formats, FileZilla historically stored passwords in base64 (trivially decoded), and .rdp files may contain password hashes. Compromising these sessions enables lateral movement to additional hosts.

findings.title: Credential Files on Disk
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or securely delete all deployment files (unattend.xml, sysprep.xml) after provisioning. Encrypt connection strings in web.config using aspnet_regiis -pe. Replace cleartext passwords in applicationHost.config with encrypted alternatives. Audit the file system for credential remnants periodically using endpoint detection rules.
findings.description: Files containing plaintext or easily reversible credentials were found on disk. This includes unattend.xml/autounattend.xml (deployment passwords), sysprep.xml/sysprep.inf files, web.config connection strings, applicationHost.config bindings, and/or McAfee SiteList.xml files.
findings.impact: These files often contain local administrator passwords, database connection strings, service account credentials, or encryption keys in cleartext or trivially reversible formats. An attacker can use these credentials for privilege escalation, database access, or lateral movement. Deployment files (unattend.xml) frequently contain the initial administrator password used during Windows installation.

findings.title: GPP cpassword Credential Exposure
findings.remediation_brief: Install MS14-025 (KB2962486) which prevents creation of new GPP passwords. Delete all existing GPP XML files in SYSVOL that contain cpassword attributes. Rotate all passwords that were stored in GPP. Migrate to LAPS or gMSA for local administrator password management. Search SYSVOL: Get-ChildItem -Path '\\domain\SYSVOL' -Recurse -Include Groups.xml,Services.xml,Scheduledtasks.xml,DataSources.xml,Printers.xml,Drives.xml | Select-String 'cpassword'.
findings.description: Group Policy Preferences (GPP) XML files containing the 'cpassword' attribute were found in SYSVOL. Microsoft published the AES-256 key used to encrypt these passwords in MSDN documentation, making all cpassword values trivially decryptable by any domain user.
findings.impact: Any authenticated domain user can read SYSVOL and decrypt GPP passwords using the publicly known AES key. These passwords typically belong to local administrator accounts, service accounts, or scheduled task accounts configured via Group Policy. This is a well-known, trivially exploitable vulnerability that provides immediate privilege escalation in most Active Directory environments.

findings.title: Cloud Credential Files Found
findings.remediation_brief: Remove long-lived cloud credential files from endpoints. Use short-lived tokens via IAM roles, instance profiles, or managed identities instead. For development machines, use aws-vault, Azure CLI managed identity, or workload identity federation. Rotate any credentials that were stored on disk. Implement cloud credential scanning in CI/CD pipelines.
findings.description: Cloud provider credential files were found on this system. This includes AWS credentials (~/.aws/credentials), Azure profiles (~/.azure/), and/or GCP service account key JSON files. These files contain access keys, tokens, or private keys that authenticate to cloud services.
findings.impact: Compromised cloud credentials can grant an attacker access to cloud infrastructure, including compute instances, storage buckets, databases, and IAM controls. Depending on the permissions associated with the credentials, this can lead to data exfiltration, resource hijacking (cryptomining), or full cloud account compromise. Cloud credentials are frequently over-provisioned with excessive permissions.

findings.title: Windows Credential Manager Entries

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager

findings.remediation_brief: Review stored credentials periodically and remove entries for systems or services no longer accessed. Educate users not to save domain credentials in Credential Manager for sensitive systems. Implement Credential Guard to protect LSASS-derived credentials from extraction.
findings.description: Windows Credential Manager (Vault) contains stored credential entries. These may include web credentials, Windows credentials for network shares, and application-specific credentials protected by DPAPI.
findings.impact: While Credential Manager entries are protected by DPAPI (tied to the user's logon session), they can be decrypted by any process running as that user. If an attacker gains user-level access, they can extract all Vault credentials using tools like mimikatz or built-in vaultcmd commands. This finding is informational — the presence of stored credentials is expected behavior.

findings.title: DPAPI Master Key Accessible

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Windows Credential Manager

findings.remediation_brief: Implement Credential Guard to protect DPAPI master keys with virtualization-based security. Enforce strong passwords to make DPAPI key derivation computationally expensive. Restrict local admin access to limit offline DPAPI attacks. Use hardware-backed credential storage (TPM, smart cards) for the most sensitive credentials.
findings.description: DPAPI (Data Protection API) master key material was found to be accessible on this system. DPAPI protects user credentials, browser passwords, WiFi keys, and other sensitive data. If an attacker can access the master key or derive it from the user's password, all DPAPI-protected secrets can be decrypted.
findings.impact: DPAPI is the underlying encryption mechanism for Windows Credential Manager, browser saved passwords (Chrome, Edge), WiFi passwords, and many application secrets. An attacker with access to the DPAPI master key (stored in %APPDATA%\Microsoft\Protect\) and knowledge of the user's password can decrypt all DPAPI-protected data, providing access to a wide range of stored credentials.

findings.title: KeePass Database Files Found

mitre_attack.name: Credentials from Password Stores: Password Managers

findings.remediation_brief: Ensure KeePass databases use strong master passwords (20+ characters) combined with key files. Keep KeePass updated to the latest version. Restrict KeePass plugin loading to signed/approved plugins. Consider migrating to an enterprise password manager with centralized audit logging and MFA enforcement.
findings.description: KeePass password database files (.kdbx) were found on this system. While KeePass databases are encrypted, their presence indicates this system stores a password vault that may be targeted by attackers for credential harvesting.
findings.impact: KeePass databases, if protected by a weak master password, can be cracked offline. CVE-2023-32784 demonstrated that KeePass master passwords could be recovered from process memory. Additionally, KeePass plugin loading, trigger mechanisms, and configuration file manipulation have been used for credential theft. The database itself is a high-value target for exfiltration.

findings.title: SSH Private Keys Found
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure all SSH private keys are protected with strong passphrases. Use ssh-agent for key caching rather than storing unprotected keys. Implement SSH certificate-based authentication for managed environments. Audit and rotate SSH keys regularly. Remove keys for systems no longer accessed. Consider hardware-backed keys (FIDO2/PIV).
findings.description: SSH private key files were found on this system. These keys may provide passwordless authentication to remote systems (Linux servers, network devices, cloud instances). Keys without passphrases are immediately usable by anyone who can read them.
findings.impact: SSH private keys provide direct authentication to remote systems without requiring a password. If a key has no passphrase (or a weak one), an attacker can immediately use it for lateral movement. Keys in authorized_keys on target systems often have broad permissions. A single compromised SSH key can provide access to many systems in the environment.

findings.title: Brute Force Attack Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Implement account lockout policies (5-10 attempts), enable multi-factor authentication, and block offending source IPs at the firewall. Investigate targeted accounts for compromise indicators. Consider implementing Azure AD Smart Lockout for adaptive protection.
findings.description: Brute-force login activity detected with multiple failed authentication attempts from the same source within the past 7 days. Sources with more than 10 failures indicate automated credential guessing attacks targeting the system.
findings.impact: Sustained brute-force attacks may eventually succeed, especially against accounts with weak or reused passwords. Successful compromise grants the attacker interactive access to the system and may lead to lateral movement, privilege escalation, and data exfiltration.

findings.title: Account Lockouts Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate the source of lockouts for each affected account. For user accounts, verify no credential compromise occurred. For service accounts, check for stale cached credentials in scheduled tasks, services, or mapped drives. Consider migrating to Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA).
findings.description: Account lockout events (Event ID 4740) were detected in the security event log, indicating accounts are being locked due to repeated failed authentication. Lockouts may be caused by brute-force attacks, misconfigured services, or stale cached credentials.
findings.impact: Account lockouts from brute-force attempts confirm active credential attacks against the system. Service account lockouts can cause application outages and business disruption.

findings.title: Security Log Cleared — Evidence Tampering
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate the account that cleared the logs for compromise. Configure event log forwarding to a SIEM to preserve logs centrally. Restrict log management permissions to dedicated admin accounts. Enable alerting on Event ID 1102.
findings.description: Event log clearing events detected (Event ID 1102/104). Clearing security logs destroys forensic evidence and is a strong indicator of attacker activity or insider threat attempting to cover their tracks.
findings.impact: Cleared security logs eliminate the audit trail of authentication events, privilege escalation, and policy changes, preventing incident investigation and regulatory compliance verification. This is a common anti-forensics technique.

findings.title: Suspicious PowerShell Activity in Event Logs
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate each suspicious PowerShell event. Check the executing user and originating process. Enable PowerShell ScriptBlock Logging, Transcription, and Constrained Language Mode. Consider deploying AppLocker or WDAC to restrict PowerShell usage to authorized administrators.
findings.description: PowerShell events contain suspicious patterns including encoded commands (-EncodedCommand), download cradles (Invoke-WebRequest/IEX), AMSI bypass attempts, or known offensive tool invocations such as Mimikatz or PowerView.
findings.impact: Suspicious PowerShell activity may indicate post-exploitation activity, malware execution, or attacker reconnaissance. PowerShell is the most commonly abused living-off-the-land tool on Windows systems.

findings.title: New Service Installations Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Review each new service installation for legitimacy. Verify the service executable path, signing status, and the account used for installation. Remove unauthorized services and investigate how they were installed.
findings.description: New service installation events (Event ID 7045/4697) recorded in event logs. Service installations are a common persistence mechanism used by malware and attackers to maintain access that survives reboots.
findings.impact: Attackers install malicious services to maintain persistent access. Services run with elevated privileges and can be configured to start automatically, ensuring the attacker's code runs at every boot.

findings.title: User Account Created
findings.remediation_brief: Verify each account creation was authorized through the proper provisioning workflow. Remove unauthorized accounts. Monitor for group membership changes (Event ID 4732) on newly created accounts.
findings.description: User account creation events (Event ID 4720) detected in security event logs. Account creation outside of normal provisioning workflows may indicate persistence or unauthorized access by an attacker.
findings.impact: Attackers create local accounts to maintain persistent access. Unauthorized accounts may be added to privileged groups to escalate privileges and maintain a foothold on the compromised system.

findings.title: UAC Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Re-enable UAC by setting the EnableLUA registry value to 1 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System. Set ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to at least 2 (prompt for consent on secure desktop). Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > User Account Control.
findings.description: User Account Control (UAC) is completely disabled on this endpoint. The registry value EnableLUA under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\System is set to 0.
findings.impact: All applications run with full administrative privileges without prompting. Malware and exploit payloads execute with elevated privileges immediately upon infection, greatly increasing the severity of any compromise.

findings.title: UAC Prompt Behavior Weak
findings.remediation_brief: Configure ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin to 2 (prompt for consent on the secure desktop) via Group Policy or registry. Also ensure PromptOnSecureDesktop is set to 1 to prevent interception of the elevation dialog by malicious software.
findings.description: The UAC elevation prompt for administrators is configured to auto-elevate without prompting (ConsentPromptBehaviorAdmin is 0) or to prompt on a non-secure desktop.
findings.impact: Weak UAC prompt settings allow malware to silently elevate privileges through auto-elevation or intercept elevation prompts on the interactive desktop, enabling privilege escalation without user awareness.

findings.title: SMBv1 Protocol Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable SMBv1 by running: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName SMB1Protocol. For Server: Remove-WindowsFeature FS-SMB1. Alternatively set HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters\SMB1 to 0. Verify no legacy applications or devices require SMBv1 before disabling.
findings.description: The deprecated SMBv1 protocol is enabled on this endpoint, either as a server or client component.
findings.impact: SMBv1 has known critical vulnerabilities including EternalBlue (MS17-010) and lacks modern security features. It enables remote code execution, credential relay attacks, and was the primary propagation vector for WannaCry and NotPetya ransomware.

findings.title: SMB Signing Not Required
findings.remediation_brief: Enable mandatory SMB signing by setting RequireSecuritySignature to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and LanmanWorkstation\Parameters. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Microsoft network server/client: Digitally sign communications (always).
findings.description: SMB message signing is not required on this endpoint, allowing unsigned SMB communications.
findings.impact: Without mandatory SMB signing, an attacker in a man-in-the-middle position can intercept and modify SMB traffic, perform relay attacks (NTLM relay), and hijack authenticated SMB sessions to access file shares or execute commands on other systems.

findings.title: NTLMv1 Authentication Allowed
findings.remediation_brief: Set LmCompatibilityLevel to 5 (Send NTLMv2 response only. Refuse LM & NTLM) at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: LAN Manager authentication level. Test thoroughly as legacy devices may require NTLMv1.
findings.description: The LAN Manager authentication level allows NTLMv1 responses, a weak authentication protocol that is trivially crackable.
findings.impact: NTLMv1 hashes can be cracked in seconds using rainbow tables or GPU-accelerated attacks, exposing user passwords. An attacker capturing NTLMv1 traffic on the network can recover plaintext credentials for lateral movement.

findings.title: LM Password Hashes Stored
findings.remediation_brief: Set NoLMHash to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa to prevent storage of LM hashes. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Local Policies > Security Options > Network security: Do not store LAN Manager hash value on next password change. Force all users to change passwords after enabling.
findings.description: The system is configured to store LAN Manager (LM) hash values for passwords, a severely weak hash format.
findings.impact: LM hashes split passwords into two 7-character halves, are case-insensitive, and use DES without salt. They can be cracked in minutes even for complex passwords, giving an attacker who obtains the SAM database or captures authentication traffic immediate access to plaintext passwords.

findings.title: AutoRun Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Set NoDriveTypeAutoRun to 255 (0xFF) at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer to disable AutoRun on all drive types. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > AutoPlay Policies > Turn off Autoplay (All drives).
findings.description: AutoRun/AutoPlay is enabled, allowing automatic execution of programs from removable media and network drives.
findings.impact: Malware can be automatically executed when a USB drive, CD/DVD, or network share is accessed. This is a classic initial access vector used by worms (Conficker) and targeted attacks using planted USB devices.

findings.title: WDigest Plaintext Credentials Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Set UseLogonCredential to 0 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest. On Windows 8.1/Server 2012 R2 and later with KB2871997 installed, WDigest plaintext caching is disabled by default. Verify the registry value is explicitly set to 0 to prevent re-enablement by malware.
findings.description: WDigest authentication is configured to store plaintext credentials in memory (UseLogonCredential set to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SecurityProviders\WDigest).
findings.impact: An attacker who achieves local administrator access can use tools like Mimikatz to extract plaintext passwords from LSASS process memory for all currently logged-in users, including domain administrators. This enables immediate lateral movement without any cracking.

findings.title: LSA Protection Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable LSA protection by setting RunAsPPL to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. A system restart is required. Test application compatibility first as some security products may not function with PPL enabled. On Windows 11 22H2+, LSA protection is enabled by default.
findings.description: Local Security Authority (LSA) protection is not enabled. The RunAsPPL registry value is not set to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa.
findings.impact: Without LSA protection, the LSASS process can be accessed by any process running as local administrator. Attackers can dump credentials from LSASS memory using standard tools, bypassing most endpoint security controls.

findings.title: Credential Guard Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Credential Guard by setting EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\DeviceGuard and RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures to 1 or 3. Prerequisites: UEFI firmware, Secure Boot, TPM 2.0, and 64-bit Windows 10/11 Enterprise or Server 2016+. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard.
findings.description: Windows Defender Credential Guard (Virtualization Based Security for credential isolation) is not enabled on this endpoint.
findings.impact: Without Credential Guard, NTLM hashes and Kerberos TGTs stored in LSASS memory can be extracted by tools running as local administrator. Credential Guard isolates these secrets in a hardware-backed virtual enclave that even kernel-level attackers cannot access.

findings.title: LLMNR Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Network > DNS Client > Turn off multicast name resolution. Set EnableMulticast to 0 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\DNSClient. Ensure proper DNS infrastructure is in place as a replacement.
findings.description: Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR) is enabled, allowing unauthenticated name resolution on the local network.
findings.impact: An attacker on the local network can respond to LLMNR queries to capture NTLMv2 hashes from connecting clients using tools like Responder. These hashes can be cracked offline or relayed to other services for unauthorized access.

findings.title: WPAD Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the WinHTTP Auto-Proxy Service (WinHttpAutoProxySvc) and set its startup to Disabled. In Internet Options, uncheck 'Automatically detect settings'. If proxy auto-configuration is needed, use explicit PAC file URLs rather than WPAD discovery.
findings.description: Web Proxy Auto-Discovery (WPAD) protocol is enabled, allowing automatic proxy configuration via DNS or DHCP.
findings.impact: An attacker can poison WPAD queries via LLMNR/NBNS or rogue DHCP to redirect all HTTP traffic through a malicious proxy, enabling credential interception, session hijacking, and man-in-the-middle attacks on all web traffic.

findings.title: PowerShell Script Block Logging Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell script block logging via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Script Block Logging. Set EnableScriptBlockLogging to 1 at HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\ScriptBlockLogging.
findings.description: PowerShell script block logging is not enabled, preventing the recording of PowerShell script content in Windows Event Logs.
findings.impact: Without script block logging, PowerShell-based attacks (obfuscated download cradles, in-memory execution, AMSI bypasses) leave no forensic evidence. Incident response teams cannot determine what malicious PowerShell commands were executed.

findings.title: PowerShell Module Logging Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell module logging via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on Module Logging. Configure the module names to log (use * for all modules).
findings.description: PowerShell module logging is not enabled, which would record pipeline execution details for specified modules.
findings.impact: Module logging provides a detailed record of which PowerShell cmdlets and functions were invoked. Without it, forensic investigators have reduced visibility into the specific operations performed during an attack.

findings.title: PowerShell Transcription Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable PowerShell transcription via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows PowerShell > Turn on PowerShell Transcription. Configure the output directory to a secured file share for centralized collection. Ensure adequate disk space and proper NTFS permissions on the transcript directory.
findings.description: PowerShell transcription (recording of all PowerShell input and output to text files) is not enabled.
findings.impact: Transcription provides a complete record of interactive and scripted PowerShell sessions including output. Without it, defenders lose a valuable forensic data source for investigating PowerShell-based attacks.

findings.title: PowerShell v2 Engine Available
findings.remediation_brief: Remove the PowerShell v2 engine: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName MicrosoftWindowsPowerShellV2Root. For Server: Remove-WindowsFeature PowerShell-V2. Verify no applications depend on PowerShell v2 before removal.
findings.description: The PowerShell v2 engine is still installed as a Windows feature, providing a downgrade path that bypasses modern logging and security controls.
findings.impact: Attackers can invoke PowerShell v2 (powershell -version 2) to bypass AMSI, script block logging, constrained language mode, and other security features that only exist in PowerShell v5+. This is a well-documented defense evasion technique.

findings.title: Windows Defender Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Re-enable Windows Defender by removing any Group Policy that disables it (DisableAntiSpyware registry key), starting the WinDefend service, and ensuring real-time protection is turned on. If a third-party antivirus is intended, verify it is properly installed and running. Ensure at minimum one antimalware solution is active at all times.
findings.description: Windows Defender Antivirus is completely disabled or not running on this endpoint with no alternative antimalware solution detected.
findings.impact: Without antimalware protection, all known malware including commodity threats, ransomware, and trojans can execute without detection. The system has no real-time file scanning, web filtering, or behavior monitoring.

findings.title: Windows Defender Exclusions Present
findings.remediation_brief: Review all Windows Defender exclusions and remove any that are not strictly necessary for application compatibility. Document the business justification for each remaining exclusion. Avoid broad exclusions (entire drives, common directories). Monitor excluded paths for suspicious file creation via separate detection mechanisms.
findings.description: Windows Defender has file, folder, process, or extension exclusions configured that exempt certain paths or processes from scanning.
findings.impact: Attackers frequently target known exclusion paths to stage and execute malware. Common exclusion paths like temp directories, development folders, or application paths become safe havens for malicious payloads that will never be scanned.

findings.title: Windows Defender Real-Time Protection Off
findings.remediation_brief: Enable real-time protection in Windows Security settings or via PowerShell: Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $false. If Group Policy is preventing this, update the policy to allow real-time protection. Verify protection is active with Get-MpComputerStatus.
findings.description: Windows Defender is installed but real-time protection is turned off, leaving the system without active file scanning.
findings.impact: Files downloaded, copied, or created are not scanned until a manual or scheduled scan occurs. Malware can execute immediately upon arrival without triggering any detection, potentially running for hours or days before a scheduled scan.

findings.title: Remote Desktop Without NLA
findings.remediation_brief: Enable NLA for Remote Desktop by setting UserAuthentication to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Terminal Server\WinStations\RDP-Tcp. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Remote Desktop Services > Remote Desktop Session Host > Security > Require user authentication for remote connections by using Network Level Authentication.
findings.description: Remote Desktop Protocol is enabled without requiring Network Level Authentication (NLA), allowing unauthenticated users to reach the RDP login screen.
findings.impact: Without NLA, attackers can establish RDP sessions without credentials, consuming server resources (DoS) and reaching the Windows login screen where they can attempt credential attacks. This also exposes the system to pre-authentication RDP vulnerabilities like BlueKeep.

findings.title: DEP Not Enabled System-Wide
findings.remediation_brief: Configure DEP to protect all programs by running: bcdedit /set nx AlwaysOn. Alternatively, configure via System Properties > Advanced > Performance Settings > Data Execution Prevention > Turn on DEP for all programs and services except those I select. Add specific exceptions only for applications that are confirmed incompatible.
findings.description: Data Execution Prevention (DEP) is not configured to protect all programs, only essential Windows programs and services.
findings.impact: Without system-wide DEP, buffer overflow exploits can execute shellcode in data memory regions. DEP prevents code execution from non-executable memory pages, making many common exploitation techniques significantly harder.

findings.title: Anonymous Access to Named Pipes
findings.remediation_brief: Clear the NullSessionPipes registry value at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanmanServer\Parameters and set RestrictNullSessAccess to 1. Apply via Group Policy: Network access: Restrict anonymous access to Named Pipes and Shares (Enabled).
findings.description: Anonymous (null session) access to named pipes is permitted, allowing unauthenticated users to connect to specific named pipes on the system.
findings.impact: Attackers can enumerate sensitive information through named pipes without authentication, including user lists, group memberships, share lists, and security policies. This information aids in planning targeted credential attacks and privilege escalation.

findings.title: Null Session Access Allowed
findings.remediation_brief: Set RestrictAnonymousSAM to 1 and RestrictAnonymous to 1 at HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa. Apply via Group Policy: Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts (Enabled) and Network access: Do not allow anonymous enumeration of SAM accounts and shares (Enabled).
findings.description: The system allows null session (anonymous) connections for SAM enumeration and share enumeration.
findings.impact: Attackers can connect without credentials to enumerate all user accounts, groups, and network shares. This provides a complete map of the attack surface and user accounts to target for password spraying or brute force attacks.

findings.title: Audit Policy Insufficient
findings.remediation_brief: Configure advanced audit policy via Group Policy to log at minimum: Logon/Logoff (Success+Failure), Account Logon (Success+Failure), Privilege Use (Success+Failure), Object Access (Failure), Policy Change (Success+Failure), System (Success+Failure). Use auditpol to verify: auditpol /get /category:*.
findings.description: The Windows audit policy does not log critical security events. Key audit categories such as logon events, privilege use, object access, or policy changes are not configured for success and/or failure auditing.
findings.impact: Without comprehensive audit logging, security incidents go undetected and uninvestigated. Login attempts, privilege escalation, file access, and policy changes occur without any record, severely impacting incident response and forensic capabilities.

findings.title: Print Spooler Running on Server
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the Print Spooler service on servers that do not need printing: Stop-Service -Name Spooler -Force; Set-Service -Name Spooler -StartupType Disabled. On domain controllers, the Spooler should always be disabled as it exposes the DC to coercion attacks via the MS-RPRN protocol.
findings.description: The Print Spooler service is running on a server where printing functionality is likely not required.
findings.impact: The Print Spooler service has been the target of multiple critical vulnerabilities including PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527) enabling remote code execution and privilege escalation. Running it on servers unnecessarily increases the attack surface.

findings.title: Application Whitelisting Not Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Implement AppLocker or Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC). Start in audit mode to identify legitimate applications, then switch to enforce mode. At minimum, implement script rules to block unauthorized script execution. For WDAC: create a base policy with Microsoft recommended block rules, then supplement with organization-specific allow rules. For AppLocker: configure default rules plus explicit allow rules for approved applications.
findings.description: Neither AppLocker nor Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) is configured on this system. Without application whitelisting, any executable, script, or DLL can run without restriction.
findings.impact: Without application control, an attacker can execute arbitrary malware, scripts, and tools on the system without restriction. Application whitelisting is consistently rated as one of the most effective endpoint security controls by ACSC Essential Eight, NIST, and CIS. Its absence significantly increases the attack surface for malware execution, lateral movement tools, and post-exploitation frameworks.

findings.title: Hypervisor Code Integrity Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable HVCI via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Device Guard > Turn On Virtualization Based Security > Virtualization Based Protection of Code Integrity = Enabled with UEFI lock. Alternatively, enable via Windows Security > Device Security > Core isolation > Memory integrity. Prerequisites: compatible CPU with virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x/AMD-V), UEFI firmware, Secure Boot enabled.
findings.description: Hypervisor-Protected Code Integrity (HVCI / Memory Integrity) is not enabled on this system. HVCI uses virtualization-based security (VBS) to protect the Windows kernel code integrity verification process, preventing kernel-mode code injection and driver-based attacks.
findings.impact: Without HVCI, the kernel is vulnerable to code injection attacks via malicious drivers, kernel exploits, and rootkits. HVCI prevents unsigned or improperly signed kernel-mode code from executing, significantly raising the bar for kernel-level attacks. Its absence leaves the system vulnerable to bootkit/rootkit installations and kernel-mode exploit payloads.

findings.title: CredSSP Delegation Enabled

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

findings.remediation_brief: Disable CredSSP delegation via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Credentials Delegation > Allow delegating fresh credentials = Disabled. If CredSSP is required for specific administrative tasks, restrict delegation to specific trusted servers only (never use '*'). Apply CVE-2018-0886 patches. Consider using Remote Credential Guard instead of CredSSP for RDP sessions.
findings.description: Credential Security Support Provider (CredSSP) delegation is enabled, allowing this system to forward user credentials to remote servers. The AllowFreshCredentials or AllowFreshCredentialsDomain policies permit credential delegation to specified or all remote hosts.
findings.impact: CredSSP delegation sends the user's cleartext credentials to the remote server. If the remote server is compromised, these credentials are immediately available to the attacker. CredSSP delegation to '*' (all servers) is especially dangerous as it enables credential forwarding to any host, including attacker-controlled machines. This defeats the purpose of Restricted Admin mode and other credential protection mechanisms.

findings.title: AMSI Provider Not Registered

mitre_attack.name: Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

findings.remediation_brief: Verify that Windows Defender or a third-party antimalware solution with AMSI support is installed and active. Check AMSI provider registration: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\AMSI\Providers" /s. If no providers are listed, reinstall or re-register the antimalware solution. If AMSI was deliberately tampered with, investigate as a potential compromise indicator.
findings.description: No Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) provider is registered on this system. AMSI is a Windows interface that allows applications to send content (scripts, macro code, .NET assemblies) to the installed antimalware solution for scanning before execution.
findings.impact: Without AMSI, script-based attacks (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, .NET) can execute malicious code without real-time scanning. AMSI is the primary defense against fileless malware, obfuscated scripts, and in-memory attacks. Its absence or deregistration is a common attacker technique (T1562.001) to disable defenses before deploying payloads.

findings.title: .NET Framework v2/v3.5 Installed
findings.remediation_brief: Remove .NET Framework 3.5 (includes 2.0 and 3.0) if no application requires it: Disable-WindowsOptionalFeature -Online -FeatureName NetFx3. On Server: Remove-WindowsFeature NET-Framework-Core. Before removing, verify no application dependencies by auditing installed software and testing in a pre-production environment.
findings.description: .NET Framework version 2.0 or 3.5 is installed on this system. These legacy .NET versions include the CLR v2 runtime which has weaker security controls than CLR v4 and can be leveraged by attackers to bypass application-level security restrictions.
findings.impact: The .NET CLR v2 runtime can be invoked by PowerShell v2 and other tools to bypass AMSI, script block logging, constrained language mode, and other security controls that are only enforced in CLR v4. Attackers specifically target legacy .NET to downgrade the runtime and evade security monitoring. If .NET 2.0/3.5 is not required by any application, it represents unnecessary attack surface.

findings.title: PowerShell Constrained Language Mode Not Enforced
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce Constrained Language Mode via WDAC/AppLocker code integrity policies (the most robust method — CLM activates automatically when UMCI is enforced). Alternatively, set the __PSLockdownPolicy environment variable to 4 (system-wide), though this is less robust than WDAC enforcement. Test with administrative scripts first — CLM restricts .NET and COM access that some admin scripts require.
findings.description: PowerShell is running in Full Language Mode rather than Constrained Language Mode (CLM). Full Language Mode allows unrestricted access to .NET types, COM objects, and Win32 APIs, enabling powerful post-exploitation capabilities.
findings.impact: Full Language Mode enables attackers to load arbitrary .NET assemblies, invoke Win32 APIs via P/Invoke or Add-Type, create COM objects, and execute complex exploitation frameworks (Invoke-Mimikatz, PowerView, etc.) entirely in memory. Constrained Language Mode blocks these capabilities while preserving administrative scripting functionality.

findings.title: Attack Surface Reduction Rules Not Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Enable ASR rules via Group Policy or Intune. Recommended rules to enable in block mode: Block Office apps from creating child processes (D4F940AB-401B-4EFC-AADC-AD5F3C50688A), Block credential stealing from LSASS (9e6c4e1f-7d60-472f-ba1a-a39ef669e4b2), Block executable content from email/webmail (BE9BA2D9-53EA-4CDC-84E5-9B1EEEE46550), Use advanced protection against ransomware (c1db55ab-c21a-4637-bb3f-a12568109d35). Start in audit mode for 2 weeks, then switch to block.
findings.description: Windows Defender Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) rules are not configured or are set to audit-only mode. ASR rules block specific behaviors commonly used by malware, such as Office macros creating child processes, obfuscated scripts, credential theft from LSASS, and untrusted USB process execution.
findings.impact: Without ASR rules, the system lacks behavioral protection against common attack techniques: Office macro malware, script-based attacks, credential dumping, ransomware file encryption patterns, and lateral movement techniques. ASR rules are one of the most effective free security controls available on Windows 10/11 and Server 2016+.

findings.title: Controlled Folder Access Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Controlled Folder Access via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard > Controlled Folder Access > Configure Controlled folder access = Enabled (Block mode). Alternatively: Set-MpPreference -EnableControlledFolderAccess Enabled. Whitelist legitimate applications that need write access to protected folders.
findings.description: Windows Defender Controlled Folder Access is not enabled. This feature protects designated folders (Documents, Desktop, Pictures, etc.) from unauthorized modification by untrusted applications, serving as anti-ransomware protection.
findings.impact: Without Controlled Folder Access, ransomware and destructive malware can freely encrypt or delete files in user profile folders and other protected locations. CFA provides a last line of defense against ransomware by blocking unauthorized write operations, even from elevated processes, unless the application is explicitly whitelisted.

findings.title: Network Protection Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Network Protection via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Microsoft Defender Antivirus > Microsoft Defender Exploit Guard > Network Protection > Prevent users and apps from accessing dangerous websites = Enabled (Block mode). Alternatively: Set-MpPreference -EnableNetworkProtection Enabled. Start in audit mode to identify false positives before enforcing.
findings.description: Windows Defender Network Protection is not enabled. Network Protection extends SmartScreen capabilities to block outbound connections to low-reputation or malicious domains and IP addresses, protecting against phishing, exploit hosting sites, and command-and-control infrastructure.
findings.impact: Without Network Protection, the system can establish connections to known-malicious domains, phishing sites, and C2 infrastructure without being blocked. This feature provides network-layer defense against web-based threats and can prevent initial access (drive-by downloads, phishing), malware download, and C2 communication.

findings.title: Exploit Protection Not Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Configure Exploit Protection system-wide and per-application: Windows Security > App & browser control > Exploit protection settings. Enable for high-risk applications (browsers, Office, PDF readers, Java). Key mitigations: DEP (AlwaysOn), ASLR (ForceRelocateImages, BottomUp), CFG (enabled), SEHOP (enabled). Deploy via Group Policy using an XML configuration file: Set-ProcessMitigation -PolicyFilePath exploit-protection-settings.xml.
findings.description: Windows Exploit Protection (successor to EMET) process mitigations are not configured. Exploit Protection applies per-process exploit mitigations such as DEP, ASLR, CFG (Control Flow Guard), heap integrity validation, and image load restrictions to protect against memory corruption exploits.
findings.impact: Without process-level exploit mitigations, applications are more vulnerable to memory corruption exploits (buffer overflows, use-after-free, ROP chains). Exploit Protection mitigations make exploit development significantly harder and can prevent known exploitation techniques from succeeding, even against unpatched vulnerabilities.

findings.title: Suspicious Outbound Connection Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Firewall for the Domain profile via Group Policy or PowerShell: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Domain -Enabled True. Review and configure appropriate inbound/outbound rules before enabling to avoid disrupting legitimate services.
findings.description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Domain network profile.
findings.impact: All inbound and outbound traffic is unfiltered when connected to a domain network. Any service listening on any port is exposed to all hosts on the network, enabling lateral movement and direct exploitation.

findings.title: High-Risk Port Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Firewall for the Private profile: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Private -Enabled True.
findings.description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Private network profile.
findings.impact: All network traffic is unfiltered when connected to private networks. Services and ports that should be restricted are accessible to all devices on the local network segment.

findings.title: System Proxy Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately enable the Windows Firewall for the Public profile: Set-NetFirewallProfile -Profile Public -Enabled True. The Public profile should have the most restrictive ruleset with all inbound connections blocked by default.
findings.description: The Windows Firewall is disabled for the Public network profile, the most exposed profile.
findings.impact: When connected to any public or untrusted network (airports, hotels, coffee shops), all services are exposed without any filtering. This is the highest-risk firewall misconfiguration as public networks are inherently hostile.

findings.title: DNS Pointing to External Servers on Domain-Joined System
findings.remediation_brief: Close or restrict access to unnecessary high-risk ports using Windows Firewall rules. For required services, restrict inbound access to specific authorized IP ranges. Consider using IPsec or VPN for administrative access to sensitive services.
findings.description: A high-risk network port is listening on this endpoint (e.g., 445/SMB, 135-139/RPC, 3389/RDP, 23/Telnet, 21/FTP, 1433/MSSQL, 3306/MySQL, 5432/PostgreSQL).
findings.impact: High-risk ports are frequent targets for automated scanning and exploitation. Exposed database ports enable direct SQL injection and credential brute-forcing. Exposed management ports enable remote administration attacks.

findings.title: WMI Event Subscription Persistence

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Windows Management Instrumentation Event Subscription

findings.remediation_brief: Review all WMI event subscriptions: Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventFilter; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __EventConsumer; Get-WMIObject -Namespace root\Subscription -Class __FilterToConsumerBinding. Remove any unknown or suspicious subscriptions. Deploy Sysmon with WMI monitoring (Event IDs 19-21). Implement WMI activity logging via Group Policy.
findings.description: Active WMI event subscriptions (EventFilter + EventConsumer + FilterToConsumerBinding) were found on this system. WMI subscriptions execute automatically in response to system events and survive reboots, making them a powerful persistence mechanism.
findings.impact: WMI event subscriptions run with SYSTEM privileges and are difficult to detect through standard monitoring. An attacker can use them to execute malicious scripts or binaries when specific events occur (user logon, process creation, time-based triggers). WMI persistence is used by APT groups and is notoriously resistant to removal — it survives reinstallation of applications and many cleanup procedures.

findings.title: COM Object Hijacking Detected

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Component Object Model Hijacking

findings.remediation_brief: Audit HKCU\Software\Classes\CLSID for entries that shadow HKLM CLSID registrations. Remove unauthorized CLSID overrides. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring (Event IDs 12-14) targeting CLSID paths. Implement application whitelisting (AppLocker/WDAC) to prevent loading of unauthorized DLLs from user-writable locations.
findings.description: COM object registrations in the HKCU registry hive override HKLM registrations for CLSIDs that are loaded by privileged processes. This COM object hijacking technique allows a user-level modification to cause a privileged process to load an attacker-controlled DLL.
findings.impact: COM hijacking is a stealthy persistence and privilege escalation technique. When a legitimate, privileged application loads a hijacked CLSID, it executes the attacker's DLL with the application's privileges. This survives reboots, is difficult to detect without specific monitoring, and blends with normal COM activity. Many legitimate Windows processes load COM objects during startup.

findings.title: AppInit_DLLs Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Clear the AppInit_DLLs registry value: reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows" /v AppInit_DLLs /f. Also clear the WOW64 key: reg delete "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Wow6432Node\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Windows" /v AppInit_DLLs /f. Set LoadAppInit_DLLs to 0 to disable the mechanism entirely. Enable Secure Boot and RequireSignedAppInit_DLLs to restrict to signed DLLs only.
findings.description: The AppInit_DLLs registry value is configured with one or more DLL paths. Windows loads any DLL listed in AppInit_DLLs into every process that loads user32.dll — which includes virtually all GUI applications. This mechanism is a well-known persistence and injection technique.
findings.impact: DLLs specified in AppInit_DLLs are loaded into every GUI process on the system, providing system-wide code injection. An attacker can use this for keylogging, credential interception, API hooking, or persistent backdoor access. The injected DLL runs with the privileges of each host process, potentially including SYSTEM-level services.

findings.title: Image File Execution Options Debugger Set

mitre_attack.name: Event Triggered Execution: Image File Execution Options Injection

findings.remediation_brief: Audit IFEO registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Image File Execution Options" /s /v Debugger. Remove any unauthorized Debugger values. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring (Event IDs 12-14) targeting IFEO keys. Legitimate IFEO uses include application compatibility shims — verify with the application vendor before removing.
findings.description: Image File Execution Options (IFEO) registry entries have a 'Debugger' value set for one or more executables. This causes Windows to launch the specified debugger program instead of (or before) the target executable, effectively hijacking the execution of legitimate programs.
findings.impact: An attacker can set an IFEO debugger entry for commonly used programs (cmd.exe, powershell.exe, taskmgr.exe) to redirect their execution to a malicious binary. This is a stealthy persistence mechanism that activates whenever the legitimate program is launched. It is also used to prevent security tools from running by redirecting them to an empty program or a kill command.

findings.title: Accessibility Feature Binary Modified
findings.remediation_brief: Restore original accessibility binaries from a known-good source or Windows installation media: sfc /scannow or DISM /Online /Cleanup-Image /RestoreHealth. Verify file hashes against Microsoft published hashes. Investigate as a potential compromise — this finding indicates the system may have been backdoored. Deploy file integrity monitoring on %SystemRoot%\System32\sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe, DisplaySwitch.exe.
findings.description: One or more Windows accessibility feature binaries (sethc.exe, utilman.exe, osk.exe, narrator.exe, magnify.exe, DisplaySwitch.exe) have been modified or replaced. The modification timestamp does not align with the OS installation date or last Windows Update, indicating potential tampering.
findings.impact: Replacing accessibility binaries with cmd.exe or a backdoor is a classic persistence technique that provides SYSTEM-level command prompt access from the Windows login screen — before any user has authenticated. An attacker can press Shift five times (sethc.exe), Win+U (utilman.exe), or similar shortcuts to trigger the backdoor. This survives reboots, user password changes, and most remediation attempts short of restoring the original binaries.

findings.title: Print Monitor DLL Persistence

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Port Monitors

findings.remediation_brief: Audit print monitor registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors" /s. Compare against known legitimate monitors (Standard TCP/IP Port, WSD Port, USB Monitor, Local Port). Remove any unknown or suspicious monitor entries. Verify DLL signatures for all registered monitor DLLs. Deploy Sysmon with registry monitoring on the Print\Monitors key.
findings.description: Custom print monitor DLLs were found registered in the system. Print monitors are loaded by the Print Spooler service (spoolsv.exe) which runs as SYSTEM. An unauthorized print monitor DLL provides persistent, SYSTEM-level code execution.
findings.impact: Print monitor DLLs are loaded by the spoolsv.exe service at startup and run with SYSTEM privileges. An attacker who registers a malicious DLL as a print monitor achieves persistence that survives reboots and is difficult to detect — the DLL appears as a legitimate print subsystem component. This technique is used by APT groups for long-term persistence.

findings.title: LSA Authentication Package Modified

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Authentication Package

findings.remediation_brief: Audit LSA registry entries: reg query "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v "Authentication Packages" and "Security Packages". Default values are 'msv1_0' for Authentication Packages and '' (empty) or 'kerberos msv1_0 schannel wdigest tspkg pku2u' for Security Packages. Remove any unauthorized entries. Enable LSA Protection (RunAsPPL) to prevent unauthorized DLL loading into lsass.exe. Enable Credential Guard for additional protection. Investigate as potential compromise.
findings.description: Non-default authentication packages or security support providers (SSPs) are registered in the LSA registry configuration. LSA authentication packages are loaded by lsass.exe at boot and run with SYSTEM privileges. Unauthorized packages can intercept credentials during authentication.
findings.impact: A malicious LSA authentication package runs inside lsass.exe with SYSTEM privileges and intercepts every authentication event on the system. This allows credential harvesting of all user passwords (including domain admin) in cleartext as they authenticate. This is one of the most powerful persistence mechanisms available, used by advanced threat actors and tools like mimilib.

findings.title: AlwaysInstallElevated Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable AlwaysInstallElevated by setting both registry values to 0: HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer\AlwaysInstallElevated=0 and HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer\AlwaysInstallElevated=0. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Installer > Always install with elevated privileges = Disabled.
findings.description: The AlwaysInstallElevated policy is enabled in both HKLM and HKCU registry hives. This Windows Installer policy allows any user to install MSI packages with SYSTEM-level privileges, regardless of the user's actual privilege level.
findings.impact: Any standard user can create a malicious MSI package (e.g., using msfvenom) and install it with SYSTEM privileges. This is a trivial, reliable privilege escalation path that requires no exploitation of software vulnerabilities — only the misconfiguration itself. Tools like PowerUp, WinPEAS, and Metasploit all check for and exploit this setting.

findings.title: Modifiable Service Binary

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Services File Permissions Weakness

findings.remediation_brief: Audit and correct file system permissions on all service binary paths. Service executables should be owned by Administrators/SYSTEM with write access restricted to Administrators only. Use icacls to verify: icacls "C:\path\to\service.exe". Install services only in protected directories (C:\Program Files\). Remove write permissions for Users/Authenticated Users groups on service binary paths.
findings.description: One or more Windows service executables reside in directories that are writable by non-administrative users, or the service binary file itself has permissive ACLs. This allows a standard user to replace the service binary with a malicious one.
findings.impact: An attacker can replace or modify a service binary that runs as SYSTEM or a privileged account. On the next service restart (or system reboot), the attacker's code executes with the service account's privileges, typically SYSTEM. This is a reliable privilege escalation technique that persists across reboots.

findings.title: DLL Search Order Hijacking Risk

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: DLL Search Order Hijacking

findings.remediation_brief: Audit all directories in the system PATH and remove write permissions for non-administrative users. Remove unnecessary directories from PATH. Enable SafeDllSearchMode (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\SafeDllSearchMode=1). Consider implementing Windows Defender Application Control (WDAC) to restrict DLL loading to signed binaries.
findings.description: One or more directories in the system PATH are writable by non-administrative users.
