Windows DLL search order loads DLLs from the application directory first, then the system directory, then each PATH directory in order. A writable PATH directory allows an attacker to place a malicious DLL that will be loaded by legitimate applications.
findings.impact: An attacker can place a crafted DLL in a writable PATH directory with the same name as a DLL that a privileged application expects to load. When the application runs, it loads the attacker's DLL instead, executing arbitrary code with the application's privileges. This is particularly dangerous for services and scheduled tasks running as SYSTEM.

findings.title: Dangerous Token Privileges Held
findings.remediation_brief: Review and minimize token privileges assigned to service accounts. Remove SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege from service accounts where not operationally required. Use Group Managed Service Accounts (gMSA) with minimal privileges. Audit User Rights Assignments via: secpol.msc > Local Policies > User Rights Assignment. Consider running services in Windows containers or AppContainers which restrict available privileges.
findings.description: The current process or service accounts hold dangerous Windows token privileges. SeImpersonatePrivilege and SeAssignPrimaryTokenPrivilege enable token impersonation attacks (Potato family exploits). SeDebugPrivilege allows debugging any process including LSASS. SeBackupPrivilege/SeRestorePrivilege bypass file ACLs. SeTcbPrivilege acts as part of the operating system.
findings.impact: Token impersonation privileges (SeImpersonate, SeAssignPrimaryToken) enable immediate SYSTEM-level privilege escalation via tools like JuicyPotato, PrintSpoofer, RoguePotato, or GodPotato. SeDebugPrivilege allows LSASS memory dumping for credential extraction. These privileges are commonly held by IIS application pool accounts, SQL Server service accounts, and other service identities.

findings.title: Unquoted Service Path with Writable Directory

mitre_attack.name: Hijack Execution Flow: Path Interception by Unquoted Path

findings.remediation_brief: Quote all service binary paths that contain spaces. Fix via registry: reg add "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\<ServiceName>" /v ImagePath /t REG_EXPAND_SZ /d '"C:\Program Files\...\service.exe"' /f. Additionally, restrict write permissions on all intermediate directories in service paths. Identify all unquoted paths: wmic service get name,pathname | findstr /i /v "C:\Windows" | findstr /i "  ".
findings.description: One or more Windows services have unquoted executable paths containing spaces, AND at least one intermediate directory in the path is writable by non-administrative users. Windows resolves unquoted paths by trying each space-delimited segment as a potential executable.
findings.impact: An attacker can place an executable at a space-boundary in the unquoted path. For example, if the service path is 'C:\Program Files\Some Service\service.exe' (unquoted), placing 'C:\Program.exe' or 'C:\Program Files\Some.exe' in a writable directory causes it to execute with the service's privileges. This requires both the unquoted path AND a writable intermediate directory to be exploitable.

findings.title: Named Pipe Permission Weakness
findings.remediation_brief: Audit named pipe ACLs using pipelist.exe (Sysinternals) and accesschk.exe. Restrict pipe permissions to the minimum required identities. Remove write/connect access for Authenticated Users and Everyone groups on privileged service pipes. Implement pipe security descriptors in service configurations.
findings.description: Named pipes on this system have overly permissive access controls, allowing non-administrative users to read, write, or impersonate connections on pipes used by privileged services.
findings.impact: Improperly secured named pipes can be exploited for privilege escalation or lateral movement. An attacker can connect to a weakly-permissioned pipe to capture or relay authentication tokens, inject commands into service communication channels, or impersonate the pipe server's identity. Named pipe impersonation is a core technique in several Potato-family privilege escalation exploits.

findings.title: Known Malicious Process Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately isolate the system from the network. Capture memory and disk images for forensic analysis before remediation. Identify the malware family and check for persistence mechanisms (scheduled tasks, services, registry run keys, WMI subscriptions). Re-image the system after forensics are complete.
findings.description: One or more running processes match known malicious software signatures in the threat intelligence database. This is a strong indicator of active system compromise requiring immediate incident response.
findings.impact: Known malicious processes indicate active malware execution. Depending on the malware type (RAT, keylogger, cryptominer, ransomware dropper), the attacker may have full remote access, be exfiltrating data, or preparing for destructive action. The system should be considered compromised.

findings.title: Process Running from Temporary Directory
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate each process: check file hash against VirusTotal, examine parent process chain, check for associated network connections. Implement AppLocker or WDAC policies to block executable execution from temp directories. Enable Windows Defender ASR rules to block execution from temp paths.
findings.description: One or more processes are executing from temporary directories (%TEMP%, %TMP%, C:\Windows\Temp). Legitimate software rarely runs from temp folders; this pattern is a strong indicator of malware, dropper activity, or exploitation payload execution.
findings.impact: Malware commonly stages and executes from temporary directories because they are user-writable, loosely monitored, and files there are expected to be transient. Ransomware droppers, fileless malware stagers, and post-exploitation payloads frequently use temp paths as their execution location.

findings.title: Process with No Executable Path
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate each process: capture a memory dump for forensic analysis, check the parent process chain for suspicious lineage, examine loaded DLLs and handles. Implement Sysmon with process creation logging (Event ID 1) to capture full command lines and parent process details.
findings.description: One or more running processes have no associated executable path on disk. This may indicate fileless malware executing entirely from memory, process hollowing, or a process whose binary was deleted after execution.
findings.impact: Processes without a disk-backed executable path can indicate fileless malware executing entirely from memory, process hollowing (where a legitimate process is replaced in memory with malicious code), or an attacker who deleted the binary after launching it to hinder forensic analysis.

findings.title: SYSTEM Process Running from User-Writable Path
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately investigate: capture memory and disk forensics, identify the privilege escalation vector (service binary hijacking, DLL search order hijacking, unquoted service path). Fix the underlying vulnerability. Deploy WDAC/AppLocker to prevent execution from user-writable paths.
findings.description: One or more processes are running as SYSTEM from user-writable locations (Users, AppData, Downloads, ProgramData, Temp). Legitimate SYSTEM processes run from protected directories (System32, Program Files). This is a strong indicator of privilege escalation or malware with elevated privileges.
findings.impact: A process running as SYSTEM from a user-writable directory indicates successful privilege escalation. The attacker has achieved the highest local privilege level and can install rootkits, create backdoor accounts, modify security settings, access any file on the system, and pivot to other systems.

findings.title: Unauthorized Remote Management Tool Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Remove unauthorized remote management tools and block their installation via application control policies. If the tool was installed by an attacker, initiate incident response. Maintain an approved remote access solution with centralized logging and multi-factor authentication.
findings.description: A remote management tool (TeamViewer, AnyDesk, LogMeIn, ConnectWise, Splashtop, etc.) was detected that is not part of the organization's approved toolset.
findings.impact: Unauthorized remote access tools create unmonitored backdoors into the network. They bypass VPN, firewall, and network security controls by tunneling through standard HTTPS. Attackers frequently install these tools for persistent remote access.

findings.title: RDP Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable RDP if not required. If required, enforce Network Level Authentication (NLA), restrict access via firewall rules to authorized IP ranges, use an RDP gateway, and enable account lockout policies.
findings.description: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) is enabled on this system. RDP exposes the system to brute-force attacks, credential stuffing, and known RDP vulnerabilities including BlueKeep (CVE-2019-0708) and DejaBlue.
findings.impact: An attacker who gains RDP access obtains full interactive control of the system. Without NLA, unauthenticated attackers can reach the login screen and exploit pre-authentication vulnerabilities.

findings.title: WinRM Service Running
findings.remediation_brief: Disable WinRM if not required. If required, enforce HTTPS transport, disable basic authentication, configure TrustedHosts to restrict connections, and monitor WinRM event logs for unauthorized access.
findings.description: Windows Remote Management (WinRM) is running on this system. WinRM allows remote command execution via PowerShell remoting and is a common lateral movement vector used by attackers.
findings.impact: An attacker with valid credentials can use WinRM to execute arbitrary commands remotely. If basic authentication or unencrypted traffic is allowed, credentials may be captured in transit.

findings.title: SSH Server Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the OpenSSH Server Windows feature if not required. If required, enforce key-based authentication, disable password login, and restrict access via firewall rules to authorized source IPs.
findings.description: An SSH server (OpenSSH) is running on this Windows system. SSH on Windows endpoints is uncommon and may indicate unauthorized installation, developer tools, or a persistence mechanism installed by an attacker.
findings.impact: SSH provides encrypted remote shell access that can be used for lateral movement, tunneling, and persistent access. On Windows endpoints, SSH is rarely business-justified and represents an additional attack surface.

findings.title: Multiple Remote Management Tools Installed
findings.remediation_brief: If OpenSSH is authorized, ensure it is configured securely: disable root login, use key-based authentication, limit allowed users, and monitor SSH logs. If not authorized, disable the sshd service.
findings.description: The OpenSSH Server service is running on this Windows endpoint, providing SSH remote access.
findings.impact: OpenSSH on Windows provides command-line remote access. While potentially legitimate for administration, it adds an additional remote access vector that should be documented and monitored.

findings.title: End-of-Life Software Installed
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade or replace end-of-life software with supported versions. If no replacement is available, implement compensating controls (network isolation, application whitelisting) and document the risk acceptance.
findings.description: Software that has reached end-of-life and no longer receives security updates is installed on this endpoint.
findings.impact: EOL software accumulates unpatched vulnerabilities over time with no vendor fixes available. Publicly known exploits continue to work indefinitely. This represents a permanent and growing security gap.

findings.title: Remote Access Software Installed
findings.remediation_brief: Update the software to the latest patched version. If updates are not immediately possible, implement compensating controls such as network segmentation and application-level monitoring. Prioritize based on CVSS score and network exposure.
findings.description: An installed software version is known to contain security vulnerabilities with available updates.
findings.impact: Running known-vulnerable software versions exposes the system to exploits targeting those specific vulnerabilities. Attackers routinely scan for known vulnerable software versions using automated tools.

findings.title: Suspicious Startup Item
findings.remediation_brief: Remove development tools from production systems. If development work is needed, use separate development environments. Document any exceptions with business justification and compensating controls.
findings.description: Development tools (compilers, debuggers, IDEs, scripting language interpreters beyond what the system requires) are installed on a production system.
findings.impact: Development tools enable an attacker to compile and run custom tools directly on the compromised system, create sophisticated payloads, and debug security controls. Their presence on production systems violates hardening baselines.

findings.title: P2P/Torrent Software Installed
findings.remediation_brief: Review unauthorized software with the system owner to determine if it should be added to the approved list or removed. Implement application control policies (AppLocker, WDAC) to prevent installation of unapproved software.
findings.description: Software not included in the organization's approved software list was detected. This finding requires per-engagement policy configuration.
findings.impact: Unauthorized software may introduce vulnerabilities, licensing issues, or compliance violations. It may also indicate shadow IT or user-installed tools that bypass change management.

findings.title: SQL Server Using Mixed Authentication Mode
findings.remediation_brief: Switch to Windows Authentication mode unless SQL authentication is strictly required. If mixed mode must remain, disable the 'sa' account, enforce strong passwords on all SQL logins, and enable SQL Server Audit for login events.
findings.description: SQL Server is configured with mixed authentication mode, allowing both Windows and SQL Server authentication. SQL authentication transmits credentials that may be weaker and harder to audit than Windows/Kerberos authentication.
findings.impact: Mixed mode enables SQL logins (like 'sa') which are frequently targeted by brute-force attacks. SQL passwords are not subject to Active Directory password policies, may be stored in application config files, and bypass centralized authentication controls.

findings.title: IIS Running with Default Site
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or stop the 'Default Web Site' if it is not needed. For production sites, create named sites with specific bindings and remove all default content, sample applications, and documentation.
findings.description: IIS is running with the default web site active. The default site exposes server information, may serve default pages, and typically lacks application-specific hardening that production deployments require.
findings.impact: The default IIS site reveals the web server platform, may expose debug pages or sample applications, and often lacks proper access controls. Attackers use default sites to fingerprint the server and find known vulnerabilities.

findings.title: Unnecessary Server Roles Installed on Workstation
findings.remediation_brief: Remove unnecessary server roles via Server Manager or DISM. Workstations should not run server infrastructure services unless specifically authorized and hardened.
findings.description: Server roles (DHCP, DNS, AD DS, Hyper-V, IIS, etc.) are installed on this workstation. Server roles on workstations expand the attack surface with services not intended for endpoint use.
findings.impact: Each server role introduces additional listening services, open ports, and potential vulnerabilities. On a workstation, these roles are rarely monitored or patched with the same rigor as production servers.

findings.title: Web Server Running on Endpoint Workstation
findings.remediation_brief: Remove web server software from workstations. Use dedicated servers or containerized development environments. If a local dev server is required, ensure it binds only to localhost (127.0.0.1).
findings.description: A web server (IIS, Apache, Nginx, XAMPP, WAMP, etc.) is running on this workstation. Web servers on endpoints are often development installations with default configurations and no hardening.
findings.impact: Web servers on workstations are typically unmonitored, lack WAF protection, may expose sensitive development data, and are frequently misconfigured with directory listing, debug modes, or default credentials enabled.

findings.title: End-of-Life Windows Version
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade the operating system to a currently supported version of Windows that receives regular security updates. For Windows Server environments, plan a migration path to Server 2019 or later. For desktop systems, upgrade to Windows 10 22H2 or Windows 11. Coordinate with application owners to verify compatibility before migration.
findings.description: The Windows operating system version running on this endpoint has reached end-of-life and no longer receives security updates from Microsoft.
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit publicly disclosed vulnerabilities that will never be patched, leading to full system compromise. The organization also faces compliance violations as most frameworks require supported software.

findings.title: Missing Critical Security Updates
findings.remediation_brief: Install all pending critical and important security updates immediately. Configure Windows Update or WSUS to automatically download and install security updates on a regular schedule. Establish a patch management process with a maximum 30-day window for critical updates and 90 days for important updates.
findings.description: The endpoint has critical or important security updates pending installation, leaving known vulnerabilities unpatched.
findings.impact: Attackers can exploit publicly known vulnerabilities with available patches. Delayed patching is one of the most common vectors for ransomware and lateral movement within enterprise networks.

findings.title: Windows Update Service Disabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable the Windows Update service by setting its startup type to Automatic and starting the service. Verify that Group Policy is not overriding this setting. If WSUS or SCCM is used for update management, ensure the client agent is properly configured and communicating with the update server.
findings.description: The Windows Update service (wuauserv) is disabled or stopped, preventing automatic security update installation.
findings.impact: Without the update service running, the system will not receive security patches, accumulating vulnerabilities over time. This creates a growing attack surface that adversaries can exploit.

findings.title: WSUS Not Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Configure a centralized update management solution such as WSUS, SCCM, or Intune. Point this endpoint to the organization's WSUS server via Group Policy (Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > Windows Components > Windows Update > Specify intranet Microsoft update service location).
findings.description: No Windows Server Update Services (WSUS) or equivalent centralized update management solution is configured for this endpoint.
findings.impact: Without centralized update management, there is no visibility into the patch compliance status of this endpoint. Updates depend on individual machine settings, making enterprise-wide patch compliance difficult to enforce and verify.

findings.title: System Uptime Exceeds 90 Days
findings.remediation_brief: Schedule a maintenance window to restart the system and apply any pending updates that require a reboot. Establish a regular reboot schedule aligned with the organization's patch management cycle, typically monthly following Patch Tuesday.
findings.description: The system has been running for over 90 days without a reboot, which may indicate that kernel-level patches requiring a restart have not been applied.
findings.impact: Many Windows security updates require a system restart to take effect. Extended uptime suggests these updates have been downloaded but not fully installed, leaving kernel-level vulnerabilities unpatched.

findings.title: No Windows Backup Configured
findings.remediation_brief: Configure Windows Server Backup or a third-party backup solution to perform regular system state and data backups. Store backups on a separate, isolated storage target. Test backup restoration procedures regularly to ensure recoverability.
findings.description: No Windows backup solution (Windows Server Backup, System Restore, or third-party backup) is configured on this endpoint.
findings.impact: Without backups, data loss from ransomware, hardware failure, or accidental deletion is unrecoverable. This significantly increases the business impact of any destructive attack or system failure.

findings.title: Last Backup Older Than 30 Days
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate why backups have not completed recently. Check backup job schedules, storage target availability, and backup service health. Resume regular backup operations and configure alerting for backup failures.
findings.description: The most recent backup on this system is older than 30 days, indicating that backup jobs may have failed or been disabled.
findings.impact: A stale backup means up to 30+ days of data would be lost in a disaster recovery scenario. Critical business data, configuration changes, and system state captured after the last backup cannot be restored.

findings.title: BitLocker Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable BitLocker Drive Encryption on all fixed drives. Use TPM+PIN for pre-boot authentication where possible. Store recovery keys in Active Directory or a centralized key management solution. For systems without TPM, use USB key-based or password-based protectors.
findings.description: BitLocker Drive Encryption is not enabled on one or more fixed drives, leaving data at rest unprotected.
findings.impact: If the device is stolen or a hard drive is physically removed, all data on unencrypted volumes is accessible without authentication. This includes cached credentials, local databases, documents, and application data.

findings.title: TPM Not Available or Not Ready
findings.remediation_brief: If the hardware supports TPM, enable it in the BIOS/UEFI firmware settings and initialize it through the TPM Management console (tpm.msc). For virtual machines, enable virtual TPM through the hypervisor. If the hardware does not support TPM, consider hardware replacement during the next refresh cycle.
findings.description: No Trusted Platform Module (TPM) is available or the TPM is not in a ready state on this endpoint.
findings.impact: Without a functional TPM, hardware-rooted security features such as BitLocker with TPM-based protectors, Credential Guard, and Measured Boot cannot be used. The system must rely on software-only security mechanisms which are more susceptible to tampering.

findings.title: Secure Boot Not Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Secure Boot in the system's UEFI firmware settings. Ensure the operating system was installed in UEFI mode (not legacy BIOS). Verify that all boot components (bootloader, kernel, drivers) are properly signed. Note that enabling Secure Boot on a legacy BIOS-installed system requires OS reinstallation in UEFI mode.
findings.description: UEFI Secure Boot is not enabled on this endpoint, allowing unsigned or tampered boot components to execute during system startup.
findings.impact: An attacker with physical access or kernel-level privileges can install a bootkit or rootkit that loads before the operating system, persisting across reinstalls and evading all OS-level security controls including antivirus and EDR.

findings.title: Sysmon Not Installed
findings.remediation_brief: Install Sysmon from Microsoft Sysinternals: sysmon64.exe -accepteula -i sysmonconfig.xml. Use a community-maintained configuration such as SwiftOnSecurity/sysmon-config or olafhartong/sysmon-modular as a starting point. Key event types to enable: Process creation (Event 1), Network connection (Event 3), File creation (Event 11), Registry modification (Event 13), WMI events (Events 19-21). Forward Sysmon logs to a SIEM for detection and alerting.
findings.description: Sysmon (System Monitor) is not installed on this system. Sysmon provides detailed telemetry about process creation, network connections, file creation, registry modifications, WMI events, and other security-relevant activities that are essential for threat detection and incident response.
findings.impact: Without Sysmon, the system lacks granular visibility into process execution (with command lines and parent process chains), network connections per-process, file creation timestamps and hashes, registry modifications, WMI activity, and named pipe operations. This severely limits the ability to detect and investigate malicious activity, lateral movement, and persistence mechanisms. Native Windows event logs lack the detail that Sysmon provides.

findings.title: PrintNightmare Vulnerable Configuration

mitre_attack.name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution: Print Processors

findings.remediation_brief: 1) Install all PrintNightmare patches (KB5004945 and later cumulative updates). 2) Set RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators=1: reg add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint" /v RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f. 3) Set NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall=0 and UpdatePromptSettings=0 in the same key. 4) On servers that do not need printing, disable the Print Spooler service entirely: Stop-Service Spooler; Set-Service Spooler -StartupType Disabled. 5) On domain controllers, always disable Print Spooler.
findings.description: The system is vulnerable to PrintNightmare (CVE-2021-34527 / CVE-2021-1675). The Print Spooler service is running AND the RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators registry key is not set to 1, or the NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall / UpdatePromptSettings Point-and-Print restriction keys are configured unsafely.
findings.impact: PrintNightmare allows any authenticated user (local or remote) to execute arbitrary code with SYSTEM privileges by exploiting the Print Spooler service's driver installation functionality. This vulnerability was actively exploited in the wild and provides reliable remote code execution. On domain controllers, it enables immediate domain compromise. Multiple exploit variants exist in public tooling.

findings.title: DNS Zone Transfer Allowed
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondary DNS servers only. In DNS Manager: right-click zone > Properties > Zone Transfers > uncheck 'Allow zone transfers' or select 'Only to the following servers' and list authorized secondaries. For AD-integrated zones, consider disabling zone transfers entirely and relying on AD replication. Verify with: nslookup > set type=AXFR > ls -d <domain>.

validation_tools.name: dnsx
validation_tools.command:
subfinder -d TARGET -all | dnsx -a -aaaa -cname -mx -txt -resp
dnsx -d TARGET -w dns-wordlist.txt -a
validation_tools.description: Fast DNS resolver and bulk DNS enumeration with wildcard filtering

validation_tools.name: fierce
validation_tools.command: fierce --domain TARGET --subdomains --delay 0.5
validation_tools.description: DNS reconnaissance tool for subdomain discovery and zone transfer testing

validation_tools.name: nmap
validation_tools.install: apt-get install nmap  OR  brew install nmap
validation_tools.command:
nmap -sV -sC --script vuln -p TARGET
nmap -sV --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 TARGET
validation_tools.description: Network discovery and security scanning with 600+ NSE scripts

validation_tools.name: nuclei
validation_tools.command:
nuclei -u TARGET -t cves/ -t vulnerabilities/ -t exposures/
nuclei -u TARGET -tags sqli,xss,ssrf
validation_tools.description: Fast template-based vulnerability scanner with 5000+ community templates

findings.description: The DNS server role is installed and zone transfers (AXFR) are allowed to any requestor, or are not restricted to specific secondary DNS servers. This allows any host to download the complete contents of DNS zones, including all hostnames, IP addresses, and service records.
findings.impact: Unrestricted DNS zone transfers expose the entire internal DNS namespace to any attacker who can reach the DNS server. This provides a complete map of internal hosts, services, domain controllers, and other infrastructure without triggering typical detection mechanisms. The information enables targeted attacks against specific systems and services identified through the zone data.

findings.title: Built-in Administrator Account Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the built-in Administrator account and create named individual admin accounts. If the built-in account must remain enabled for emergency access, rename it and set a complex password stored in a password vault. Consider implementing LAPS for local admin password management.
findings.description: The built-in Administrator account (RID 500) is enabled on this endpoint.
findings.impact: The built-in Administrator is a well-known target for brute force attacks and cannot be locked out by default. If compromised, it provides full system control. Attackers specifically target this account during password spraying and pass-the-hash attacks.

findings.title: Guest Account Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the Guest account immediately: net user Guest /active:no. Verify via Group Policy that it remains disabled.
findings.description: The built-in Guest account is enabled on this endpoint, allowing unauthenticated or minimally-authenticated access.
findings.impact: The Guest account provides a foothold for unauthenticated access to the system. Even with limited privileges, it can be used for local enumeration, accessing public shares, and as a stepping stone for privilege escalation.

findings.title: Password Never Expires on User Account
findings.remediation_brief: Review the local Administrators group and remove unnecessary members. Implement the principle of least privilege using standard user accounts for daily operations. Consider implementing LAPS and just-in-time admin access solutions.
findings.description: The local Administrators group contains more than 3 members, indicating excessive administrative access.
findings.impact: Each local administrator account is a potential credential for full system compromise. Excessive admin accounts increase the attack surface for pass-the-hash, credential theft, and privilege abuse. Lateral movement is easier when admin credentials are widespread.

findings.title: Excessive Local Administrators
findings.remediation_brief: Remove the 'Password never expires' flag from interactive user accounts. Implement a maximum password age policy (60-90 days). Service accounts should use managed service accounts (gMSA) or be documented with compensating controls if password expiry would break functionality.
findings.description: One or more interactive user accounts have the 'Password never expires' flag set.
findings.impact: Passwords that never expire may remain unchanged for years, increasing the window for compromise through credential theft or brute force. Compliance frameworks universally require periodic password rotation.

findings.title: Weak Password Policy
findings.remediation_brief: Set minimum password length to at least 12 characters and enable complexity requirements. Configure via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Password Policy. Consider implementing a password filter or Azure AD Password Protection to block common passwords.

validation_tools.name: Hydra
validation_tools.install: apt-get install hydra  OR  brew install hydra
validation_tools.command: hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt TARGET http-post-form '/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:F=incorrect'
validation_tools.description: Fast network logon cracker supporting 50+ protocols

validation_tools.name: hashcat
validation_tools.install: apt-get install hashcat  OR  brew install hashcat
validation_tools.command:
hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt  # MD5
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt  # NTLM
validation_tools.description: World's fastest password recovery tool — GPU-accelerated with 300+ hash types

validation_tools.name: CrackMapExec
validation_tools.install: pip install crackmapexec  OR  apt-get install crackmapexec
validation_tools.command:
crackmapexec smb TARGET -u '' -p ''
crackmapexec smb TARGET -u users.txt -p passwords.txt
validation_tools.description: Post-exploitation framework for Active Directory, SMB, and credential testing

findings.description: The local password policy does not meet security baselines: minimum length is less than 8 characters and/or password complexity requirements are disabled.
findings.impact: Weak password policies allow users to set easily guessable passwords. Short passwords without complexity requirements can be cracked in seconds using modern hardware, making brute force and dictionary attacks trivially successful.

findings.title: Account Lockout Not Configured or Too Permissive
findings.remediation_brief: Configure account lockout policy: set lockout threshold to 5-10 failed attempts, lockout duration to 30 minutes, and reset counter after 30 minutes. Apply via Group Policy: Computer Configuration > Windows Settings > Security Settings > Account Policies > Account Lockout Policy.
findings.description: The account lockout threshold is set to 0 (disabled), allowing unlimited failed login attempts without locking the account.
findings.impact: Without account lockout, attackers can perform unlimited password guessing attacks against all accounts without triggering any lockout defense. Password spraying and brute force attacks can continue indefinitely.

findings.title: Wireless Reconnection Successful
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. This is an expected operational event confirming normal wireless stack behaviour.
findings.description: The wireless interface successfully disconnected from and reconnected to the target SSID within the expected time window. The SSID association was confirmed by polling the interface state.

findings.title: Wireless Reconnection Failed or Timed Out
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the device remains within AP range. Check whether the access point enforces re-association rate limits or client flood protection. Investigate whether WPA Enterprise RADIUS timeout is causing delays.
findings.description: The reconnect command was issued but the interface did not confirm association with the target SSID within the 20-second polling window. This may indicate a weak signal, aggressive rate-limiting of (re)association requests by the AP, or a WPA Enterprise authentication delay.

findings.title: SSID Mismatch After Reconnect
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate whether a rogue AP broadcasting the same or similar SSID is present. Confirm that the wireless client prefers the intended BSSID. Consider enabling BSSID-pinning or 802.11w Management Frame Protection.
findings.description: After issuing the reconnect command for the target SSID, the interface associated with a different SSID. This may indicate the presence of a rogue access point with a stronger signal, or unintended roaming to an adjacent network.

findings.title: Wireless Interface Not Found
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the wireless adapter is physically connected and recognised by the OS. Run 'iw dev' (Linux) or 'airport -I' (macOS) to confirm available interfaces. Ensure the correct interface name is passed via --interface.
findings.description: The specified or auto-detected wireless interface could not be found on the system. The tool is unable to perform any disconnect/reconnect operations.

findings.title: Target Network Not Available
findings.remediation_brief: Confirm the device is in range of the target AP. Check whether the AP has de-authenticated the client. Investigate AP availability or DHCP lease expiry causing loss of association.
findings.description: The interface is not currently associated with the expected SSID at the start of a cycle. The target network may be temporarily unavailable, out of range, or the interface has roamed to a different network.

findings.title: Cycle Completed Successfully
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Normal operational event.
findings.description: A full disconnect/reconnect cycle completed without error. Both the disconnect and reconnect commands succeeded, and the association with the target SSID was confirmed.

findings.title: Maximum Cycle Count Reached
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Re-run with a higher --count value or 0 for continuous operation if additional testing cycles are needed.
findings.description: The configured maximum number of disconnect/reconnect cycles has been reached. The tool has exited normally.

findings.title: Disconnect Command Returned Non-Zero Exit Code
findings.remediation_brief: Verify that the process has sufficient privileges (sudo). Confirm the wireless stack is responsive. On Linux, check whether wpa_supplicant is running and accessible via the DBUS interface.
findings.description: The OS wireless disconnect command (iw, wpa_cli, nmcli, or airport) returned a non-zero exit code. The interface may not have cleanly disassociated before the reconnect attempt.

findings.title: Reconnect Command Returned Non-Zero Exit Code
findings.remediation_brief: Confirm the SSID has a saved connection profile (NetworkManager connection or wpa_supplicant configuration block). On macOS, ensure the network was previously joined and is in the keychain.
findings.description: The OS wireless reconnect command returned a non-zero exit code. The network may not have been joined. This may indicate the SSID is not in the system's known network profiles, or that the wireless daemon rejected the connection attempt.

findings.title: Dry-Run Cycle Completed (Simulated)
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Remove --dry-run for live testing.
findings.description: A cycle completed in dry-run mode. No actual wireless commands were issued. This confirms the timing logic and argument parsing are functioning correctly.

findings.title: Privilege Escalation Required for Wireless Commands
findings.remediation_brief: Configure passwordless sudo for the specific wireless commands used by drift (e.g., /usr/bin/iw, /usr/sbin/nmcli, /usr/bin/wpa_cli) in /etc/sudoers.d/drift.
findings.description: Wireless management commands (iw, nmcli, airport) require elevated privileges. The tool invokes these via sudo. If passwordless sudo is not configured, interactive prompts may interrupt automated testing.

findings.title: Interface Auto-Detection Fallback Used
findings.remediation_brief: Specify the intended interface explicitly using --interface to avoid ambiguity in multi-adapter environments.
findings.description: The wireless interface was not explicitly specified. The tool fell back to parsing /proc/net/wireless or airport output to determine the active interface. The selected interface may not be the intended test adapter.

findings.title: Azure Storage Account allows HTTP: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: az storage account update --name <name> --https-only true
findings.description: Azure storage account does not enforce HTTPS-only. Data in transit may traverse plaintext.
findings.impact: Attackers on-path can intercept blob/queue/file data and Shared Access Signatures. SAS tokens captured this way grant persistent access until their expiry.

findings.title: Azure Storage Account publicly accessible: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: az storage account update --default-action Deny + add specific IP/VNet rules.
findings.description: Storage account network ACL defaults to Allow with no IP restrictions configured.
findings.impact: Blob endpoints are reachable from the entire internet. Authentication still applies, but any leaked SAS, key, or AD token is immediately exploitable from any source.

findings.title: Azure Key Vault soft-delete disabled: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: az keyvault update --name <kv> --enable-soft-delete true
findings.description: Soft-delete is not enabled on this Key Vault — accidental deletions cannot be recovered within the retention window.
findings.impact: An attacker (or careless operator) who deletes a key, secret, or certificate causes permanent loss; downstream applications that depend on the material break and cannot be restored.

findings.title: Azure Key Vault purge-protection disabled: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: az keyvault update --name <kv> --enable-purge-protection true
findings.description: Purge-protection is disabled — soft-deleted keys / secrets can be immediately purged by an attacker with delete permission.
findings.impact: Attacker with Contributor or Key Vault Contributor can soft-delete then immediately purge, bypassing the soft-delete grace window and destroying evidence.

findings.title: Azure VM OS disk unencrypted: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: az vm encryption enable --resource-group <rg> --name <vm> --disk-encryption-keyvault <kv-id>
findings.description: Azure Disk Encryption is disabled on the OS disk.
findings.impact: If the underlying VHD is exfiltrated (snapshot abuse, storage-account compromise), the OS volume can be mounted offline and credentials, keys, and data extracted.

findings.title: GCS bucket uniform access disabled: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: gcloud storage buckets update gs://<bucket> --uniform-bucket-level-access
findings.description: Uniform bucket-level access is disabled; legacy per-object ACLs are in effect.
findings.impact: Object ACLs can grant unintended public-read or all-authenticated-users access bypassing IAM policy. Inventory of object ACLs is hard to audit at scale.

findings.title: GCE instance uses default service account: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: Create a least-privilege custom SA and re-attach: gcloud compute instances set-service-account.
findings.description: Compute instance is attached to the default Compute Engine service account.
findings.impact: Default SA is granted Editor by default in legacy projects and supplies broad scopes (cloud-platform). Workload compromise becomes project-wide compromise.

findings.title: GCE instance has public IP: {name}
findings.remediation_brief: If unneeded, remove the access-config: gcloud compute instances delete-access-config.
findings.description: Compute instance has an external IP configured.
findings.impact: Direct internet exposure increases attack surface; ensure firewall rules and IAP/Cloud Armor are in place. INFO unless the workload has no internet-egress requirement.

findings.title: GCP project-level {role} granted to {member}
findings.remediation_brief: Replace with narrower predefined or custom roles scoped to specific resources.
findings.description: Project-level owner or editor role granted to a user / service account.
findings.impact: Owner/editor at project scope can disable logging, modify any resource, and pivot to other resources. Lateral movement is trivial within the project boundary.

findings.title: Internal Redirect: Trailing Slash Mismatch
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure consistent URL handling and redirect policies are configured on the web server.
findings.description: The server issued an internal redirect due to a trailing slash mismatch on the target URL. This may expose URL normalization behavior.

findings.title: HTTP Redirect to In-Scope URL
findings.remediation_brief: Review redirect configurations to ensure they are intentional and do not expose sensitive routing information.
findings.description: The target URL issues an HTTP redirect to another in-scope URL. Redirect chains may expose internal routing logic.

findings.title: HTTP Redirect to External URL
findings.remediation_brief: Validate and whitelist all redirect destinations. Avoid unvalidated redirects to external URLs.
findings.description: The target URL issues an HTTP redirect to an external domain. This could be leveraged in open redirect or phishing scenarios.

findings.title: WordPress readme.html Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or restrict access to readme.html via web server configuration.
findings.description: The WordPress readme.html file is publicly accessible. This file may disclose the WordPress version and other installation details.

findings.title: WordPress license.txt Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or restrict access to license.txt via web server configuration.
findings.description: The WordPress license.txt file is publicly accessible. While not directly exploitable, it confirms a WordPress installation.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: WordPress Version
findings.remediation_brief: Remove version disclosure from meta generator tags and restrict access to files that reveal version information. Keep WordPress updated.
findings.description: The WordPress version was identified from publicly accessible files or meta tags. A known version allows attackers to target specific vulnerabilities.

findings.title: WordPress Login Page Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict access to wp-login.php by IP, add CAPTCHA, implement account lockout, or use a WAF rule to limit login attempts.
findings.description: The WordPress admin login page (wp-login.php) is publicly accessible. This exposes the authentication endpoint to brute-force and credential stuffing attacks.

findings.title: WordPress User Registration Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable user registration if not required. If required, implement email verification and role restrictions for new registrations.
findings.description: WordPress user self-registration is enabled. Attackers may create accounts to gain authenticated access or exploit subscriber-level vulnerabilities.

findings.title: WordPress Password Reset Form Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Implement rate limiting on the password reset endpoint and ensure username/email enumeration is not possible through error messages.
findings.description: The WordPress password reset form is accessible. Combined with user enumeration, this could facilitate account takeover via password reset abuse.

findings.title: WordPress X-Pingback Header Present
findings.remediation_brief: Disable XML-RPC or remove the X-Pingback header via web server configuration if XML-RPC functionality is not required.
findings.description: The X-Pingback HTTP header is present, advertising the XML-RPC pingback endpoint. This confirms XML-RPC is enabled and may facilitate SSRF or DDoS amplification.

findings.title: WordPress XML-RPC Interface Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable XML-RPC entirely if not required. If required, restrict access by IP and disable the multicall method.
findings.description: The WordPress XML-RPC interface (xmlrpc.php) is enabled and accessible. This legacy interface enables brute-force attacks, SSRF via pingback, and DDoS amplification.

findings.title: WordPress XML-RPC Multicall Brute-Force Vector
findings.remediation_brief: Disable XML-RPC or specifically block the system.multicall method. Implement per-IP rate limiting at the web server level.
findings.description: The XML-RPC system.multicall method is enabled, allowing an attacker to test hundreds of username/password combinations in a single HTTP request, bypassing standard rate limiting.

findings.title: WordPress XML-RPC Pingback SSRF Vector
findings.remediation_brief: Disable XML-RPC or block the pingback.ping method. Implement egress filtering to restrict outbound requests from the web server.
findings.description: The XML-RPC pingback.ping method is accessible. An attacker can abuse this to perform Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) or use the WordPress server as a DDoS reflector.

findings.title: WordPress XML-RPC Interface Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Disable xmlrpc.php entirely unless required. If required, restrict access by IP whitelist.
findings.description: The WordPress XML-RPC endpoint responds to requests. The full list of available methods was retrieved, confirming the attack surface exposed by this legacy interface.

findings.title: WordPress REST API Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict REST API access to authenticated users where possible. Disable specific endpoints that expose sensitive data.
findings.description: The WordPress REST API is publicly accessible without authentication. This may expose site structure, user data, and plugin information to unauthenticated users.

findings.title: WordPress Users Exposed via REST API
findings.remediation_brief: Disable or restrict the /wp/v2/users endpoint. Use a security plugin or custom code to require authentication for user enumeration endpoints.
findings.description: The WordPress REST API /wp/v2/users endpoint returns a list of registered usernames and IDs without authentication. This facilitates targeted brute-force and social engineering attacks.

findings.title: WordPress Media Files Enumerable via REST API
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict the media REST API endpoint to authenticated users or disable it if not needed for public consumers.
findings.description: The WordPress REST API /wp/v2/media endpoint exposes a list of uploaded media files without authentication, revealing site content structure and potentially sensitive file paths.

findings.title: WordPress User Enumeration via Author Archives
findings.remediation_brief: Disable author archive pages or suppress the username slug from archive URLs using a security plugin or custom rewrite rules.
findings.description: WordPress author archive pages (/?author=N) redirect to /author/<username>/, disclosing valid usernames. Enumerated usernames can be used for targeted brute-force attacks.

findings.title: WordPress Username Disclosed via oEmbed API
findings.remediation_brief: Disable the oEmbed endpoint if not required, or customize the author name field to avoid exposing login usernames.
findings.description: The WordPress oEmbed endpoint discloses the site author username in its JSON response. This provides an additional username enumeration vector.

findings.title: WordPress Configuration Backup Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately remove all backup and temporary copies of wp-config.php from the web root. Rotate all credentials disclosed. Configure the web server to deny access to .bak, .swp, and ~ files.
findings.description: A WordPress configuration backup file (e.g., wp-config.php.bak, wp-config.php~) was found accessible on the web server. These files typically contain database credentials, authentication keys, and salts.

findings.title: WordPress Plugin Detected
aliases: WordPress Plugins Detected in Page Source
findings.remediation_brief: Keep all WordPress plugins updated to the latest release. Remove readme.txt from plugin directories on production servers. Remove unused plugins to reduce attack surface.

validation_tools.install: gem install wpscan  OR  docker pull wpscanteam/wpscan
validation_tools.command: wpscan --url https://TARGET --enumerate vp,vt,u --api-token YOUR_TOKEN
validation_tools.description: WordPress vulnerability scanner — enumerates plugins, themes, users, and known CVEs

validation_tools.command:
nuclei -u TARGET -t cves/ -t vulnerabilities/ -t exposures/
nuclei -u TARGET -tags sqli,xss,ssrf
validation_tools.description: Fast template-based vulnerability scanner with 5000+ community templates

findings.description: WordPress plugin(s) confirmed via readme.txt enumeration. Version disclosure enables targeted CVE lookups. Plugin names and versions are listed in the Affected field.

findings.title: WordPress Theme Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Keep themes updated. Remove inactive themes. Restrict access to theme readme and style.css version disclosures.
findings.description: The active WordPress theme was detected via static asset paths. Theme identification aids in locating theme-specific vulnerabilities.

findings.title: WordPress Debug Log Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Disable WP_DEBUG in production. Move the debug log outside the web root or restrict access via web server configuration.
findings.description: The WordPress debug log file (wp-content/debug.log) is publicly accessible. Debug logs may contain PHP errors, stack traces, file paths, database queries, and credentials.

findings.title: WordPress uploads Directory Browsing Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable directory listing in the web server configuration. Add an Options -Indexes directive or equivalent.
findings.description: Directory listing is enabled on the WordPress uploads directory. Attackers can enumerate all uploaded files, potentially finding sensitive documents or user data.

findings.title: Robots.txt Discloses Hidden Paths
findings.remediation_brief: Review paths listed in robots.txt. Ensure sensitive paths are protected by authentication, not just excluded from crawlers.
findings.description: The robots.txt file contains Disallow directives that reveal hidden or sensitive application paths. These paths are often administrative interfaces, backup files, or unlinked endpoints.

findings.title: Sitemap.xml Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Review all URLs listed in sitemap.xml to ensure none expose sensitive functionality without proper access controls.
findings.description: A sitemap.xml file was found. Sitemaps enumerate application URLs and can reveal non-linked endpoints and application structure.

findings.title: Server Banner Disclosure
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the web server to suppress or genericize the Server header. Remove version information from all HTTP response headers.
findings.description: The HTTP Server header discloses the web server software name and version. This information assists attackers in identifying applicable CVEs and exploit modules.

findings.title: X-Powered-By Header Discloses Technology Stack
findings.remediation_brief: Remove or suppress the X-Powered-By header in web server and application framework configuration.
findings.description: The X-Powered-By HTTP response header discloses the backend technology (e.g., PHP version, ASP.NET version, Express). This aids fingerprinting and CVE targeting.

findings.title: Application Error Message Disclosure
findings.remediation_brief: Configure custom error pages for all HTTP error codes. Ensure verbose errors are logged server-side only and not returned to clients.
findings.description: Verbose error messages are returned by the application, potentially revealing stack traces, file paths, database queries, or framework internals.

findings.title: Directory Listing Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable directory listing in web server configuration (Options -Indexes for Apache, autoindex off for Nginx).
findings.description: Directory listing is enabled on one or more paths, allowing unauthenticated users to browse file and directory contents. This may expose source code, configuration files, or sensitive documents.

findings.title: WSDL/WADL Service Description Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict access to WSDL/WADL files by IP or authentication. Remove them from public-facing endpoints in production.
findings.description: A WSDL or WADL service description file is publicly accessible. These files describe all available service methods, parameters, and data types, providing a full attack surface map.

findings.title: GraphQL Endpoint Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Disable introspection in production. Implement query depth limiting, rate limiting, and field-level authorization checks.
findings.description: A GraphQL endpoint was detected. GraphQL endpoints expose a queryable schema and may be subject to introspection, batching attacks, and authorization bypass.

findings.title: Swagger/OpenAPI Documentation Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict access to API documentation in production. If public documentation is required, ensure it does not expose internal or administrative endpoints.
findings.description: Swagger UI or OpenAPI specification files are publicly accessible without authentication. These documents expose the full API surface including endpoints, parameters, authentication schemes, and data models.

findings.title: Admin Interface Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict admin interface access by IP whitelist. Move admin interfaces to non-standard ports or behind a VPN. Enforce MFA on all administrative accounts.
findings.description: An administrative interface was discovered at a predictable path. Admin interfaces exposed to the internet are high-value targets for brute-force, credential stuffing, and authentication bypass attacks.

findings.title: Backup File Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Remove all backup files from the web root. Add web server rules to deny access to common backup file extensions.
findings.description: A backup file (e.g., .bak, .old, .orig, ~, .zip) was discovered in the web root. Backup files often contain source code, configuration, or credentials.

findings.title: Configuration File Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Remove configuration files from the web root immediately. Store configuration outside the document root. Rotate all exposed credentials.
findings.description: A configuration file (e.g., .env, config.php, settings.py, database.yml) is publicly accessible. Configuration files typically contain database credentials, API keys, secret keys, and other sensitive values.

findings.title: Git Repository Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately block access to .git directories via web server configuration. Rotate all credentials ever committed to the repository. Audit git history for secrets.
findings.description: A .git directory or git repository index is accessible from the web root. An attacker can reconstruct the full source code, commit history, and any secrets ever committed.

findings.title: SVN/CVS Repository Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Block access to .svn and CVS directories via web server configuration. Remove version control directories from the web root.
findings.description: A Subversion (.svn) or CVS repository directory is accessible from the web root. Repository metadata can be used to reconstruct source files.

findings.title: Log File Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Move log files outside the web root. Restrict access via web server configuration. Ensure log rotation is implemented.
findings.description: An application or server log file is publicly accessible. Log files may contain IP addresses, usernames, session tokens, stack traces, and sensitive application data.

findings.title: Database File Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Remove all database files from the web root immediately. Store database files outside the document root and restrict filesystem permissions.
findings.description: A database file (e.g., .sqlite, .db, .mdb) is directly accessible from the web server. This exposes the entire database contents to unauthenticated download.

findings.title: TLS Certificate Expired
findings.remediation_brief: Renew the TLS certificate immediately. Implement automated certificate renewal (e.g., Let's Encrypt with certbot or ACME protocol) to prevent future expirations.
findings.description: The TLS certificate presented by the server has expired. Browser warnings will be displayed, and the certificate can no longer be trusted to guarantee the server's identity.

findings.title: TLS Certificate Not Yet Valid
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure server time is synchronized via NTP. Verify the certificate was issued correctly and replace if the issue persists.
findings.description: The TLS certificate presented by the server has a notBefore date in the future, meaning it is not yet valid. Clients may reject the connection.

findings.title: TLS Certificate Hostname Mismatch
findings.remediation_brief: Obtain and install a certificate that matches the server's hostname. Use Subject Alternative Names (SANs) to cover all required hostnames.
findings.description: The Common Name or Subject Alternative Names in the TLS certificate do not match the hostname being accessed. This breaks trust validation and may indicate a misconfiguration or MITM condition.
findings.impact: A TLS certificate hostname mismatch indicates the certificate was not issued for the requested domain, causing browser warnings. Users who bypass these warnings become vulnerable to MITM attacks, and automated systems may silently accept invalid certificates.

findings.title: TLS Certificate Self-Signed
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted CA. Use Let's Encrypt for free, automatically renewed certificates.
findings.description: The TLS certificate is self-signed and not issued by a trusted Certificate Authority. Clients cannot validate the server's identity, making the connection susceptible to MITM attacks.

findings.title: Weak TLS Protocol Supported (SSLv2/SSLv3/TLS 1.0/TLS 1.1)
findings.remediation_brief: Disable SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1. Configure the server to support only TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3.
findings.description: The server supports one or more deprecated TLS/SSL protocol versions (SSLv2, SSLv3, TLS 1.0, or TLS 1.1). These protocols have known cryptographic weaknesses exploitable by POODLE, BEAST, and similar attacks.

findings.title: Weak Cipher Suite Supported
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the server to support only strong cipher suites (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Use Mozilla SSL Configuration Generator for recommended cipher lists.
findings.description: The server supports weak cipher suites including NULL encryption, RC4, DES, 3DES, or export-grade ciphers. Weak ciphers can be exploited to decrypt TLS-protected traffic.

findings.title: TLS BEAST Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable TLS 1.0. Prefer TLS 1.2+ with GCM cipher suites. Enable server-side cipher preference.
findings.description: The server is vulnerable to the BEAST (Browser Exploit Against SSL/TLS) attack due to the use of TLS 1.0 with CBC cipher suites. An attacker with network position can decrypt portions of encrypted traffic.

findings.title: TLS POODLE Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable SSLv3 entirely. Implement TLS_FALLBACK_SCSV to prevent protocol downgrade attacks.
findings.description: The server supports SSLv3, making it vulnerable to the POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) attack. An attacker can force a downgrade to SSLv3 and decrypt session cookies.

findings.title: TLS DROWN Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable SSLv2 on all servers sharing the same private key. Regenerate private keys if SSLv2 was enabled.
findings.description: The server supports SSLv2, making modern TLS connections vulnerable to the DROWN attack. An attacker can decrypt RSA-encrypted TLS sessions by exploiting SSLv2 export cipher weaknesses.

findings.title: TLS HEARTBLEED Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade OpenSSL to 1.0.1g or later immediately. After patching, revoke and regenerate all TLS certificates and private keys. Invalidate all active sessions.
findings.description: The server is running a version of OpenSSL vulnerable to Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160). An attacker can read up to 64KB of server memory per request, potentially extracting private keys, session tokens, and credentials.

findings.title: TLS LOGJAM Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable export-grade DHE cipher suites. Generate and configure strong (2048-bit or 4096-bit) DH parameters. Prefer ECDHE over DHE.
findings.description: The server supports DHE key exchange with weak (export-grade) Diffie-Hellman parameters (512-bit), making it vulnerable to the LOGJAM downgrade attack.

findings.title: TLS FREAK Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable all EXPORT cipher suites. Update OpenSSL to a patched version. Enforce server-side cipher preference.
findings.description: The server supports RSA_EXPORT cipher suites, making it vulnerable to the FREAK (Factoring RSA Export Keys) attack. An attacker can force the use of weak 512-bit RSA keys.

findings.title: TLS ROBOT Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable RSA key exchange cipher suites. Use ECDHE for forward secrecy. Patch the TLS library to a version with ROBOT mitigations.
findings.description: The server is vulnerable to the ROBOT (Return Of Bleichenbacher's Oracle Threat) attack, allowing an attacker to perform RSA decryption and signing operations with the server's private key.

findings.title: TLS CCS Injection Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade OpenSSL to 0.9.8za, 1.0.0m, or 1.0.1h or later. Restart the server after patching.
findings.description: The server is vulnerable to the OpenSSL CCS Injection vulnerability (CVE-2014-0224). An attacker with MITM position can force the use of weak key material.

findings.title: TLS Ticketbleed Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Apply the vendor patch from F5. Disable TLS session tickets as a temporary mitigation.
findings.description: The server is vulnerable to Ticketbleed (CVE-2016-9244) in F5 BIG-IP TLS implementations, allowing an attacker to read up to 31 bytes of uninitialized memory via TLS session tickets.

findings.title: TLS SWEET32 Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Disable 3DES (TRIPLE_DES, 3DES_EDE) cipher suites. Prefer AES-GCM cipher suites.
findings.description: The server supports 3DES cipher suites, making long-lived TLS connections vulnerable to the SWEET32 birthday attack, which can recover plaintext from encrypted traffic.

findings.title: HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) Not Enforced
findings.remediation_brief: Add the Strict-Transport-Security header with a max-age of at least 31536000 seconds (1 year), includeSubDomains, and preload directives.
findings.description: The Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header is not present or has an insufficient max-age. Without HSTS, browsers may connect over HTTP, enabling SSL stripping attacks.
findings.impact: Without HSTS enforcement, browsers permit plaintext HTTP connections, enabling SSL stripping attacks where an attacker downgrades the connection to intercept credentials and session tokens in transit.

findings.title: TLS Certificate Uses Weak Signature Algorithm (MD5/SHA-1)
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one using SHA-256 or stronger signature algorithm (SHA-2 family).
findings.description: The TLS certificate is signed with a weak signature algorithm (MD5 or SHA-1). SHA-1 certificates are deprecated by major browsers and CAs, and MD5 certificates are cryptographically broken.

findings.title: TLS Certificate Short Key Length
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the certificate with one using at least 2048-bit RSA keys, or preferably 4096-bit RSA or ECDSA P-256/P-384.
findings.description: The TLS certificate uses an RSA key shorter than 2048 bits. Short RSA keys are susceptible to factoring attacks with sufficient computational resources.

findings.title: Subdomain Takeover Vulnerability
findings.remediation_brief: Remove dangling DNS records immediately. Claim or delete the referenced external resource. Implement DNS monitoring to detect future dangling records.
findings.description: A subdomain DNS record points to an external service (e.g., GitHub Pages, S3, Heroku, Netlify) that is no longer claimed. An attacker can register the unclaimed resource and serve malicious content from the trusted subdomain.

findings.title: Missing Content-Security-Policy Header
findings.remediation_brief: Implement a restrictive Content-Security-Policy header. Start with a report-only policy, monitor violations, then enforce. Avoid 'unsafe-inline' and 'unsafe-eval' directives.
findings.description: The Content-Security-Policy (CSP) header is absent. Without CSP, the application has no defense against Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) and data injection attacks through browser-enforced policy.

findings.title: Missing X-Frame-Options Header
findings.remediation_brief: Add 'X-Frame-Options: DENY' or 'X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN'. Alternatively, use the CSP frame-ancestors directive.
findings.description: The X-Frame-Options header is absent. Without this header, the page can be embedded in an iframe on any origin, enabling clickjacking attacks that trick users into performing unintended actions.

findings.title: Missing X-Content-Type-Options Header
findings.remediation_brief: Add 'X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff' to all HTTP responses.
findings.description: The X-Content-Type-Options header is absent. Without this header, browsers may perform MIME type sniffing, potentially executing uploaded files as scripts.

findings.title: Missing Referrer-Policy Header
findings.remediation_brief: Add 'Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or a more restrictive policy to prevent sensitive URL data leakage.
findings.description: The Referrer-Policy header is absent. Without this header, the browser's default behavior may leak the full URL (including query parameters and path) in the Referer header to third-party origins.

findings.title: Missing Permissions-Policy Header
findings.remediation_brief: Add a Permissions-Policy header that disables browser features not required by the application (e.g., camera, microphone, geolocation).
findings.description: The Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy) header is absent. This header controls which browser features and APIs are available to the page and embedded third-party content.

findings.title: Missing Strict-Transport-Security Header
findings.remediation_brief: Add 'Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload' to all HTTPS responses.

validation_tools.name: testssl.sh
validation_tools.command:
testssl.sh TARGET:443
testssl.sh --full --json TARGET:443
validation_tools.description: Comprehensive TLS/SSL configuration testing including cipher suites, protocols, BEAST/POODLE/HEARTBLEED

validation_tools.name: nuclei
validation_tools.command:
nuclei -u TARGET -t cves/ -t vulnerabilities/ -t exposures/
nuclei -u TARGET -tags sqli,xss,ssrf

validation_tools.name: nmap
validation_tools.install: apt-get install nmap  OR  brew install nmap
validation_tools.command:
nmap -sV -sC --script vuln -p TARGET
nmap -sV --script ssl-enum-ciphers -p 443 TARGET
validation_tools.description: Network discovery and security scanning with 600+ NSE scripts

findings.description: The HTTP Strict-Transport-Security (HSTS) header is absent. Without HSTS, browsers may connect over plain HTTP, and SSL stripping attacks can downgrade HTTPS connections to HTTP.

findings.title: Insecure Content-Security-Policy (Unsafe-Inline Allowed)
findings.remediation_brief: Replace 'unsafe-inline' with nonce-based or hash-based CSP. Refactor inline scripts to external files.
findings.description: The Content-Security-Policy header contains 'unsafe-inline', which negates XSS protection by allowing inline JavaScript and CSS. This is the most common CSP misconfiguration.

findings.title: Insecure Content-Security-Policy (Wildcard Source)
findings.remediation_brief: Replace wildcard sources with specific, trusted origin allowlists. Audit all third-party resource dependencies.
findings.description: The Content-Security-Policy header contains a wildcard (*) source directive, allowing scripts or resources to be loaded from any origin. This effectively disables CSP's XSS protection.

findings.title: Session Cookie Missing Secure Flag
findings.remediation_brief: Set the Secure flag on all session cookies. Ensure the application forces HTTPS for all authenticated requests.
findings.description: One or more session cookies are set without the Secure flag. Without the Secure flag, the cookie will be transmitted over unencrypted HTTP connections, exposing session tokens to network interception.

findings.title: Session Cookie Missing HttpOnly Flag
findings.remediation_brief: Set the HttpOnly flag on all session and authentication cookies to prevent JavaScript access.
findings.description: One or more session cookies are set without the HttpOnly flag. Without HttpOnly, client-side JavaScript can read the cookie value, enabling session token theft via XSS.

findings.title: Session Cookie Missing SameSite Attribute
findings.remediation_brief: Set SameSite=Strict or SameSite=Lax on all session cookies. Use SameSite=None only for legitimate cross-site cookie sharing, and always with Secure.
findings.description: Session cookies are set without the SameSite attribute, or with SameSite=None without Secure. This enables Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks in browsers that do not implement SameSite by default.

findings.title: JWT Token in Local Storage
findings.remediation_brief: Store JWTs in HttpOnly, Secure cookies instead of localStorage. This prevents JavaScript access and protects tokens from XSS-based theft.
findings.description: JSON Web Tokens (JWTs) are stored in browser localStorage. localStorage is accessible to JavaScript, making JWT tokens vulnerable to theft via XSS attacks.

findings.title: JWT Algorithm Confusion (None Algorithm)
findings.remediation_brief: Explicitly validate the JWT algorithm on the server side. Reject tokens with 'alg: none'. Use a strict allowlist of permitted algorithms.
findings.description: The server accepts JWTs with the algorithm set to 'none', bypassing signature verification entirely. An attacker can forge arbitrary JWT payloads and impersonate any user.

findings.title: JWT Algorithm Confusion (RS256 to HS256)
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce algorithm validation server-side. Use separate code paths for asymmetric (RS256) and symmetric (HS256) verification. Never use the public key as an HMAC secret.
findings.description: The server is vulnerable to JWT algorithm confusion. By changing the algorithm from RS256 to HS256 and signing the token with the public key as the HMAC secret, an attacker can forge valid JWTs.

findings.title: JWT Weak HMAC Secret
findings.remediation_brief: Use a cryptographically random secret of at least 256 bits for HMAC-signed JWTs. Store the secret securely and rotate it periodically.
findings.description: The JWT HMAC signing secret is weak or uses a common/guessable value. An attacker can brute-force the secret offline and forge arbitrary JWT tokens.

findings.title: JWT Signature Not Verified
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure the JWT verification library is correctly configured to always verify the signature. Never decode without verification.
findings.description: The server accepts JWTs with an invalid or tampered signature. The server is processing the JWT payload without verifying its integrity, allowing full token forgery.

findings.title: JWT Sensitive Data in Payload
findings.remediation_brief: Remove sensitive data from JWT payloads. Use JWE (JSON Web Encryption) if sensitive data must be embedded in tokens.
findings.description: Sensitive data (e.g., passwords, PII, internal IDs) was found in the JWT payload. JWT payloads are base64-encoded but not encrypted, making them readable to any party with the token.

findings.title: JWT Token Accepted After Expiry
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce 'exp' claim validation in JWT processing. Reject tokens with past expiration times. Use short token lifetimes with refresh token rotation.
findings.description: The server accepts JWT tokens after their 'exp' (expiration) claim has passed. This allows indefinite reuse of stolen or leaked tokens.

findings.title: JWT kid Header Injection
findings.remediation_brief: Validate and sanitize the 'kid' header value. Use a whitelist of known key IDs. Never use the kid value directly in SQL queries or file system lookups.
findings.description: The JWT 'kid' (Key ID) header parameter is used in an unsafe SQL query or file path lookup without validation. An attacker can inject a SQL payload or path traversal sequence into the kid header to manipulate key selection.

findings.title: JWT jwk Header Injection
findings.remediation_brief: Never trust keys embedded in the JWT header. Use only server-side trusted key stores for JWT verification. Ignore or reject tokens with 'jwk' or 'jku' headers unless explicitly required.
findings.description: The server trusts the 'jwk' (JSON Web Key) header embedded in the JWT itself for signature verification. An attacker can embed their own public key in the jwk header and sign a forged token with the corresponding private key.

findings.title: SQL Injection
findings.remediation_brief: Use parameterized queries or prepared statements for all database interactions. Never concatenate user input into SQL strings. Apply the principle of least privilege to database accounts.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — Reflected
findings.remediation_brief: Encode all user-supplied data before rendering it in HTML context. Implement a strict Content-Security-Policy. Use a template engine with auto-escaping enabled.
findings.description: Reflected Cross-Site Scripting was detected. User-supplied input is returned in the HTTP response without proper encoding, allowing an attacker to inject client-side scripts that execute in the victim's browser.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — Stored
findings.remediation_brief: Encode all stored user data before rendering. Validate and sanitize input on write. Implement CSP with nonce-based script policy.
findings.description: Stored Cross-Site Scripting was detected. Malicious scripts submitted by an attacker are persisted in the application's data store and executed in the browser of every user who views the affected content.

findings.title: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) — DOM-Based
findings.remediation_brief: Review all client-side JavaScript for unsafe DOM manipulation. Use textContent instead of innerHTML. Validate and encode data before passing to DOM sinks.
findings.description: DOM-based Cross-Site Scripting was detected. Client-side JavaScript reads attacker-controlled data (e.g., from URL fragments, postMessage, or localStorage) and writes it to a dangerous sink (innerHTML, eval, document.write) without sanitization.

findings.title: LDAP Injection
findings.remediation_brief: Use an LDAP library that supports parameterized queries. Escape all special LDAP characters (\, *, (, ), NUL) in user-supplied input before using it in filters.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Javascript Secret
findings.remediation_brief: Remove all hardcoded secrets from client-side JavaScript. Move sensitive keys to server-side configuration. Rotate any exposed secrets immediately. Implement secret scanning in the CI/CD pipeline.
