findings.description: The GraphQL endpoint processes queries with many duplicated fields without limiting the result set.
findings.impact: An attacker can amplify response size by duplicating fields, potentially causing increased bandwidth usage.

findings.title: GraphQL Debug Extensions Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Disable GraphQL debug extensions in production environments.
findings.description: The GraphQL response includes an extensions field containing debug information.
findings.impact: Debug information reveals internal implementation details, query performance characteristics, and potential injection points.

findings.title: HTTP/2 Cleartext Upgrade (h2c) Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the reverse proxy to reject Upgrade: h2c requests or strip the header before forwarding.
findings.description: The server or reverse proxy accepts HTTP/2 cleartext upgrade requests.
findings.impact: An attacker can use h2c smuggling to bypass proxy-level security controls, WAF rules, and access restrictions.

findings.title: h2c Smuggling — Internal Endpoint Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Block h2c upgrades at the reverse proxy and implement authentication on all internal endpoints regardless of network position.
findings.description: An internal endpoint that is blocked at the proxy level becomes accessible when requested via an h2c upgrade connection.
findings.impact: An attacker can access admin panels, monitoring dashboards, or internal APIs by tunneling through the h2c upgrade.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal IP in HTTP Response
aliases: RFC 1918 Address Leakage in HTTP Response
findings.remediation_brief: Remove internal IP addresses from HTTP response bodies, error messages, and headers. Configure application error handling to suppress internal details. Review proxy and load-balancer configurations to strip internal addresses from forwarded headers.
findings.description: The HTTP response body or headers contain one or more RFC 1918 private IP addresses (10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16), disclosing internal network topology.
findings.impact: An attacker learns internal addressing, which aids lateral-movement planning, infrastructure mapping, and targeted exploitation of internal services.

findings.title: Application Responses Identify Valid Accounts
findings.remediation_brief: Return identical responses (status code, body length, content, and timing) for all login attempts regardless of whether the username exists. Use generic error messages like 'Invalid credentials'.
findings.description: Login endpoint responses differ between valid and invalid usernames, allowing attackers to enumerate valid accounts through status codes, body length, error messages, or timing differences.
findings.impact: An attacker can confirm which usernames exist in the system, enabling targeted credential attacks (brute force, credential stuffing) and social engineering.

findings.title: Authorization Gaps — Unauthenticated Access to Restricted Paths
aliases: Missing access control on admin paths
findings.remediation_brief: Implement proper access controls on all administrative and restricted paths. Deny access by default and require authentication and appropriate authorization.
findings.description: Administrative or restricted paths are accessible without authentication, indicating missing or misconfigured access controls.
findings.impact: An attacker can access administrative functions, sensitive data, or configuration interfaces without valid credentials, potentially leading to full application compromise.

findings.title: HTTP Parameter Pollution (Reflected)
findings.remediation_brief: Validate and reject duplicate parameters. Use framework-level parameter parsing that selects only the first occurrence. Encode all reflected user input.
findings.description: Duplicate HTTP parameters are processed and reflected in responses, potentially allowing attackers to bypass input validation or inject malicious content.
findings.impact: An attacker can inject a second parameter value that overrides or appends to the first, bypassing WAF rules, input filters, or business logic validation.

findings.title: Improper Error Handling — Server Error Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Implement custom error pages that suppress stack traces. Disable debug mode in production. Log detailed errors server-side only.
findings.description: Server returns HTTP 5xx error responses with detailed error information including stack traces, database errors, or debug output.
findings.impact: Detailed error messages disclose implementation details (language, framework, file paths, database type, SQL queries) that aid targeted exploitation.

findings.title: Insecure HTTPS to HTTP Redirect Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure all redirects maintain HTTPS. Configure HSTS to prevent protocol downgrades. Review server redirect configurations.
findings.description: Redirect chains downgrade from HTTPS to HTTP, exposing session tokens, credentials, and sensitive data to network-level interception.
findings.impact: An attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack can intercept credentials, session tokens, and sensitive data transmitted over the unencrypted HTTP connection.

findings.title: Form Submits to HTTP from HTTPS Page
findings.remediation_brief: Change all form action URLs to use HTTPS. Enable HSTS.
findings.description: Forms on HTTPS pages submit data to HTTP endpoints, exposing form data (potentially including credentials) to network interception.
findings.impact: Credentials or sensitive data submitted through the form travel over unencrypted HTTP, vulnerable to man-in-the-middle interception.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in HTTP Response
findings.remediation_brief: Remove internal hostnames from HTTP response headers (Server, Via, X-Powered-By, X-Backend-Server) and response bodies. Configure reverse proxies to strip internal routing headers.
findings.description: HTTP response headers or body contain internal hostnames (.local, .internal, .corp, .lan, etc.), disclosing naming conventions and network topology.
findings.impact: Internal hostnames reveal infrastructure naming patterns and topology, aiding reconnaissance and potentially enabling blind SSRF attacks when callback parameters exist.

findings.title: Unhandled Application Exception Disclosed
findings.remediation_brief: Implement custom error pages. Disable debug mode in production. Log exceptions server-side only. Never expose stack traces in HTTP responses.
findings.description: HTTP responses contain exception class names, stack traces, or debug output patterns from various frameworks (Python, Java, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Ruby, SQL).
findings.impact: Exception details disclose implementation language, framework version, file paths, database type, and SQL queries, significantly reducing the effort needed for targeted exploitation.

findings.title: Outdated or Unnecessary Website Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Review whether this website is still needed. If not, decommission it. If needed, update its content and underlying software.
findings.description: The website shows indicators of being outdated, abandoned, or unnecessary: old copyright dates, 'under construction' text, default CMS/server pages, or stale Last-Modified headers.
findings.impact: Outdated or unnecessary websites expand the attack surface with unpatched software and forgotten configurations that are less likely to be monitored.

findings.title: Log File Publicly Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Remove log files from web-accessible directories. Configure web servers to deny access to log file extensions (.log). Move log storage outside the document root. In Apache: <FilesMatch ".log$"> Require all denied </FilesMatch>. In nginx: location ~* \.log$ { deny all; }.
findings.description: The web server exposes log file(s) to unauthenticated users. Log files commonly contain internal IP addresses, stack traces, usernames, session tokens, SQL queries, and file system paths. CWE-532, CWE-200.
findings.impact: Attackers can harvest internal paths, database query patterns, user data, session tokens, and credentials from exposed log files. This information enables targeted exploitation of backend systems, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.

findings.title: Password Field With Autocomplete Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Set autocomplete='off' or autocomplete='new-password' on all password input fields.
findings.description: Password input fields do not set autocomplete='off', allowing browsers to cache entered passwords.
findings.impact: On shared workstations, cached passwords can be retrieved by subsequent users, compromising accounts.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Cloud Credentials in File
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately rotate all credentials found in exposed files. Remove credential files from the web-accessible directory. Add dot-files and credential paths to the web server deny list. Use IAM roles and managed identities instead of static credential files. Never store credential files in the document root.
findings.description: Cloud or CI/CD credential file(s) are accessible via the web, containing API keys, access tokens, database passwords, and service account credentials. Covers AWS credentials, Docker config, Kubernetes config, NPM config, Git credentials, and PostgreSQL password files. CWE-540, CWE-200.
findings.impact: Attackers gain direct access to cloud infrastructure, container registries, Kubernetes clusters, or package repositories using the disclosed credentials. This enables data exfiltration, resource hijacking, supply chain attacks, and full infrastructure compromise.

findings.title: Terraform State File Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Store Terraform state in a secure remote backend (S3+DynamoDB, Terraform Cloud). Never serve state files via a web server.
findings.description: Terraform state file is accessible via the web, containing infrastructure secrets, API keys, database passwords, and complete cloud resource inventory.
findings.impact: Full infrastructure credential compromise — database passwords, API keys, cloud resource details enabling lateral movement and data exfiltration.

findings.title: Sensitive Data Exposed in HTML Comments
findings.remediation_brief: Remove sensitive data from HTML comments. Implement build processes that strip comments from production output. Conduct code reviews for comment hygiene.
findings.description: HTML comments in page source contain sensitive keywords such as passwords, API keys, connection strings, or tokens.
findings.impact: Credentials, API keys, or connection strings in HTML comments are visible to any user viewing page source, enabling direct account or service compromise.

findings.title: Exposed Admin/Debug Endpoint: /_ray/api/health
findings.owasp_web: A09:2025 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.remediation_brief: Remove Spatie Ray from production. Restrict debug tools to development environments only.
findings.description: Spatie Ray debug tool is accessible at /_ray/api/health. Ray allows remote code inspection and can expose application internals in production.
findings.impact: Attackers can inspect application state, variables, queries, and stack traces through the Ray debug interface, gaining deep application knowledge for exploitation.

findings.title: Exposed Admin/Debug Endpoint: Express.js Default Error
findings.owasp_web: A09:2025 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.remediation_brief: Implement custom error handlers in Express.js. Set NODE_ENV=production to suppress stack traces. Never return error details to clients.
findings.description: Express.js default error handler returns stack traces to clients, disclosing file paths, module versions, and application structure.
findings.impact: Stack traces reveal internal file paths, module names, and line numbers that attackers use to plan targeted exploitation of known framework vulnerabilities.

findings.title: WebDAV PROPFIND Response Discloses Server Information
findings.remediation_brief: Disable WebDAV on the web server unless required. Restrict PROPFIND to authenticated users. Block PROPFIND at the reverse proxy.
findings.description: The server responds to unauthenticated PROPFIND requests with WebDAV property data, disclosing file metadata and directory structure.
findings.impact: Attackers can enumerate server directory structure and file metadata without authentication, mapping the application for targeted attacks.

findings.title: WebDAV Methods Enabled
findings.remediation_brief: Disable WebDAV unless explicitly required. If required, enforce authentication and restrict to authorized users only.
findings.description: The web server advertises WebDAV methods (PROPFIND, MKCOL, COPY, MOVE, LOCK, UNLOCK), enabling remote file manipulation capabilities.
findings.impact: WebDAV methods can allow unauthenticated file upload, modification, or deletion. Historical vulnerabilities like CVE-2017-7269 demonstrate RCE risk.

findings.title: Password Reset Token Exposed in URL
aliases: Reset Token in URL Query String
findings.remediation_brief: Transmit reset tokens via POST body or HTTP headers, not URL query parameters. Implement short-lived, single-use tokens.
findings.description: Password reset functionality includes the reset token in URL query parameters, exposing it in logs, browser history, and Referer headers.
findings.impact: Reset tokens in URLs can be harvested from server logs, proxy caches, browser history, and Referer headers, enabling account takeover.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: ETag
findings.remediation_brief: Configure Apache: FileETag MTime Size (remove INode). For nginx, ETag is based on modification time and size by default.
findings.description: The ETag response header follows the Apache inode-size-mtime format, disclosing filesystem inode numbers that can fingerprint shared hosting.
findings.impact: Inode values reveal file identity and can be used to detect shared hosting, map filesystem structure, and fingerprint specific web servers.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal Hostname in SAN
findings.remediation_brief: Issue separate certificates for internal and external services. Remove internal hostnames from externally visible certificate SANs.
findings.description: The TLS certificate's Subject Alternative Names include internal hostnames that disclose naming conventions and network topology.
findings.impact: Internal hostnames in certificates reveal naming conventions, infrastructure topology, and internal service locations to external attackers.

findings.title: Cloud Storage Bucket URL Exposed
findings.remediation_brief: Serve static assets through a CDN with a custom domain. Restrict bucket access policies. Do not store sensitive data in publicly referenced buckets.
findings.description: Cloud storage bucket URLs (AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob) are exposed in page content, enabling cloud infrastructure reconnaissance.
findings.impact: Exposed bucket URLs enable attackers to test for misconfigured public access, potentially accessing sensitive data stored in the cloud.

findings.title: Exposed Admin/Debug Endpoint: /_ignition/execute-solution
findings.owasp_web: A09:2025 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.remediation_brief: Upgrade Laravel Ignition to a patched version. Remove debug tools from production. Set APP_DEBUG=false.
findings.description: Laravel Ignition execute-solution endpoint is accessible, potentially enabling remote code execution via CVE-2021-3129.
findings.impact: CVE-2021-3129 allows unauthenticated RCE through the Ignition execute-solution endpoint by chaining log file manipulation with PHP deserialization.

findings.title: Overly Permissive Permissions-Policy Header
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict sensitive features in the Permissions-Policy header to self only or disable them entirely. Replace wildcard (*) values with specific origins or empty allowlists: Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=(), usb=().
findings.description: The Permissions-Policy (or Feature-Policy) header grants wildcard (*) access to sensitive browser features such as camera, microphone, geolocation, or payment. This allows any third-party iframe or embedded content to access these device capabilities, increasing the risk of privacy violations and data exfiltration. CWE-16.
findings.impact: Third-party content embedded in iframes can access the user's camera, microphone, geolocation, or payment APIs without restriction. A compromised or malicious third-party script can silently activate these features for surveillance or data theft.

findings.title: Expired TLS Certificate Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Renew the TLS certificate immediately through the issuing Certificate Authority. Configure automated certificate renewal (e.g. via certbot/ACME) and monitoring alerts for certificates approaching expiration.
findings.description: The TLS certificate presented by the server has passed its notAfter date and is no longer valid. Expired certificates break trust chain validation and cause browser warnings, which train users to bypass security prompts. An expired certificate may also indicate a forgotten or unmaintained service.
findings.impact: Users encounter certificate warnings and may click through them, normalizing the bypass of TLS trust validation. An attacker could perform a man-in-the-middle attack more easily when users are conditioned to ignore certificate errors. The expired certificate may also indicate the service is unmaintained and potentially vulnerable.

findings.title: Self-Signed TLS Certificate
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the self-signed certificate with one issued by a trusted public Certificate Authority (e.g. Let's Encrypt, DigiCert). If a private CA is required, ensure its root certificate is distributed to all intended clients.
findings.description: The server presents a self-signed TLS certificate that is not issued by a trusted Certificate Authority. Self-signed certificates are not validated by browsers or TLS clients by default, indicating the service may not be production-hardened or is using a private PKI without proper trust distribution.
findings.impact: Users must manually trust the certificate or bypass browser warnings, which normalizes ignoring TLS errors and makes man-in-the-middle attacks feasible. A self-signed certificate on an internet-facing service suggests it may be a development, staging, or unmaintained system with weaker security controls.

findings.title: Revoked TLS Certificate Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Replace the revoked certificate immediately with a new certificate from a trusted CA. Investigate the reason for revocation — if key compromise is suspected, generate a new key pair. Rotate any credentials or secrets that may have been exposed.
findings.description: The TLS certificate presented by the server has been revoked by its issuing Certificate Authority. Certificate revocation typically occurs due to key compromise, CA compromise, or administrative decommission. A revoked certificate should not be trusted for any purpose.
findings.impact: A revoked certificate may indicate that the private key was compromised, potentially allowing an attacker to impersonate the server. Clients that check CRL/OCSP will reject the connection, but not all clients perform revocation checking, leaving some users vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks using the compromised key.

findings.title: TLS Certificate SAN Enumeration

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Digital Certificates

findings.remediation_brief: Review SAN entries to ensure no unintended hostnames (internal names, staging environments, decommissioned services) are exposed. Use separate certificates for services that should not be associated publicly.
findings.description: The TLS certificate presented by the server contains multiple Subject Alternative Name (SAN) entries, revealing additional hostnames and services hosted on this infrastructure. SAN enumeration is a passive reconnaissance technique that exposes the scope of services behind a single certificate.
findings.impact: An attacker can enumerate additional attack surface by reviewing SAN entries, discovering internal hostnames, staging environments, or related services that may have weaker security controls. Shared certificates also indicate infrastructure relationships between the listed domains.

findings.title: Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance (CSA) Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the Ivanti CSA is running the latest patched firmware version. Apply all available security patches immediately. If running CSA 4.6, migrate to CSA 5.0 as version 4.6 has reached end-of-life. Monitor CISA KEV catalogue for new Ivanti advisories.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as an Ivanti Cloud Services Appliance (CSA). Ivanti CSA has been the target of multiple critical actively-exploited zero-day vulnerabilities including path traversal (CVE-2024-8963), SQL injection (CVE-2024-9379), OS command injection (CVE-2024-8190), and another OS command injection (CVE-2024-9380).
findings.impact: An attacker can chain these vulnerabilities to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution on the CSA appliance. Successful exploitation provides full administrative access to the appliance and the ability to pivot into the internal network. CISA has issued emergency directives for these vulnerabilities.

findings.title: Pulse Secure / Ivanti Connect Secure VPN Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the Ivanti Connect Secure appliance is running the latest patched firmware. Apply vendor mitigation XML and patches as directed by Ivanti advisories. Run the Ivanti Integrity Checker Tool (ICT) to detect signs of compromise. Consider factory-resetting the appliance if compromise is suspected.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Pulse Secure / Ivanti Connect Secure VPN appliance. This product line has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including authentication bypass (CVE-2023-46805) and command injection (CVE-2024-21887), which were chained for unauthenticated RCE.
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit known vulnerabilities to bypass authentication and execute arbitrary commands on the VPN appliance, gaining access to the internal network. VPN appliances are high-value targets as they provide direct access to corporate networks and are internet-facing by design.

findings.title: F5 BIG-IP Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the F5 BIG-IP is running the latest patched firmware version. Restrict management interface access to trusted networks only. Disable iControl REST on external interfaces if not required.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as an F5 BIG-IP appliance. F5 BIG-IP has had critical remote code execution vulnerabilities including CVE-2023-46747 (authentication bypass to RCE) and CVE-2022-1388 (iControl REST unauthenticated RCE).
findings.impact: An attacker exploiting known F5 BIG-IP vulnerabilities can achieve unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on the appliance. As a load balancer/ADC, BIG-IP sits in a privileged network position with visibility into all traffic it proxies, including credentials and session tokens.

findings.title: Citrix NetScaler / ADC Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Apply Citrix security patches immediately. After patching Citrix Bleed, terminate all active sessions and rotate all credentials — the patch does not invalidate stolen session tokens. Run Citrix-provided IoC scanning tools to check for compromise.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Citrix NetScaler or ADC appliance. Citrix ADC has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including CVE-2023-4966 ('Citrix Bleed', session token leakage) and CVE-2023-3519 (unauthenticated RCE).
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit Citrix Bleed (CVE-2023-4966) to steal valid session tokens without authentication, bypassing MFA and gaining access to internal resources. CVE-2023-3519 allows unauthenticated remote code execution on the appliance itself. Both were widely exploited in the wild by ransomware operators.

findings.title: Fortinet FortiGate Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the Fortinet appliance is running the latest patched FortiOS firmware. Disable SSL VPN if not required. Restrict management interfaces to trusted networks. Enable logging and monitor for indicators of compromise.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Fortinet appliance (FortiGate, FortiWeb, or FortiOS-based). FortiOS has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including CVE-2024-21762 (out-of-bound write in SSL VPN) and CVE-2023-27997 (heap buffer overflow in SSL VPN, 'XORtigate').
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit known FortiOS vulnerabilities to achieve pre-authentication remote code execution on the firewall appliance. As a perimeter firewall/VPN, FortiGate sits at the network boundary with full visibility into traffic and provides a pivot point into the internal network.

findings.title: Palo Alto Networks Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the Palo Alto appliance is running the latest patched PAN-OS version. Apply hotfixes for CVE-2024-3400 immediately. Restrict management interface access and disable unused GlobalProtect portals. Monitor for indicators of compromise using Palo Alto's threat prevention signatures.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Palo Alto Networks appliance. PAN-OS has been the target of critical zero-day exploitation including CVE-2024-3400 (GlobalProtect command injection with CVSS 10.0), which was actively exploited before a patch was available.
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit CVE-2024-3400 to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution with root privileges on the firewall through the GlobalProtect gateway. As a next-generation firewall, Palo Alto devices provide full network visibility and can be used to intercept traffic, modify firewall rules, or pivot into the internal network.

findings.title: SonicWall Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the SonicWall appliance is running the latest patched firmware version. Restrict SSLVPN and management interface access. Enable MFA for all VPN connections. Monitor for unauthorized access attempts.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a SonicWall appliance. SonicWall has had critical vulnerabilities including CVE-2024-40766 (improper access control in SonicOS management and SSLVPN) which was actively exploited by ransomware operators.
findings.impact: An attacker can exploit known SonicWall vulnerabilities to gain unauthorized access to the firewall management interface or VPN services. SonicWall appliances are perimeter security devices and their compromise provides direct access to the internal network.

findings.title: Cisco ASA Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the Cisco ASA is running the latest patched firmware version. Restrict management access to trusted networks. Disable unused VPN profiles and WebVPN features. Monitor syslog for unauthorized access attempts.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Cisco Adaptive Security Appliance (ASA). Cisco ASA is a widely-deployed firewall/VPN platform that has had numerous critical vulnerabilities over its lifetime, including path traversal, authentication bypass, and remote code execution flaws.
findings.impact: A Cisco ASA appliance at the network perimeter provides firewall, VPN, and NAT services. Its compromise gives an attacker the ability to modify access control rules, intercept VPN traffic, and pivot into the internal network. ASA's WebVPN and AnyConnect components have historically been targeted.

findings.title: VMware vSphere / ESXi Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify VMware ESXi/vCenter is running the latest patched version. Restrict management interfaces (port 443, 902) to a dedicated management VLAN. Disable SSH on ESXi hosts unless actively needed. Enable lockdown mode on ESXi hosts.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a VMware vSphere, vCenter, or ESXi host. VMware hypervisor products have been targeted by critical vulnerabilities and are high-value targets for ransomware operators who encrypt entire virtual machine datastores.
findings.impact: Compromise of a VMware hypervisor gives an attacker control over all virtual machines running on it, including the ability to access VM disks, snapshot memory, and intercept network traffic between VMs. ESXi-targeting ransomware (e.g. ESXiArgs) can encrypt entire datastores, taking down all hosted services simultaneously.

findings.title: Sophos Firewall Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Verify the Sophos firewall is running the latest firmware version. Disable the User Portal on WAN-facing interfaces if not required. Restrict management access to trusted internal networks only. Enable automatic hotfix installation.
findings.description: The TLS certificate fingerprint identifies this host as a Sophos firewall appliance (XG Firewall, Sophos Firewall OS, or legacy Cyberoam). Sophos firewalls have had critical vulnerabilities including SQL injection and code injection flaws in their user portal and management interfaces.
findings.impact: An attacker exploiting Sophos firewall vulnerabilities can gain unauthorized access to the firewall management interface, modify security policies, and potentially achieve remote code execution. As a perimeter device, compromise provides a pivot point into the internal network and visibility into all traversing traffic.

findings.title: Technology Stack Identified (Wappalyzer)

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

findings.remediation_brief: Ensure all identified technologies are running their latest patched versions. Remove version information from HTTP response headers where possible (e.g. ServerTokens Prod, server_tokens off). Remove unused technologies and frameworks to reduce attack surface.
findings.description: Webanalyze (Wappalyzer engine) identified the technology stack running on the target web application. Technologies detected may include web servers, application frameworks, CMS platforms, JavaScript libraries, analytics tools, CDNs, and other components. Each identified technology can be checked against known vulnerability databases for version-specific issues.
findings.impact: Technology fingerprinting reveals the exact software stack in use, enabling targeted vulnerability research. An attacker can search for CVEs, default credentials, and known misconfigurations specific to each detected technology and version. Identifying the CMS, framework, and server version narrows the attack surface to known weaknesses.

findings.title: Hidden HTTP Parameters Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Review all discovered hidden parameters for security implications. Remove any debug, test, or administrative parameters from production deployments. Ensure all accepted parameters are documented and subject to the same input validation and authorization controls as public parameters.
findings.description: arjun discovered hidden HTTP parameters that are not present in crawled forms, links, or visible page elements. These parameters are accepted by the server but not publicly advertised, potentially exposing additional attack surface for injection, authentication bypass, or information disclosure.
findings.impact: Hidden parameters may accept unexpected input that bypasses client-side validation. An attacker who discovers hidden debug, admin, or configuration parameters can probe them for injection vulnerabilities, privilege escalation, or information disclosure. These parameters are often less hardened than publicly documented ones because developers assume they are not discoverable.

findings.title: Security-Sensitive Hidden Parameter
findings.remediation_brief: Remove all debug, test, and administrative parameters from production deployments. If debug functionality is required, gate it behind strong authentication and restrict access to authorized personnel. Audit parameter names for sensitive patterns during code review.
findings.description: arjun discovered a hidden HTTP parameter with a security-sensitive name pattern (such as admin, debug, test, secret, token, key, or password). These parameters suggest debug functionality, authentication bypasses, or configuration controls that should not be accessible in production.
findings.impact: Security-sensitive hidden parameters frequently enable debug modes, expose verbose error output, bypass authentication, or reveal API keys and tokens. An attacker who discovers a 'debug=true' parameter may gain access to stack traces, internal paths, and database queries. Parameters named 'token' or 'key' may accept forged credentials.

findings.title: Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) — SSTImap Confirmed
findings.remediation_brief: Use sandboxed template engines that restrict template directives to safe operations. Never pass user input directly into template rendering functions. Use template engines' built-in auto-escaping features. If dynamic templates are required, use a strict allowlist of permitted template operations and sanitize all input before rendering.
findings.description: SSTImap confirmed that the target application is vulnerable to Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI). User-supplied input is rendered directly within a server-side template engine without proper sanitization, allowing an attacker to inject template directives that execute arbitrary code on the server.
findings.impact: A confirmed SSTI vulnerability allows full remote code execution (RCE) on the server. An attacker can read/write arbitrary files, exfiltrate database credentials, pivot to internal networks, and fully compromise the application server. SSTI is one of the highest-impact web vulnerabilities because template engines run with the full privileges of the application process.

findings.title: SSTI — Template Engine Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure the template engine is properly sandboxed with restricted directive capabilities. Verify that user input does not reach template rendering functions. Apply input sanitization and output encoding at the template layer.
findings.description: SSTImap identified the template engine in use on the target application (e.g., Jinja2, Twig, Freemarker, Mako, Velocity, Smarty) but was unable to achieve code execution. The engine may have sandboxing or input filtering that prevents exploitation, but the presence of a detectable engine suggests user input reaches the template layer.
findings.impact: Template engine identification narrows the attack surface for targeted exploitation. Even if SSTImap could not achieve RCE, manual techniques or future bypass discoveries may succeed. The detection confirms that user input interacts with the template engine, which is a prerequisite for SSTI attacks.

findings.title: OS Command Injection — commix Confirmed
findings.remediation_brief: Use parameterized OS commands or language-native APIs instead of shell execution. Never concatenate user input into shell commands. Apply strict input validation with allowlists for expected parameter values. Use subprocess calls with argument arrays instead of shell=True. Implement the principle of least privilege for the web application process.
findings.description: commix confirmed that the target application is vulnerable to OS command injection. User-supplied input is incorporated into operating system commands without proper sanitization, allowing an attacker to execute arbitrary system commands on the underlying server with the privileges of the web application process.
findings.impact: Confirmed OS command injection allows full remote code execution. An attacker can read/write files, dump databases, install backdoors, establish reverse shells, pivot to internal networks, and fully compromise the server. This is a maximum-severity vulnerability that provides complete control over the affected system.

findings.title: Blind Command Injection (Time-Based) — commix
findings.remediation_brief: Use parameterized OS commands or language-native APIs instead of shell execution. Never concatenate user input into shell commands. Apply strict input validation with allowlists. Use subprocess calls with argument arrays instead of shell=True.
findings.description: commix detected blind OS command injection via time-based techniques. The application's response time varied when time-delay payloads (e.g., sleep) were injected, indicating that user input is incorporated into operating system commands. While output is not directly reflected, the time-delay confirmation proves command execution occurs on the server.
findings.impact: Blind command injection is exploitable for full remote code execution even though command output is not returned in the response. An attacker can exfiltrate data character-by-character via time-based inference, establish out-of-band channels (DNS, HTTP callbacks), or write webshells to achieve interactive access. The impact is equivalent to confirmed command injection, with only exploitation complexity increased.

findings.title: Unkeyed Header in Cache Response
findings.remediation_brief: Include all security-relevant HTTP headers in the cache key configuration. Review cache configuration to ensure that any header whose value appears in responses is either included in the cache key or stripped before caching.
findings.description: toxicache detected that the web cache does not include a specific HTTP header in its cache key, but the header's value is reflected in the cached response. This means the header could potentially be used for cache poisoning if an exploitable reflection point is found.
findings.impact: An unkeyed header that is reflected in the response is a prerequisite for web cache poisoning. While this finding alone does not confirm exploitation, it indicates that the cache configuration does not properly account for all inputs that influence the response. This is the foundation for cache poisoning attacks that can lead to stored XSS, phishing, or defacement at scale.

findings.title: Session Token Exposed in URL
findings.remediation_brief: Transmit session tokens only via cookies (with Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite attributes) or Authorization headers. Never embed session identifiers in URL query parameters or path segments.
findings.description: Session-related parameter(s) appear in the URL query string. Tokens in URLs leak through browser history, Referer headers, proxy logs, and server access logs.
findings.impact: An attacker who obtains the URL (via Referer header, shared link, browser history, or proxy logs) gains immediate authenticated access to the victim's session without needing to compromise cookies or credentials directly.

findings.title: Session Token in Page Links
findings.remediation_brief: Remove session tokens from all hyperlinks. Use cookie-based session management exclusively. Set Referrer-Policy to no-referrer or same-origin.
findings.description: Page links embed session tokens in URL query parameters within href attributes, leaking tokens through Referer headers when users navigate to external sites.
findings.impact: Session tokens are transmitted to third-party servers via Referer headers when users click external links, allowing third parties or network observers to hijack user sessions.

findings.title: Overly Broad Cookie Domain Scope
findings.remediation_brief: Set the cookie Domain attribute to the exact hostname of the application. Avoid using parent domain cookies unless required for cross-subdomain SSO.
findings.description: Session cookies are scoped to a parent domain rather than the application's specific hostname, allowing any subdomain under the parent to read these cookies.
findings.impact: A compromised sibling application on any subdomain under the parent domain can read and replay session cookies, enabling cross-application session hijacking without attacking the target directly.

findings.title: Cookie Path Scoped to Root
findings.remediation_brief: Set the cookie Path attribute to the application's base URL path to limit cookie visibility to the application's URL space.
findings.description: Session cookies use Path=/ while the application resides at a subpath. Other applications on the same hostname can read these cookies.
findings.impact: Other applications sharing the same hostname (common in shared hosting or multi-tenant environments) can access session cookies, creating a cross-application information disclosure risk.

findings.title: JWT Algorithm None Accepted

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a strong signing algorithm (RS256, ES256) server-side. Reject tokens with alg=none. Use an allowlist of accepted algorithms.
findings.description: A JWT token uses algorithm 'none', meaning the token has no signature verification. Any attacker can forge arbitrary tokens with any claims.
findings.impact: Complete authentication bypass. An attacker can craft JWTs with arbitrary claims (admin roles, any user identity) without needing the signing key, gaining unrestricted access to all application functionality.

findings.title: JWT Missing Expiration Claim

mitre_attack.name: Use Alternate Authentication Material: Application Access Token

findings.remediation_brief: Include an 'exp' claim in all JWTs with a reasonable lifetime (15 minutes for access tokens, hours for refresh tokens). Validate expiration server-side on every request.
findings.description: A JWT token has no 'exp' (expiration) claim. Without expiration, a stolen token remains valid indefinitely.
findings.impact: A stolen or leaked JWT can be replayed indefinitely since it never expires, giving an attacker persistent unauthorized access until the signing key is rotated or the token is explicitly blacklisted.

findings.title: JWT Excessive Lifetime
findings.remediation_brief: Reduce JWT lifetime to 15-60 minutes for access tokens. Use refresh tokens for session continuity. Implement token revocation for compromised tokens.
findings.description: A JWT token has an excessively long lifetime (>24 hours). Long-lived tokens increase the window for token theft and replay attacks.
findings.impact: Extended token lifetimes give attackers a wider window to intercept, steal, and reuse tokens. If a token is compromised, the attacker maintains access for the full remaining lifetime without needing to re-authenticate.

findings.title: JWT Contains Sensitive Data
findings.owasp_api: API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization
findings.remediation_brief: Remove sensitive data from JWT payloads. Store sensitive data server-side and reference it by ID. Use JWE (encrypted JWT) if payload confidentiality is required.
findings.description: A JWT payload contains sensitive fields (passwords, SSNs, credit card numbers). JWT payloads are base64url-encoded (not encrypted) and readable by anyone with access to the token.
findings.impact: Sensitive information embedded in the JWT is exposed to anyone who intercepts the token (via logs, browser storage, network capture, or Referer headers). This is a direct data exposure vulnerability since JWTs are not encrypted by default.

findings.title: JWT Missing Audience Claim
findings.remediation_brief: Include an 'aud' claim in all JWTs identifying the intended recipient. Validate the audience server-side and reject tokens with unexpected audience values.
findings.description: A JWT token has no 'aud' (audience) claim. Without audience restriction, tokens intended for one service may be replayed against a different service that shares the same signing key.
findings.impact: Tokens can be cross-replayed between services that share signing infrastructure. An attacker with a token from a lower-privilege service can replay it against a higher-privilege service if no audience validation is performed.

findings.title: Session Persists After Password Change
aliases: Session Not Invalidated on Password Change
Password Change Does Not Revoke Sessions
findings.remediation_brief: Invalidate all existing sessions for the user when their password is changed. Force re-authentication on all devices.
findings.description: Existing sessions remain valid after a password change. If an attacker has compromised a session, changing the password does not revoke their access.
findings.impact: A user who changes their password to recover from a compromise cannot fully revoke attacker access. The compromised session persists, and the attacker retains authenticated access until natural session expiry.

findings.title: Excessive Session Cookie Lifetime
findings.remediation_brief: Set session cookie Max-Age/Expires to a reasonable duration (4-8 hours for standard apps, shorter for sensitive apps). Implement absolute server-side session timeout independent of cookie expiry.
findings.description: A session cookie has an excessively long lifetime (>30 days), increasing the window for session hijacking via stolen cookies.
findings.impact: Extremely long-lived session cookies remain valid for weeks or months, giving attackers an extended window to exploit stolen cookies. Even if the user logs out from one device, the cookie on another compromised device remains usable.

findings.title: Missing Referrer-Policy With External Links
findings.remediation_brief: Set Referrer-Policy header to 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin' or 'no-referrer' to prevent URL leakage. Apply via HTTP header or <meta> tag.
findings.description: The authenticated page contains external links but no Referrer-Policy header is set. Browsers default to sending the full URL as the Referer header when users click external links, potentially leaking session tokens or sensitive URL parameters.
findings.impact: Session tokens, CSRF tokens, or other sensitive URL parameters are transmitted to third-party servers via the Referer header when users click external links. Third parties can use leaked tokens for session hijacking.

findings.title: Mixed Content on Authenticated Page
findings.remediation_brief: Load all resources over HTTPS. Use Content-Security-Policy: upgrade-insecure-requests to automatically upgrade HTTP to HTTPS.
findings.description: The authenticated HTTPS page loads resources over plain HTTP. Mixed content allows a network attacker to inject malicious resources into the authenticated page via MITM.
findings.impact: A network-positioned attacker can modify HTTP-loaded resources (scripts, styles, images) in transit, injecting malicious content into the authenticated HTTPS page. This can lead to session hijacking, credential theft, or arbitrary code execution in the user's browser context.

findings.title: Potential Session Puzzling
findings.remediation_brief: Use separate session variables for each functional context (authentication, registration, password reset). Regenerate session IDs at each privilege boundary. Do not reuse session objects across security contexts.
findings.description: The same session cookie name is assigned different values across functionally distinct paths (login, registration, password reset, profile). This may indicate session variable overloading where authentication state from one context can be leveraged in another.
findings.impact: An attacker may exploit session puzzling to escalate privileges by initiating a session in one security context (e.g. password reset flow) and presenting it to another context (e.g. authenticated dashboard) where the session variables carry unintended authority.

findings.title: CEC Bus Devices Discoverable Without Authentication — {self.ctx.instance_key}
CEC Power State Exposed — Unauthorised Control Possible — {self.ctx.instance_key}
CEC Scan Complete — No Devices Responded — {self.ctx.instance_key}
Zigbee Device Susceptible to Flooding on {self.ctx.instance_key}
DB9 Port: No Active Protocol Detected —
Bluetooth Device Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile every discovered radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield Bluetooth interfaces that are not required.
findings.description: A Bluetooth (BR/EDR or BLE) device was detected during zero-knowledge scanning, along with its advertising data (address, address type, RSSI, name, service UUIDs, manufacturer data).
findings.impact: Confirms a live wireless attack surface and provides the address and advertised metadata needed to target every subsequent enumeration, pairing, and exploitation test.

findings.title: BLE GATT Service Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Where the GATT layout itself is sensitive, require an encrypted, bonded link before service discovery is permitted.
findings.description: The GATT server of a BLE device was enumerated without prior knowledge, revealing its services, characteristics, handles and properties (read/write/notify).
findings.impact: Discloses device function and defines the read/write/subscribe attack surface; unauthenticated enumeration is the first step toward characteristic abuse.

findings.title: Classic Bluetooth SDP Service Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Disable unused BR/EDR profiles; restrict SDP exposure and require authentication for sensitive services.
findings.description: Classic Bluetooth (BR/EDR) SDP service records were enumerated (RFCOMM/L2CAP channels, profiles such as SPP/DUN/PAN).
findings.impact: Exposed SDP records widen the BR/EDR attack surface and can reveal legacy profiles (PAN/BNEP, DUN) with their own vulnerability history.

findings.title: Static or Public Bluetooth Address — Device Trackable
findings.remediation_brief: Enable LE Privacy with frequently-rotating Resolvable Private Addresses; distribute the IRK only to bonded peers.
findings.description: The device advertises with a Public or Static-Random Bluetooth address that does not rotate, rather than a rotating Resolvable Private Address (RPA).
findings.impact: A stable address lets any passive listener track and correlate a body-worn or clinical device (and by extension a patient) across time and location, and leaks the OUI/vendor.

findings.title: Sensitive Identifier Broadcast in Advertising Data
findings.remediation_brief: Remove serials and patient identifiers from the advertised device name and manufacturer data; expose per-unit IDs only via an authenticated, bonded GATT read; consider BT 5.4 Encrypted Advertising Data.
findings.description: The device broadcasts a serial number, patient identifier, or other per-unit token in its advertising name or manufacturer-specific data, in the clear.
findings.impact: A stable unique identifier in advertising defeats address privacy (the string becomes the tracking key) and discloses asset/patient information to any passive listener in range.

findings.title: Just Works Pairing — No MITM Protection
findings.remediation_brief: Provision real IO capability and set the MITM bit (LESC Numeric Comparison or Passkey Entry); where no IO exists, use OOB pairing or an app-layer authenticated channel.
findings.description: The device negotiated Just Works pairing (SMP MITM-protection bit = 0, or an IO capability of NoInputNoOutput on either side), which provides no man-in-the-middle protection.
findings.impact: An active attacker in radio range can interpose during pairing and relay or modify the entire connection, because Just Works authenticates neither party.

findings.title: LE Legacy Pairing — Passively Decryptable
findings.remediation_brief: Require LE Secure Connections (ECDH P-256); reject SC=0 on any hardware that supports LESC (BLE 4.2+).
findings.description: The device negotiated LE Legacy pairing (SMP Secure Connections bit = 0). Legacy derives the session key from a weak Temporary Key (Just Works TK=0; Passkey Entry TK is a ~20-bit value).
findings.impact: A passively-sniffed pairing can be decrypted offline with crackle, recovering the Long-Term Key and all past and future bonded traffic for that pair.

findings.title: Static or Reused BLE Passkey
findings.remediation_brief: Use a fresh, random, per-pairing passkey that is never hard-coded, printed, or reused across units; prefer Numeric Comparison or OOB where the UI allows.
findings.description: The device authenticates LE Secure Connections pairing with a static or reused 6-digit passkey — printed on the enclosure, embedded in firmware/manual, or identical across units — rather than a fresh random per-pairing value.
findings.impact: A hard-coded or shared passkey defeats the MITM protection of LESC Passkey Entry: anyone who can read the printed/documented value can complete an authenticated man-in-the-middle relay, reducing LESC to Just Works in practice.

findings.title: Bluetooth Pairing Method Confusion
findings.remediation_brief: Pin the negotiated association model, present an unambiguous 'enter' vs 'compare' UI, and prefer OOB pairing.
findings.description: A man-in-the-middle can negotiate Numeric Comparison with one device and Passkey Entry with the other in the same ceremony; both use a 6-digit value, so the user reads the number one device shows and enters it into the other, completing a stable MITM even under LESC.
findings.impact: Defeats the highest LESC/MITM security level via the human factor (CERT VU#534195): the attacker holds a persistent interposed position while both devices report a successful pairing.

findings.title: Bluetooth Pairing Security Downgrade Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a security floor (SC=1, MITM for sensitive functions, 16-byte key) and abort pairing on any weaker offer; re-verify the negotiated level before exposing sensitive GATT.
findings.description: The device completed pairing after a forced downgrade offer (Secure Connections cleared, IO capability set to NoInputNoOutput, and/or a reduced key size), instead of aborting.
findings.impact: A device that silently accepts SC=0 / Just Works / a short key when it can support stronger security is exploitable via an active downgrade man-in-the-middle in range.

findings.title: Short Bluetooth Encryption Key Negotiated
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce a 16-byte encryption key floor and abort pairing/connection on any shorter negotiated size.
findings.description: The device negotiated a maximum encryption key size below 16 bytes (BLE floor is 7). Short keys reduce brute-force cost and are the BLE analogue of the KNOB attack.
findings.impact: A negotiated key near the 7-byte floor allows an attacker to brute-force the session key and decrypt or inject traffic.

findings.title: Bluetooth ECDH Public Key Not Validated (CVE-2018-5383)
findings.remediation_brief: Update to post-2018 firmware/OS that mandates ECDH public-key on-curve validation.
findings.description: The pairing stack does not validate the peer's ECDH public key (Y-coordinate) during Secure Simple Pairing / LE Secure Connections, allowing a fixed-coordinate invalid-curve attack.
findings.impact: An in-range MITM present during pairing can force the shared secret into a small subgroup and recover the session key (~50% per attempt, retryable), fully compromising the session.

findings.title: KNOB — Bluetooth Encryption Key Entropy Downgrade (CVE-2019-9506)
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the host to enforce a minimum encryption key entropy (>=7 octets BR/EDR, 16 for LESC) and abort shorter negotiations.
findings.description: The BR/EDR encryption key-entropy negotiation (LMP) is not integrity-protected, letting a MITM force both devices to a 1-byte (8-bit) key.
findings.impact: The reduced-entropy key is brute-forced in real time, allowing an in-range attacker with no pairing or user interaction to decrypt and inject traffic on the link.

findings.title: BLUFFS — Bluetooth Forward/Future Secrecy Weakness (CVE-2023-24023)
findings.remediation_brief: Reject low negotiated key lengths, adopt the SIG key-derivation fix, and operate in Secure Connections Only mode.
findings.description: Weaknesses in BR/EDR session-key derivation (Core Spec 4.2-5.4) permit unilateral, repeatable session-key derivation, breaking forward and future secrecy; combined with key-length downgrade it enables MITM and impersonation across sessions.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can force reuse of a weak session key, decrypting captured traffic and impersonating a device across multiple sessions.

findings.title: BIAS — Bluetooth Impersonation (CVE-2020-10135)
findings.remediation_brief: Enable Secure Connections Only mode and require mutual authentication in both directions.
findings.description: BR/EDR authentication does not mandate mutual authentication; via role-switch and SC-to-legacy downgrade an attacker impersonates a previously-paired master or slave without possessing the link key.
findings.impact: An attacker in range who knows the victim BD_ADDR can impersonate a trusted, previously-bonded device without any key material.

findings.title: BLURtooth — Cross-Transport Key Overwrite (CVE-2020-15802)
findings.remediation_brief: Apply BT 5.1 CTKD restrictions that forbid overwriting authenticated keys or downgrading key strength.
findings.description: In dual-mode devices supporting Cross-Transport Key Derivation (spec 4.2/5.0 before 5.1), an unauthenticated attacker in range can trigger CTKD to overwrite an authenticated bonding key with an unauthenticated or lower-entropy one.
findings.impact: The paired relationship can be silently weakened without user interaction, enabling MITM on a link the user believes is securely bonded.

findings.title: BLESA — BLE Reconnection Spoofing (CVE-2020-9770)
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce mandatory authenticated and encrypted reconnection before accepting any data from a previously-bonded peer.
findings.description: BLE reconnection authentication is optional and often not enforced by the client, so a central accepts spoofed data from an impersonated peripheral without re-authentication after the first bonding.
findings.impact: An attacker spoofing the peripheral BD_ADDR can feed forged data (e.g. medical telemetry) to the consuming device on reconnect, with no user interaction.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Read
findings.remediation_brief: Set encryption/authentication-required permissions on sensitive characteristics; gate PHI behind LESC-authenticated bonding.
findings.description: One or more GATT characteristics returned data over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Read Response with a value and no 0x05/0x0F/0x08 security error).
findings.impact: Any listener in range can read the exposed data with no credential; where it is PHI, telemetry, or configuration the confidentiality impact is severe.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Characteristic Write
findings.remediation_brief: Require an authenticated, encrypted, bonded link (LESC + MITM) for all writes; add application-layer authorization (signed / challenge-response commands) to control points and OTA.
findings.description: A GATT write to a device characteristic succeeded over an unpaired, unencrypted link (ATT Write Response with no security error).
findings.impact: Unauthenticated write access permits configuration change, actuation, factory reset, or firmware/OTA abuse with no credential — the highest-impact GATT finding, and safety-critical on a medical device.

findings.title: Unauthenticated GATT Notification/Indication Stream
findings.remediation_brief: Require encryption on the CCCD and its source characteristic; do not start notifications before authenticated bonding.
findings.description: On an unpaired link the device granted a large ATT MTU and started notifications/indications after a CCCD write, streaming data without authentication.
findings.impact: Sensitive telemetry or PHI is exposed to any in-range listener without pairing; a large pre-auth MTU on a sensitive stream aggravates the leak.

findings.title: SweynTooth BLE SoC Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Update the BLE controller firmware/SDK to a patched release; where the SoC is end-of-life, apply architectural mitigations (restrict pairing, disable unused profiles, physical/RF controls).
findings.description: The device's BLE System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known SweynTooth firmware vulnerabilities in the Link Layer, L2CAP, SMP or ATT (crash, deadlock, or the Telink Zero-LTK Installation security bypass).
findings.impact: Depending on the SoC and SDK version, an in-range attacker can crash or deadlock the device (DoS, may require power-cycle) or, on affected Telink parts, install an all-zero LTK for arbitrary read/write — safety-relevant per FDA/CISA advisory ICS-ALERT-20-063-01.

findings.title: BrakTooth BR/EDR SoC Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Update the Bluetooth controller firmware to a patched release; for end-of-life SoCs, disable unused profiles, restrict connectability, and apply physical/RF controls.
findings.description: The device's BR/EDR System-on-Chip belongs to a vendor/part with known BrakTooth LMP/Baseband vulnerabilities (V1-V16), ranging from crashes and deadlocks to Espressif ESP32 arbitrary code execution.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can crash, deadlock, or (on ESP32) execute code on the controller; several affected parts (e.g. TI CC2564C, Qualcomm CSR8811/8510) were 'no fix planned', leaving only architectural mitigation.

findings.title: BleedingTooth Linux BlueZ Kernel Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the kernel to 5.9+ (or vendor backport); set CONFIG_BT_HS=n to remove the A2MP path; rfkill unused radios.
findings.description: The Linux host behind the Bluetooth controller runs an unpatched BlueZ kernel (< 5.9), exposing the BleedingTooth family: BadKarma (L2CAP heap type-confusion), BadChoice (info leak), BadVibes (BLE ext-advertising heap overflow).
findings.impact: BadKarma chains to zero-click kernel remote code execution over BR/EDR from radio range; BadVibes needs only that the victim is scanning, with no BD_ADDR required.

findings.title: BlueBorne Bluetooth Stack Vulnerability Surface
findings.remediation_brief: Apply the 2017-09+ vendor security patches; disable Bluetooth when unused.
findings.description: The host Bluetooth stack (Linux BlueZ, Android, Windows, or old iOS) predates the 2017 BlueBorne patches, exposing SDP/BNEP/L2CAP flaws that require only that Bluetooth is powered on.
findings.impact: An attacker in range can achieve remote code execution or MITM with no pairing and no user interaction; 'non-discoverable' is not a mitigation because the address is recoverable by sniffing.

findings.title: LE Secure Connections Confirmed (Passively Uncrackable)
findings.remediation_brief: Maintain LESC; additionally verify per-pairing random passkeys, no debug keys, and rejection of downgrade offers.
findings.description: The device completed LE Secure Connections pairing (ECDH P-256), confirmed on the wire by the Pairing Public Key / DHKey Check PDUs and/or a crackle result of 'LE Secure Connections'.
findings.impact: Positive assurance that the session key never crosses the air and the pairing is not passively crackable; residual risk shifts to implementation flaws (static passkey, debug keys, downgrade acceptance).

findings.title: BlueSmack / L2CAP Echo Denial of Service
findings.remediation_brief: Patch the stack for input-length validation; rate-limit/throttle L2CAP echo and connection requests; make the radio non-connectable when unused.
findings.description: The device degraded or reset under a bounded L2CAP echo / l2ping flood (BlueSmack), indicating it does not bound or rate-limit oversized echo requests.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker who knows the BD_ADDR can hang or reboot the device, denying service — critical for a safety or clinical device.

findings.title: Bluetooth Connection Exhaustion / l2ping Flood
findings.remediation_brief: Rate-limit inbound connection requests, cap concurrent connections, and recover gracefully; make the radio non-connectable when idle.
findings.description: Rapid L2CAP/ACL connection opens or a sustained l2ping flood exhausted the device's connection slots, causing it to refuse or reset connections.
findings.impact: An in-range attacker can deny service to legitimate centrals by consuming all available connection resources.

findings.title: Bluetooth Link-Layer Malformed-PDU Crash
findings.remediation_brief: Update controller firmware and host stack (PDU length/format validation, buffer bounding); disable unused profiles; rate-limit.
findings.description: The device crashed or deadlocked when sent a malformed Link-Layer / HCI PDU (the generic class covering SweynTooth/BrakTooth-style firmware defects and Android BlueFrag CVE-2020-0022).
findings.impact: A malformed advertising/connect/control PDU — often broadcast with no BD_ADDR required — crashes the target and can escalate to remote code execution on vulnerable stacks.

findings.title: Bluetooth Testing SKIPPED — No Adapter or Sniffer Available
findings.remediation_brief: Attach a BlueZ adapter for active GATT/pairing work, or flash a sniffer board via Quiver (Sniffle / nRF Sniffer / ButteRFly / Ubertooth) for passive capture, then re-run the module.
findings.description: No Bluetooth adapter or sniffer was selected/available for the instance, so Bluetooth/BLE testing was not performed.
findings.impact: The Bluetooth attack surface of the device was not assessed; the absence of findings does not indicate the interface is secure.

findings.title: BLE LESC Passkey Recovered from Passive Capture
findings.remediation_brief: Use a fresh, random, single-use passkey per pairing that is never printed, hard-coded, or reused; a passkey a single sniffed pairing reveals provides no MITM protection under LESC.
findings.description: The 6-digit LE Secure Connections Passkey Entry passkey was recovered offline from a passively-captured pairing. In LESC Passkey Entry each of the 20 passkey bits is committed with f4 (AES-CMAC over the cleartext ECDH public keys, the revealed per-round nonce, and one passkey bit); once the nonce is revealed the single bit is brute-forced by matching the captured Pairing Confirm, and the recovery is confirmed independently from the initiator and responder halves.
findings.impact: An attacker who passively sniffs ONE pairing recovers the passkey with no active MITM and no physical access to the printed value. If the passkey is static or reused it authenticates every future session and every unit that shares it, collapsing LESC Passkey Entry to Just Works — full man-in-the-middle and session compromise.

findings.title: CAN Bus Frame Captured
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure CAN bus access is physically restricted. Document observed frame IDs against expected device behaviour.
findings.description: CAN bus frames were captured from the device. Frame IDs and data payloads are documented for replay and fuzzing analysis.

findings.title: CAN Bus Injected Frame Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Implement a CAN firewall or gateway. Consider SecOC (ISO 21434) for safety-critical systems. Apply physical access controls to CAN connectors.
findings.description: An injected CAN frame was accepted and processed by the device. CAN has no built-in authentication; any node on the bus can transmit arbitrary messages.

findings.title: CAN Replay Attack
findings.remediation_brief: Implement SecOC (Secure Onboard Communication, ISO 21434 / AUTOSAR) for safety-critical CAN signals to add freshness counters and message authentication codes. Apply a CAN firewall or gateway to rate-limit and filter frames by ID and frequency. Physically restrict access to OBD-II ports and CAN bus connectors. Log and alert on unexpected frame repetition patterns.
findings.description: A previously captured CAN frame was successfully replayed and accepted as a legitimate message by one or more nodes on the bus. CAN provides no built-in authentication or sequence numbering, meaning any captured frame can be retransmitted at will to reproduce an action — such as unlocking a door, disabling a safety system, or triggering an actuator — without knowledge of the originating system. This class of attack is particularly dangerous in automotive and industrial control environments where CAN commands directly affect physical state.

findings.title: ARP / DHCP Traffic Reveals Network Configuration
findings.remediation_brief: Informational — expected behaviour. Review whether observed network configuration aligns with intended design.
findings.description: Passive ARP or DHCP traffic captured during the ConfigDiscovery phase revealed network configuration details: default gateway, DNS servers, existing DHCP leases, and VLAN membership.

findings.title: Plaintext Protocol in Boot Traffic
findings.remediation_brief: Replace plaintext boot-time protocols with TLS-protected equivalents. Use HTTPS for firmware update checks, SFTP for configuration retrieval.
findings.description: Traffic captured during device boot revealed cleartext protocols (Telnet, HTTP, FTP, TFTP) carrying potentially sensitive data including configuration pulls or update checks.

findings.title: Plaintext Protocol in Shutdown Traffic
findings.remediation_brief: Review and encrypt all shutdown-phase network communication.
findings.description: Traffic captured during device shutdown contained plaintext protocol traffic, potentially including final state synchronisation or credential exchange.

findings.title: NTLM Hash Captured via Responder
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NBT-NS as described in GB-DISC-005/006. Enforce SMB signing. Implement network segmentation. Use strong, unique passwords resistant to offline cracking.
findings.description: Responder successfully captured an NTLMv1 or NTLMv2 challenge-response hash in response to a poisoned LLMNR/NBT-NS reply. The captured hash can be subjected to offline dictionary or brute-force cracking or used directly in NTLM relay attacks.

findings.title: Cleartext Credentials in Traffic Capture
findings.remediation_brief: Replace all cleartext authentication protocols with encrypted equivalents. Use TLS for web, SSH for remote management, SNMPv3 for SNMP.
findings.description: Cleartext credentials (username/password) were observed in captured network traffic. The device transmitted authentication information over an unencrypted protocol (e.g., HTTP Basic Auth, FTP, Telnet, SNMP v1/v2c).

findings.title: Cleartext Credentials Captured
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately replace the protocol in use with an encrypted equivalent: HTTPS for web services, SSH for remote administration, SFTP/FTPS for file transfer, SMTPS or SMTP with enforced STARTTLS for mail. Rotate the captured credentials and investigate whether they are reused across other systems. Conduct a broader credential reuse assessment across the environment.
findings.description: A username and password pair was observed in plaintext within captured network traffic. The credentials were transmitted over an unencrypted protocol such as HTTP Basic Authentication, FTP, Telnet, SMTP AUTH (without STARTTLS), or SNMP v1/v2c, and are fully recoverable without any cryptographic attack. Captured credentials may be valid for the target service, other systems on the network, VPN access, or cloud console login if the user has reused them.

findings.title: Live Host Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile all discovered hosts against the authorised asset inventory and investigate any unexpected or unregistered hosts.
findings.description: A host was confirmed active on the network by responding to one or more probe types (ICMP, TCP SYN, ARP, or UDP), expanding the known attack surface.

findings.title: Open Port Discovered
findings.remediation_brief: Inventory all open ports against expected service requirements; close or restrict access to ports that serve no legitimate business purpose via host-based or network firewall rules.
findings.description: A TCP or UDP port was confirmed open on the target host, indicating an exposed service that contributes to the overall network attack surface.

findings.title: Service Version Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Suppress version information where possible. Keep all identified services up to date.
findings.description: A specific software version was identified from a service banner or nmap version detection. This information can be cross-referenced against CVE databases to identify known vulnerabilities.

findings.title: DHCP Lease Assigned to Device
findings.remediation_brief: No action required; informational record.
findings.description: The device successfully obtained a DHCP lease from the gearbox DHCP server. The assigned IP address and MAC address are documented for the assessment.

findings.title: LLMNR/NBT-NS Broadcast Poisoning Possible

mitre_attack.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle: LLMNR/NBT-NS Poisoning and SMB Relay

findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR and NetBIOS-NS via Group Policy (Network > DNS Client) and enforce DNS-only name resolution across all hosts.

validation_tools.name: Responder
validation_tools.command: python3 Responder.py -I eth0 -rdwv
validation_tools.description: LLMNR/NBT-NS/MDNS poisoner that captures NTLMv1/v2 hashes from the network

validation_tools.name: CrackMapExec
validation_tools.install: pip install crackmapexec  OR  apt-get install crackmapexec
validation_tools.command:
crackmapexec smb TARGET -u '' -p ''
crackmapexec smb TARGET -u users.txt -p passwords.txt
validation_tools.description: Post-exploitation framework for Active Directory, SMB, and credential testing

validation_tools.name: Impacket
validation_tools.command:
impacket-smbclient //TARGET/share -U 'domain/user%password'
impacket-secretsdump domain/user:pass@TARGET
validation_tools.description: Python library for low-level network protocol manipulation; includes 40+ tools

validation_tools.name: hashcat
validation_tools.install: apt-get install hashcat  OR  brew install hashcat
validation_tools.command:
hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt  # MD5
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt  # NTLM
validation_tools.description: World's fastest password recovery tool — GPU-accelerated with 300+ hash types

findings.description: LLMNR and/or NBT-NS broadcast name resolution is active on the network, allowing an attacker to poison responses with Responder and capture NTLMv1/v2 hashes for offline cracking or relay.

findings.title: Discovery: Hostname Identified
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure DNS naming conventions do not disclose sensitive infrastructure details. Restrict reverse-DNS resolution (PTR records) for internal hosts from being accessible to external resolvers. Disable NetBIOS name service (NBT-NS) where not required.
findings.description: A DNS hostname or NetBIOS name was resolved for a target IP address, providing a human-readable label for the host. Hostnames frequently encode information about the device's function, location, operating system, or network segment (e.g., dc01.corp.example.com, router-dmz-01, dev-sql-server). This information reduces the attacker's reconnaissance burden by allowing service correlation without port scanning and aids in target prioritisation during an assessment.

findings.title: HDMI CEC Command Injection Accepted
findings.remediation_brief: Disable CEC in firmware if not required. Apply command filtering to reject unauthorised CEC commands.
findings.description: Injected HDMI CEC commands were accepted and processed. An attacker with HDMI port access can issue remote control commands or exploit CEC stack vulnerabilities.

findings.title: HDMI HDCP Not Enforced
findings.remediation_brief: Enable HDCP enforcement in device firmware.
findings.description: HDCP content protection is not enforced on the HDMI interface. Video/audio streams can be captured in cleartext.

findings.title: HDMI DDC-CI Unauthorised Control
findings.remediation_brief: Disable DDC-CI in display firmware if remote monitor control is not required.
findings.description: DDC-CI commands accepted over HDMI allow monitor control (brightness, OSD) without physical interaction with the display.

findings.title: EDID Information Disclosure
findings.remediation_brief: No action required if EDID is functioning normally. Consider custom EDID for high-security deployments.
findings.description: EDID data was successfully read, disclosing monitor model, serial number, manufacturer, and capabilities.

findings.title: HDMI CEC Bus Device Enumeration
findings.remediation_brief: No immediate action required if CEC is a necessary product feature. Review whether CEC device information could aid targeted attack chains and consider disabling CEC in firmware for devices where it serves no operational purpose.
findings.description: HDMI CEC bus enumeration was performed and active devices on the CEC bus were successfully identified without any authentication requirement. Discovered information includes logical and physical addresses, device type (TV, playback device, audio system), vendor OUI, and OSD name strings. While this finding is informational, it establishes the device topology and may support more targeted CEC command injection or denial-of-service attacks.

findings.title: DDC/CI Display Control Channel Accessible
findings.remediation_brief: Disable DDC/CI in display firmware or OSD settings where remote monitor control is not operationally required. Apply application-layer access controls to software DDC/CI tools (e.g., ddcutil on Linux). For high-security deployments, use video switches that do not forward DDC/CI signals.
findings.description: The DDC/CI (Display Data Channel Command Interface) channel over HDMI or DisplayPort is accessible and accepts control commands without authentication. An attacker with physical or software access to the video source can issue DDC/CI commands to adjust brightness, contrast, input selection, colour profiles, and power state of the connected display, or to read monitor asset information (MCCS capabilities). In environments with strict physical security requirements, uncontrolled display manipulation represents a tangible risk.

findings.title: LoRa Transmission Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile the transmitting radio against the authorised asset inventory; disable or shield LoRa interfaces that are not required and document expected channels/spreading factors.
findings.description: LoRa radio transmissions were captured on the device's regional ISM band (433/868/915 MHz) during passive scanning, including frame count and observed MHDR MType(s).
findings.impact: Confirms a live LoRa wireless attack surface and provides the frames needed to target the subsequent LoRaWAN activation, key, replay, and payload tests.

findings.title: LoRaWAN Network Traffic Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Confirm the LoRaWAN deployment is authorised and inventoried; ensure the network server enforces monotonic frame counters and secure join handling.
findings.description: LoRaWAN protocol traffic (Join and/or MAC data frames identifiable by their MHDR/FHDR structure and DevAddr) was identified in the passive capture.
