findings.description: No DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) selector was discoverable for the target domain. Without DKIM, email authentication is weaker and phishing risk increases.

findings.title: Breached Email Address Found
findings.remediation_brief: Notify affected employees. Force password resets for all affected accounts. Enable MFA. Review whether compromised accounts have access to sensitive systems.
findings.description: An email address associated with the target organisation appeared in a known data breach (HIBP or Dehashed). The account holder's credentials may have been exposed.
findings.impact: Email addresses found in breach databases indicate that associated passwords may be available to attackers. Credential reuse across services means these compromised credentials may grant access to the organization's systems.

findings.title: Plaintext Credential Found in Breach Database
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately force a password reset for the affected account. Check for reuse across other systems (VPN, cloud consoles, O365). Enable MFA on all accounts.
findings.description: A plaintext or reversibly hashed password was found in a breach database (Dehashed) for a target-domain email address. Direct account compromise may be possible.
findings.impact: Plaintext credentials from data breaches provide direct access if the user has reused passwords across services. This represents an immediate, exploitable risk requiring urgent password reset and multi-factor authentication enforcement.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Github Secret / API Key
findings.remediation_brief: Revoke the exposed secret immediately. Rotate all affected credentials. Scrub the secret from git history (git filter-repo). Enable GitHub secret scanning alerts.
findings.description: GitDorker or TruffleHog identified a secret, API key, token, or private key in a public GitHub repository associated with the target organisation or its employees.

findings.title: M365 Valid User Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Enable account lockout and smart lockout in Azure AD. Implement Conditional Access policies. Consider disabling legacy authentication protocols.
findings.description: TREVORspray or Azure AD authentication confirmed that a discovered email address is a valid M365/Azure AD account (user exists in the tenant). Confirms the account is a viable spray target.

findings.title: M365 Valid Credential Found (Credential Spray Success)
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately revoke the session, reset the password, and enable MFA for the compromised account. Investigate access logs for lateral movement. Review Conditional Access policies.
findings.description: TREVORspray successfully authenticated to M365/Azure AD with a discovered credential. Full account access to Microsoft cloud services may be available to an attacker.

findings.title: Subdomain Takeover Risk
findings.remediation_brief: Remove the dangling DNS record immediately. If the external service is still needed, reclaim the resource. Implement subdomain monitoring.
findings.description: A subdomain has a CNAME pointing to an external service (e.g., GitHub Pages, S3, Heroku, Shopify) that is no longer claimed. An attacker could register the resource and serve malicious content under the organisation's subdomain.

findings.title: Employee Email Address Harvested

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Educate employees on minimising personal information exposure. Implement email security controls (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, anti-phishing).

findings.description: An employee email address was discovered via theHarvester, Hunter.io, LinkedIn, or public sources. Collected addresses support phishing and credential spray attacks.

findings.title: Web Technology Fingerprint
findings.remediation_brief: Remove version disclosure from HTTP headers (Server, X-Powered-By). Keep software up to date. Consider a WAF to obscure fingerprinting.
findings.description: The technology stack of a live host was identified (Wappalyzer, httpx, whatweb): CMS, web framework, server software, JavaScript libraries, CDN providers. Helps attackers target known vulnerabilities.
findings.impact: Technology fingerprints reveal the application stack, framework versions, and third-party components. An attacker uses this to target version-specific vulnerabilities and narrow exploit selection to applicable attack vectors.

findings.title: Wayback Machine URL with Sensitive Path
aliases: Information Disclosure: Internal Server Directory Structure
Wayback Machine URL with Sensitive Path
findings.remediation_brief: Verify whether the resource still exists. Remove sensitive files from public-facing web roots. Review server access logs for recent access to these paths.
findings.description: waybackurls or xurlfind3r discovered a historical URL containing a sensitive path (e.g., /admin, /backup, /.env, /config, /api/v1/keys) that was once publicly accessible.

findings.title: Shodan Exposure — Open Service
findings.remediation_brief: Restrict access to services that do not need to be publicly reachable. Apply firewall rules. Update exposed services to current versions.
findings.description: Shodan reports an open service on a target IP that is visible to the public internet. Banner data, software version, and service type are indexed and searchable by anyone.
findings.impact: Shodan-indexed services are visible to any internet user and often reveal version strings, default pages, and configuration details. Attackers routinely search Shodan for exposed services matching known vulnerable versions.

findings.title: Shodan Exposure — Known CVE on Service
findings.remediation_brief: Patch or update the affected service immediately. If patching is not immediately possible, apply mitigating controls (WAF rule, network restriction).
findings.description: Shodan has associated one or more CVEs with a service running on a target IP based on the service banner and version string. A known public exploit may exist.
findings.impact: Shodan-indexed services are visible to any internet user and often reveal version strings, default pages, and configuration details. Attackers routinely search Shodan for exposed services matching known vulnerable versions.

findings.title: Cloud Storage Bucket Found
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately set the bucket to private unless public access is intentional. Audit bucket contents for sensitive data. Enable bucket access logging and alerts.
findings.description: cloud_enum or manual enumeration discovered a publicly accessible cloud storage bucket (AWS S3, Azure Blob, GCP Storage) associated with the target. It may contain sensitive files.

findings.title: Certificate Transparency Log Entry
findings.remediation_brief: No direct remediation required. Review disclosed subdomains for unintended exposure. Consider certificate issuance monitoring for your domain.
findings.description: A certificate was found in CT logs (crt.sh, Certspotter, Facebook CT) for the target domain. The SAN/CN reveals subdomain names that may not be otherwise discoverable.
findings.impact: Certificate Transparency logs reveal all certificates ever issued for the domain, exposing subdomain naming patterns, internal service names, and historical infrastructure that may still be accessible.

findings.title: ASN / IP Range Identified

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: No immediate action required. Ensure only intended IP ranges are associated with the organisation's ASN. Review WHOIS/ARIN records for accuracy.

findings.title: WHOIS Data Exposure
findings.remediation_brief: Enable WHOIS privacy protection through your registrar for domains where registrant PII should not be public.
findings.description: WHOIS records for the target domain revealed registrant contact details, nameserver names, registrar information, and registration dates. This information aids in phishing and social engineering.
findings.impact: WHOIS records may reveal registrant names, email addresses, phone numbers, and physical addresses of domain administrators. This personally identifiable information enables targeted social engineering against infrastructure personnel.

findings.title: LinkedIn Employee Profile Enumerated
findings.remediation_brief: Educate staff on LinkedIn exposure. Implement strict email security (DMARC p=reject). Train employees to recognise spear-phishing.
findings.description: Employee names, titles, and organisational roles were enumerated from LinkedIn. This information supports spear-phishing, social engineering, and targeted credential spray attacks.

findings.title: Social Media Profile Linked to Employee
findings.remediation_brief: Assess employee privacy settings. Provide training on personal operational security.
findings.description: maigret discovered social media profiles (Twitter, GitHub, Reddit, etc.) linked to an employee username derived from their email address. May reveal personal information useful for social engineering.

findings.title: Sensitive File Found via Web Crawler
findings.remediation_brief: Remove the file from the web root immediately. Audit web server directory listings. Restrict access to backup and config files via .htaccess or server config.
findings.description: katana or xurlfind3r discovered a publicly accessible file containing potentially sensitive data: backup archives (.zip, .bak), configuration files (.env, .config), log files, or database dumps.

findings.title: HTTP Security Headers Missing
findings.remediation_brief: Add security headers to web server or application configuration. Verify with securityheaders.com.
findings.description: httpx detected missing security headers on a live host: Content-Security-Policy, X-Frame-Options, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options, or Referrer-Policy.

findings.title: Uncover / Internet-Wide Scan Engine Match
findings.remediation_brief: Review all indexed services. Remove unnecessary public exposure. Ensure indexed software versions are patched and up to date.
findings.description: The uncover tool found the target in internet-wide scan engine results (Shodan, Censys, FOFA, Quake360, ZoomEye, CriminalIP). Services and their versions are publicly catalogued.

findings.title: Wildcard DNS Record Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Remove wildcard records unless they serve a specific purpose. Document and review all subdomains that rely on wildcard resolution.

findings.title: Discovery: Email Address

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Educate employees on minimising professional email exposure in public contexts. Implement robust email security controls including SPF, DKIM, and DMARC at p=reject. Enable anti-phishing and impersonation protection in the email gateway. Monitor for credential spray activity against cloud identity providers.
findings.description: One or more email addresses associated with the target organisation or its employees were harvested during OSINT enumeration using tools such as theHarvester, Hunter.io, or Phonebook.cz. Exposed email addresses directly enable phishing campaigns, password spray attacks against cloud identity platforms (M365, Google Workspace), and account enumeration. Even a single valid address provides an attacker with a confirmed naming convention from which to infer additional accounts.
findings.impact: Harvested email addresses enable targeted phishing, credential stuffing against SSO portals, and username enumeration. Email naming conventions reveal the format used for all employees, allowing generation of valid email addresses for the entire organization.

findings.title: Discovery: IP Address

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Reconcile all discovered IP addresses against the authorised asset inventory. Ensure cloud-hosted instances are protected by security groups or firewall rules limiting unnecessary public exposure. Review whether any discovered IPs host unintended or forgotten services.
findings.description: One or more IP addresses were mapped to the target organisation's assets through DNS resolution, certificate transparency log analysis, ASN enumeration, WHOIS records, or OSINT sources. Confirmed IP addresses expand the known attack surface beyond the primary domain, enabling direct host scanning, service fingerprinting, and identification of infrastructure not protected by a CDN or application-layer proxy.

findings.title: Information Disclosure: Internal Server Directory Structure
aliases: Information Disclosure: Internal Server Directory Structure
Wayback Machine URL with Sensitive Path
findings.remediation_brief: Configure the web application to display generic error pages rather than stack traces or exception details in production. Suppress server-side path information from HTTP response headers and application output. Review Wayback Machine archives for pages that previously revealed directory structure and ensure those resources are no longer publicly accessible.
findings.description: Internal filesystem path components were found exposed in publicly accessible sources, including HTTP response bodies, error messages, stack traces, application comments, or historical Wayback Machine snapshots. Exposed paths such as /var/www/app/releases/20231105/, C:\inetpub\wwwroot\api\, or /home/deploy/app/ reveal the server's operating system, directory layout, deployment tooling, and technology stack. This information assists attackers in crafting targeted local file inclusion, path traversal, or directory brute-force payloads.

findings.title: Phone Number Pattern Spotted
findings.remediation_brief: Review whether the exposed telephone number serves a legitimate public-facing business purpose (e.g., a sales or support line). For internal or employee numbers, remove them from public web properties. Conduct security awareness training focused on social engineering and vishing recognition.
findings.description: A pattern matching a telephone number (e.g., +1-555-867-5309, (800) 123-4567) was identified in publicly accessible web content associated with the target domain. Exposed phone numbers can be used to conduct vishing (voice phishing) attacks impersonating employees or IT support, to enumerate internal organisational structure, or to harvest contact information for social engineering campaigns targeting staff.
findings.impact: Discovered phone numbers enable vishing (voice phishing) and SMS-based social engineering attacks. Combined with employee names and roles from other OSINT sources, phone numbers allow targeted pretexting calls that bypass email security controls entirely.

findings.title: Potential PII Pattern — Social Security Number Format Detected
aliases: Potential PII Pattern — Social Security Number Format Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Immediately investigate whether the detected values are real SSNs or test data. If real, initiate incident response per your breach notification obligations (HIPAA, state data breach laws). Remove the file or page containing the data from public access. Implement data loss prevention (DLP) scanning to detect SSN-format strings in web application output and source code repositories. Conduct a broader audit of publicly accessible content for additional PII exposure.
findings.description: Content matching the US Social Security Number format (XXX-XX-XXXX, nine digits with specific separators) was identified in publicly accessible content associated with the target domain or organisation. Exposure of SSN-format data in a publicly reachable location constitutes a potential data breach under US federal and state regulations (HIPAA, state breach notification laws, FTC Act). Even if the values are synthetic or test data, their public exposure indicates a failure in data classification and handling controls.

findings.title: DNS: DMARC record found
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure DMARC policy is set to 'reject' (p=reject) for maximum protection against email spoofing. Configure aggregate and forensic reporting endpoints to monitor policy violations.
findings.description: A DMARC (Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting and Conformance) record was found for the domain. DMARC instructs receiving mail servers on how to handle messages that fail SPF and DKIM validation checks.
findings.impact: A properly configured DMARC record instructs receiving mail servers to reject or quarantine spoofed emails. While this is a positive security control, the DMARC policy details reveal the organization's email authentication architecture and reporting endpoints, which inform phishing campaign design.

findings.title: DNS: Missing CAA Record
findings.remediation_brief: Add a CAA DNS record specifying the authorized certificate authorities for the domain. Example: 'example.com. IN CAA 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"'. This prevents unauthorized CAs from issuing certificates.
findings.description: No Certificate Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS record was found for the domain. CAA records restrict which certificate authorities are permitted to issue certificates for the domain.
findings.impact: Without a CAA record, any certificate authority worldwide can issue certificates for this domain. An attacker who compromises or social-engineers a less-secure CA can obtain a trusted certificate, enabling undetectable man-in-the-middle attacks against the organization's users and services.

findings.title: nslookup forward lookup: {record_summary}

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Review DNS records for unnecessary information disclosure. Ensure SPF, DKIM, and DMARC are properly configured. Consider restricting zone transfers and minimizing publicly exposed DNS records.
findings.description: Forward DNS lookup enumeration was performed, revealing mail exchange (MX), name server (NS), text (TXT), and other DNS records for the domain.
findings.impact: DNS record enumeration reveals mail servers, nameservers, SPF policies, and other infrastructure details that map the organization's digital footprint. An attacker uses this data to identify email providers, hosting relationships, and security mechanisms that inform subsequent attack phases.

findings.title: Typosquatting Domain Detected
findings.remediation_brief: Monitor for typosquatting domains using automated tools (dnstwist). Consider registering common misspellings of the domain proactively. Implement DMARC to prevent spoofed emails from look-alike domains. Establish a domain takedown process with registrars.
findings.description: One or more domains visually or typographically similar to the target domain were detected with active DNS resolution, indicating potential typosquatting infrastructure.
findings.impact: Typosquatting domains that resolve to active infrastructure can be used for phishing, credential harvesting, or malware distribution targeting the organization's users and customers. An attacker registers domains visually similar to the legitimate domain to intercept mistyped URLs or craft convincing phishing campaigns.

findings.title: DNS: A Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Minimize unnecessary A records. Use CDN or proxy services to obscure origin server IPs where appropriate.
findings.description: A record maps a domain to an IPv4 address, revealing the IP infrastructure behind a hostname.
findings.impact: Exposing A records allows attackers to identify hosting providers, colocated services, and network topology for targeted attacks.

findings.title: DNS: AAAA Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Ensure IPv6 hosts have equivalent security controls to IPv4. Remove AAAA records for services not intentionally dual-stacked.
findings.description: AAAA record maps a domain to an IPv6 address, revealing dual-stack infrastructure.
findings.impact: IPv6 records can expose additional attack surface on hosts that may have different firewall rules or monitoring than their IPv4 counterparts.

findings.title: DNS: MX Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Ensure MX records point only to authorized mail servers. Implement SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. Remove MX records for domains that do not send or receive email.
findings.description: MX record identifies the mail servers responsible for accepting email for the domain.
findings.impact: Attackers use MX records to identify email infrastructure, target mail servers for exploitation, and craft phishing campaigns that mimic legitimate mail routing.

findings.title: DNS: NS Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Use reputable DNS providers with DNSSEC support. Restrict zone transfers to authorized secondaries. Monitor for unauthorized NS record changes.
findings.description: NS record identifies the authoritative nameservers for the domain.
findings.impact: Knowledge of nameservers enables DNS cache poisoning attempts, zone transfer attacks, and helps map the organization's DNS infrastructure and hosting relationships.

findings.title: DNS: TXT Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Audit TXT records regularly. Remove obsolete verification tokens. Ensure SPF records use restrictive policies (-all). Implement DKIM and DMARC.
findings.description: TXT records contain arbitrary text data including SPF policies, DKIM keys, domain verification tokens, and service configuration.
findings.impact: TXT records can leak internal service configurations, reveal third-party integrations (Google Workspace, Microsoft 365, etc.), and expose verification tokens that may enable service takeover.

findings.title: DNS: SOA Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Ensure SOA contact email does not expose internal personnel. Use reasonable TTL and refresh values.
findings.description: SOA record contains the primary nameserver, responsible party email, and zone serial/refresh parameters.
findings.impact: SOA records reveal the primary DNS administrator's contact, zone update frequency, and infrastructure details useful for social engineering and timing attacks around zone refreshes.

findings.title: DNS: CNAME Record

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: DNS/Passive DNS

findings.remediation_brief: Regularly audit CNAME records for dangling references. Remove CNAMEs pointing to decommissioned services to prevent subdomain takeover.
findings.description: CNAME record creates an alias from one domain to another canonical name.
findings.impact: CNAME records can reveal internal naming conventions, third-party service dependencies, and may be vulnerable to subdomain takeover if the canonical target is decommissioned.

findings.title: GitHub Actions: Workflow Injection Vulnerability

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

findings.remediation_brief: Use intermediate environment variables instead of direct expression substitution in workflow run steps. Replace ${{ github.event.issue.title }} with an env: block that assigns the value to an environment variable, then reference the variable in the script. Use actions/github-script with the github context object instead of shell interpolation.
findings.description: gato identified a GitHub Actions workflow that uses unsanitized expression substitution (${{ }}) with attacker-controlled input (such as issue titles, PR bodies, or commit messages). This allows an attacker to inject arbitrary code that executes in the workflow runner context.
findings.impact: Workflow injection allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code in the CI/CD environment. This can lead to secret exfiltration (GitHub tokens, deployment keys, API credentials), supply chain compromise (modifying build artifacts), lateral movement to other repositories, and persistent access via self-hosted runner compromise.

findings.title: GitHub Actions: Secret Exfiltration Path

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

findings.remediation_brief: Restrict secrets to specific jobs using environment-level scoping. Use OIDC tokens instead of long-lived credentials for cloud authentication. Require approval for workflows triggered by external contributors. Avoid passing secrets to steps that handle untrusted input.
findings.description: gato identified a workflow configuration where secrets are accessible to jobs or steps that process untrusted input. An attacker who can trigger the workflow (via PR, issue, or fork) may be able to exfiltrate secrets through environment variables, workflow artifacts, or out-of-band channels.
findings.impact: Secret exfiltration from CI/CD pipelines can expose deployment credentials, cloud provider keys, signing certificates, and API tokens. Compromised secrets enable lateral movement to production environments, supply chain attacks via signed releases, and persistent access to organizational infrastructure.

findings.title: GitHub Actions: Overly Permissive Permissions
findings.remediation_brief: Apply least-privilege permissions to all workflows. Use the permissions: key at the workflow or job level to request only required scopes (e.g., contents: read, issues: write). Avoid write-all or admin permissions.
findings.description: gato identified a GitHub Actions workflow with overly permissive GITHUB_TOKEN permissions (such as write-all, admin, or contents: write). Workflows should follow the principle of least privilege and request only the minimum permissions required for their function.
findings.impact: Overly permissive workflow tokens increase the blast radius if the workflow is compromised. A write-all token can modify repository contents, create releases, manage issues/PRs, push to protected branches, and modify repository settings. If combined with a workflow injection, an attacker gains full repository control.

findings.title: GitHub Actions: Self-Hosted Runner Risk
aliases: GitHub Actions Runner on Public Repo

mitre_attack.name: Supply Chain Compromise: Compromise Software Supply Chain

findings.remediation_brief: Use ephemeral/disposable runners for public repositories. Restrict self-hosted runners to private repos only. If self-hosted runners must be used on public repos, enable the 'Require approval for all outside collaborators' setting and use separate runner groups with restricted repository access.
findings.description: gato identified self-hosted GitHub Actions runners configured on a public repository. Self-hosted runners in public repos are dangerous because any user can submit a pull request that triggers a workflow run on the runner, potentially executing arbitrary code in the organization's infrastructure.
findings.impact: Self-hosted runners on public repos allow any GitHub user to execute code on the organization's infrastructure by submitting a crafted pull request. This can lead to lateral movement into internal networks, credential theft from the runner environment, persistence via runner modification, and access to other repositories that share the same runner group.

findings.title: GitHub Actions: Audit Complete — No Issues
findings.remediation_brief: No remediation required. Continue to audit workflows periodically, especially when new workflows are added or existing ones are modified.
findings.description: gato completed a security audit of the target organization's GitHub Actions workflows and found no injection vulnerabilities, secret exfiltration paths, excessive permissions, or self-hosted runner risks.
findings.impact: No security issues were identified in the GitHub Actions configuration. This is a positive finding indicating that CI/CD workflows follow security best practices for the areas audited.

findings.title: CDN/WAF Bypass: Origin IP Exposed

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Restrict the origin server firewall to accept connections only from CDN/WAF edge IP ranges. Use the CDN provider's published IP lists (e.g., Cloudflare IPs, AWS CloudFront IPs) in firewall rules. Block all direct access to the origin from non-CDN sources. Consider using authenticated origin pulls (mTLS between CDN and origin).
findings.description: hakoriginfinder discovered the origin server IP address behind the CDN/WAF. The origin IP responds to HTTP requests directly, bypassing all CDN/WAF protections (rate limiting, DDoS mitigation, WAF rules, geo-blocking, bot detection). The origin was confirmed by matching response characteristics to the target domain.
findings.impact: Direct access to the origin server bypasses all CDN/WAF security controls. An attacker can launch DDoS attacks directly against the origin, exploit web application vulnerabilities without WAF interference, bypass rate limiting and bot detection, and circumvent geo-blocking or IP-based access controls. The origin server may also expose internal services or management interfaces not intended to be publicly accessible.

findings.title: CDN/WAF Bypass: Potential Origin IP

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Network Information: IP Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Verify whether this IP is the actual origin server. If confirmed, restrict its firewall to accept connections only from CDN edge IPs. If it is a staging or development server, ensure it is not publicly accessible.
findings.description: hakoriginfinder identified an IP address that may be the origin server behind the CDN/WAF. The IP responded to HTTP requests with content that partially matches the target domain (e.g., 2xx/3xx status code with related content). Further verification is needed to confirm this is the actual origin.
findings.impact: If this IP is confirmed as the origin server, an attacker can bypass all CDN/WAF protections. Even as a candidate, it reveals infrastructure information that narrows the attack surface and may identify related services, staging environments, or development servers.

findings.title: CDN/WAF Bypass: No Origin Exposure
findings.remediation_brief: No remediation required. Continue to ensure origin server firewall restricts access to CDN edge IPs only.
findings.description: hakoriginfinder scanned for the origin server IP behind the CDN/WAF and found no exposed origin IPs. The CDN/WAF appears to properly protect the origin server from direct access.
findings.impact: The CDN/WAF is correctly protecting the origin server. No direct access paths were discovered during the scan.

findings.title: Historical Endpoints Discovered

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases

findings.remediation_brief: Review discovered endpoints and remove or restrict access to any that should not be publicly accessible. Implement proper authentication and authorization controls on all endpoints.
findings.description: waymore discovered historical endpoints for the target domain across multiple web archive sources (Wayback Machine, Common Crawl, VirusTotal, URLScan.io, AlienVault OTX). These URLs represent the domain's historical web presence and may include endpoints that are no longer publicly linked but still accessible.
findings.impact: Historical endpoints can reveal previously accessible admin panels, configuration pages, backup files, development endpoints, and API routes. Even if removed from the current site, these endpoints may still respond to requests. Archived URLs also reveal the application's evolution, naming conventions, and internal structure.

findings.title: Sensitive Historical URL Discovered

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases

findings.remediation_brief: Remove sensitive endpoints from production. Add authentication to admin panels. Delete backup and configuration files from web-accessible directories. Disable debug/install/setup endpoints in production. Request removal of sensitive cached pages from web archives where possible.
findings.description: waymore discovered historical URLs matching security-sensitive patterns (admin, config, debug, backup, test, internal, setup, install, phpinfo, .env, wp-admin, phpmyadmin) in web archive data. These URLs may indicate administrative interfaces, configuration files, or backup resources that were previously accessible and may still respond to requests.
findings.impact: Sensitive historical URLs may reveal admin panels that still respond, configuration files with credentials, database backups, installation wizards that can be replayed, debug pages with verbose error output, and internal API documentation. These represent high-value targets for an attacker who can access them directly.

findings.title: Historical API Endpoint

mitre_attack.name: Search Open Technical Databases: Scan Databases

findings.remediation_brief: Decommission deprecated API versions. Ensure all API endpoints require proper authentication and authorization. Maintain an up-to-date API inventory and remove endpoints that are no longer needed.
findings.description: waymore discovered API endpoints in web archive data (/api/, /v1/, /v2/, /graphql, /rest/, /ws/, /webhook). These endpoints may represent current or deprecated API surfaces that can be probed for authentication bypasses, information disclosure, or injection vulnerabilities.
findings.impact: Historical API endpoints reveal the application's API structure, versioning scheme, and endpoint naming conventions. Deprecated API versions may lack security controls applied to current versions. API endpoints are high-value targets for authentication bypass, injection, and data exfiltration.

findings.title: Document Metadata: Internal Username Leaked

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Employee Names
Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

findings.remediation_brief: Strip metadata from all documents before publishing. Use document management policies that automatically remove Author, Creator, and other identifying metadata fields. Configure document creation tools to use generic or organizational names instead of personal usernames.
findings.description: exiftool extracted an internal username from the Author or Creator metadata field of a publicly accessible document. This username may correspond to an internal Active Directory account, email address, or application login credential.
findings.impact: Leaked usernames enable targeted phishing, credential stuffing, and password spraying attacks. Internal usernames often follow predictable patterns (first.last, flast) that allow enumeration of additional accounts. Combined with other OSINT, usernames can be used for social engineering or to identify high-value targets (executives, administrators).

findings.title: Document Metadata: Software Version Disclosed

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

findings.remediation_brief: Strip metadata from documents before publishing. This is informational and does not require urgent remediation.
findings.description: exiftool extracted the software name and version from the Creator or Producer metadata field of a publicly accessible document. This reveals the specific applications used to create or modify the document, including version numbers that may be checked against known vulnerability databases.
findings.impact: Software version disclosure enables targeted vulnerability research. An attacker who knows the exact version of Microsoft Office, Adobe Acrobat, or other document creation tools can search for version-specific CVEs, craft targeted exploits, and identify outdated software that may be vulnerable to known attacks.

findings.title: Document Metadata: Internal File Path Leaked

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Host Information: Client Configurations

findings.remediation_brief: Strip metadata from all documents before publishing. Use metadata removal tools (exiftool -all=, mat2) as part of the document publishing workflow. Configure document templates to avoid embedding local file paths.
findings.description: exiftool extracted an internal file system path (such as C:\Users\jsmith\Documents\... or /home/admin/reports/...) from a publicly accessible document's metadata. This reveals the internal directory structure, operating system, and potentially the username of the document creator.
findings.impact: Internal file paths reveal the organization's operating system, directory structure, username conventions, and internal project names. This information assists in crafting targeted phishing payloads, identifying high-value targets, and planning post-exploitation activities. Path structures can also reveal development vs. production environments.

findings.title: Document Metadata: Email Address Leaked

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Identity Information: Email Addresses

findings.remediation_brief: Strip metadata from documents before publishing. This is informational — email addresses may already be publicly available through other channels.
findings.description: exiftool extracted an email address from the metadata of a publicly accessible document. This email may belong to the document's author, reviewer, or the organization's document management system.
findings.impact: Email addresses extracted from document metadata can be used for targeted phishing, social engineering, and email-based attacks. They may also reveal internal email naming conventions that allow enumeration of additional email addresses across the organization.

findings.title: Document Metadata: GPS Coordinates Leaked

mitre_attack.name: Gather Victim Org Information: Determine Physical Locations

findings.remediation_brief: Strip EXIF GPS data from all images and documents before publishing. Configure mobile devices and cameras to disable GPS tagging. Use metadata removal tools (exiftool -gps:all=, mat2) as part of the content publishing workflow.
findings.description: exiftool extracted GPS coordinates from the EXIF metadata of a publicly accessible image or document. This reveals the physical location where the photo was taken or the document was created, which may include office locations, employee residences, or sensitive facility coordinates.
findings.impact: GPS coordinates in publicly accessible documents can reveal office locations, data center addresses, employee home locations, and other sensitive physical locations. This information enables physical surveillance, social engineering, and targeted attacks against specific facilities. For individuals, leaked GPS data from personal photos represents a privacy violation.

findings.title: Document Metadata: Audit Summary
findings.remediation_brief: Review individual document metadata findings for specific remediation actions. Implement organization-wide metadata stripping policies for all publicly published documents.
findings.description: exiftool completed a metadata audit of publicly accessible documents found during reconnaissance. This finding summarizes the total number of documents analyzed, metadata fields extracted, and categories of information discovered across all scanned documents.
findings.impact: This is a summary finding providing an overview of the document metadata analysis. Individual findings for specific metadata disclosures (usernames, software versions, file paths, GPS data) are reported separately.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — Task Hijack via {strategy}
aliases: AI Task Abandonment via Prompt Injection
findings.remediation_brief: Strip or sanitise all file metadata before including it in the LLM context. Enforce a fixed system prompt that explicitly forbids instruction overrides from file content. Process file content in a separate, sandboxed context from system instructions. Validate AI output against expected format/schema — flag responses containing unexpected tokens or format deviations.
findings.description: The AI pipeline abandoned its primary task entirely when processing a file containing an injected instruction in its metadata, text layer, or audio content. The AI's response contained only the injected canary token, confirming the model followed the adversarial instruction instead of performing its assigned function (transcription, classification, summarisation, etc.).
findings.impact: An attacker can embed instructions in files submitted to the AI pipeline that completely override the model's intended behaviour. This enables arbitrary output manipulation — the AI can be made to produce any attacker-chosen text, leak system prompts, or return fabricated classifications. In production pipelines processing documents, images, or audio, this means an attacker controls what downstream consumers (dashboards, databases, compliance workflows) receive as AI output.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — Prefix Inject via {strategy}
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce strict output schema validation — reject responses that do not match the expected format. Implement input sanitisation to strip embedded instructions from file metadata and text layers before LLM ingestion. Use delimiter-based prompt architecture to clearly separate system instructions from user/file content.
findings.description: The AI pipeline completed its primary task but also followed an injected instruction to prefix its output with an attacker-controlled token. The response contains both the expected task output and the injected canary, indicating the model treated the embedded instruction as authoritative alongside its system prompt.
findings.impact: An attacker can inject arbitrary prefixes or annotations into AI pipeline output without fully disrupting the primary task. This partial injection is exploitable for output tagging attacks (injecting misleading classification labels), cache poisoning (injected prefixes propagate through cached results), and trust boundary violations (downstream systems may parse the prefix as metadata).

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — Classify Override via {strategy}
findings.remediation_brief: Never allow file content to influence the classification decision prompt. Use a two-stage pipeline: extract content in a sandboxed context, then classify the extracted content with a separate prompt that cannot receive user-injected instructions. Validate classifications against a known-good label set.
findings.description: The AI pipeline returned an attacker-controlled classification label instead of performing genuine content analysis. The injected instruction directed the model to output a specific category, and the model complied — either abandoning its own classification (CRITICAL) or appending the injected label alongside its real output (HIGH).
findings.impact: An attacker can force arbitrary classification labels on submitted content, bypassing the AI's actual analysis. In document processing pipelines, this enables content to be misclassified (e.g. malware marked as benign, non-compliant documents marked as compliant, spam marked as legitimate). This directly undermines any automated decision-making that depends on the AI's classification output.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — System Probe via {strategy}
findings.remediation_brief: Never include sensitive credentials or internal URLs in system prompts. Implement output filtering to detect and block responses that contain system prompt fragments. Use instruction hierarchy (system > user > tool) enforcement so file content cannot override system-level instructions. Monitor for anomalous response patterns indicating prompt extraction attempts.
findings.description: The AI pipeline disclosed its system prompt or internal configuration in response to an injected instruction embedded in file metadata or content. The injected payload directed the model to reveal its operating instructions, and the canary token's presence in the response confirms the model attempted to comply.
findings.impact: System prompt leakage reveals the AI pipeline's internal logic, guardrails, classification rules, and potentially sensitive configuration details to an attacker. This information enables targeted follow-up attacks — an attacker who knows the system prompt can craft payloads specifically designed to bypass its guardrails. System prompts may also contain API keys, internal endpoint URLs, or business logic that should remain confidential.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — Authority Claim via {strategy}
findings.remediation_brief: Implement strict instruction hierarchy — the model must never accept authority claims from file content. Use architectural separation: system instructions arrive through a trusted channel (API system role), while file content is clearly demarcated as untrusted user input. Train or fine-tune models to recognise and reject authority claim patterns in user content.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction that claimed special authority (e.g. 'AUTHORIZED EVALUATOR', 'ADMIN OVERRIDE', 'SECURITY TEST IN PROGRESS'). The model treated the claimed role as legitimate and executed the embedded instruction, confirming it does not validate the provenance of instructions embedded in file content.
findings.impact: An attacker can invoke claimed authority roles within file content to bypass AI guardrails. The model's failure to distinguish between legitimate system instructions and authority claims embedded in user-submitted content means any attacker can escalate their privilege level within the AI's decision framework by simply asserting a role. This undermines all role-based access controls in the AI pipeline.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {strategy} (Partial Injection)
findings.remediation_brief: Implement output schema validation that rejects responses deviating from the expected format. Strip all metadata and embedded instructions from file content before LLM ingestion. Deploy anomaly detection on AI output to flag unexpected tokens or patterns.
findings.description: The AI pipeline completed its primary task but also followed the injected instruction — the canary token appeared in the response alongside legitimate task output. This indicates the model treated the embedded instruction as a secondary directive, executing it in addition to (rather than instead of) its assigned task.
findings.impact: Partial injection is more dangerous than full hijack in production contexts because it may go undetected — the pipeline still produces plausible-looking output while also executing attacker instructions. This enables data exfiltration (canary confirms the model reads and acts on embedded content), output poisoning (injected content mixed into legitimate results), and supply chain attacks (downstream consumers receive tainted output that appears valid).

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {strategy} (Stored Text Injection)
findings.remediation_brief: Sanitise AI output before persisting it to any data store. Implement content security policies on stored transcriptions and classifications. Never render stored AI output as HTML without escaping. Monitor stored results for canary-pattern tokens or instruction-like content that should not appear in legitimate transcriptions.
findings.description: The injected payload was not detected in the immediate AI response but was found persisted in stored results at the verify URL. This indicates a stored/persistent prompt injection — the AI pipeline transcribed, classified, or processed the injected content and wrote it to a database, search index, or result store where it is now accessible to other users or downstream systems.
findings.impact: Stored prompt injection is the AI equivalent of stored XSS. The injected payload persists in the application's data layer and may be rendered to other users, fed into downstream LLM calls (second-order injection), indexed by search engines, or used as training data. In Whisper/transcription pipelines, spoken injection payloads are faithfully transcribed and stored as text, creating a persistent attack vector that outlives the original file submission.

findings.title: AI Injection Resilient — {category} via {strategy}
findings.remediation_brief: No remediation required. Continue monitoring for new injection techniques and re-test periodically as the AI model or pipeline is updated.
findings.description: The AI pipeline did not follow the injected instruction. The canary token was absent from both the immediate response and any stored results. The model completed its primary task without executing the embedded adversarial payload.
findings.impact: Informational — no security impact. The pipeline demonstrated resilience against this specific injection vector, category, and delivery strategy combination. This does not guarantee resilience against other payload variants, encoding schemes, or multi-turn attacks.

findings.title: AI Injection Dry Run — {category} via {strategy}
findings.remediation_brief: No remediation required — this is an informational record of test file generation.
findings.description: A test file containing an injected adversarial payload was generated but not submitted to a target AI pipeline (--dry-run mode). The file is available in the test_files output directory for manual inspection or subsequent submission.
findings.impact: Informational — no security testing was performed. The generated file can be used for manual testing, integration into CI/CD security pipelines, or submitted to AI endpoints outside of pAIn's automated workflow.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — Task Hijack via pdf_docinfo_metadata
findings.remediation_brief: Strip all PDF metadata (Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator, Producer) before feeding document content to the LLM. Use a metadata-free text extraction pipeline that discards everything except the visible text layer.
findings.description: The AI pipeline abandoned its primary task when processing a PDF whose document-info metadata (Author, Subject, Keywords, Creator) contained an injected instruction. PDF metadata is commonly extracted by document processing pipelines and passed to LLMs as context.
findings.impact: PDFs are the most common document format in enterprise AI pipelines. Document-info metadata injection succeeds silently because the injected content is invisible to the human viewer — only the pipeline's metadata extraction step sees it. This enables zero-interaction attacks where a legitimately-appearing PDF hijacks any AI pipeline that processes it.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via pdf_hidden_text_layer
findings.remediation_brief: Implement text layer analysis that detects and strips hidden text (zero-contrast text, extremely small font, off-page positioned text) before LLM ingestion. Use render-then-OCR instead of direct text extraction to ensure only visible content reaches the model.
findings.description: The AI pipeline processed a PDF containing a hidden text layer (white text on white background) with an injected instruction. The text is invisible to human viewers but extracted by PDF text extraction libraries (pdfplumber, pdfminer, PyMuPDF) and passed to the LLM. The model followed the hidden instruction.
findings.impact: Hidden text layer injection is especially dangerous because the document appears completely legitimate to any human reviewer — the injected content is only visible to the machine pipeline. This enables supply-chain attacks where documents pass human approval processes before being fed to AI systems that then execute the hidden instructions.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via png_text_chunk_metadata
findings.remediation_brief: Strip all image metadata (EXIF, tEXt, iTXt, XMP) before passing images to AI vision models. Process only the pixel data for vision analysis. If metadata is needed for non-AI purposes, process it in a separate context that does not feed into the LLM.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction embedded in a PNG image's tEXt/iTXt metadata chunks (Comment, Description, Author, Source fields). Image metadata is commonly extracted by vision pipelines and may be included in the LLM's context alongside OCR or vision analysis results.
findings.impact: Image metadata injection targets vision-AI and document-processing pipelines. Since metadata is not visible in the rendered image, the attack is invisible to human reviewers. Pipelines that extract and include image metadata in LLM prompts are vulnerable to having their analysis influenced or overridden by injected instructions.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {format}_text_overlay_ocr
findings.remediation_brief: Implement content-type awareness in the LLM prompt — explicitly instruct the model that OCR-extracted text is untrusted content to be described, never instructions to be followed. Use a two-stage pipeline where OCR extraction and LLM analysis run in isolated contexts.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction rendered as visible text in an image. The text was extracted via OCR (optical character recognition) or multimodal vision analysis and passed to the LLM, which treated it as an instruction rather than image content to be described or classified.
findings.impact: OCR/vision-based injection targets any pipeline that extracts text from images — document digitisation, receipt processing, medical imaging, ID verification, etc. Unlike metadata injection, the payload is technically visible, but in a real attack it would be placed in inconspicuous locations (small text, low contrast, marginal annotations) that human reviewers overlook.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via wav_spoken_audio_content
findings.remediation_brief: Implement post-transcription filtering to detect and strip instruction-like patterns from ASR output before passing to downstream LLMs. Use separate processing contexts for transcription and instruction execution. Apply anomaly detection to transcriptions that contain command-like syntax.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction delivered as synthesised speech in a WAV audio file. The speech-to-text (Whisper/ASR) component transcribed the spoken payload, and the downstream LLM treated the transcribed text as an instruction to execute rather than content to process.
findings.impact: Spoken audio injection is the most dangerous delivery vector for transcription pipelines because it exploits the fundamental purpose of the pipeline — faithfully transcribing speech. The injected instruction arrives through the same channel as legitimate audio content, making it impossible to filter at the transport layer. In customer service, medical dictation, legal transcription, and meeting-notes pipelines, spoken injection can alter transcripts, inject false records, or hijack downstream AI processing.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via {format}_id3_tags
findings.remediation_brief: Strip all audio metadata (ID3, Vorbis comments, MP4 tags) before including audio file context in LLM prompts. Process only the audio waveform data for transcription and discard metadata entirely.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction embedded in audio file metadata (ID3 tags: Title, Artist, Album, Comment, Lyrics). Audio metadata is commonly extracted by media processing pipelines and may be included in the LLM's context alongside transcription results.
findings.impact: Audio metadata injection targets music cataloguing, podcast processing, and media management AI pipelines. ID3 tags are standard metadata fields that many processing pipelines extract automatically. The injected payload is invisible during audio playback but present in the file's binary structure, enabling silent injection into any pipeline that reads tag data.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via docx_body_text_extraction
findings.remediation_brief: Implement instruction boundary separation — ensure the LLM prompt clearly delineates system instructions from document content using robust delimiters. Apply content filtering to detect instruction-like patterns in extracted text before LLM ingestion.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction placed in the body text of a DOCX (Word) document. The document XML body was extracted by the pipeline's document parser and passed to the LLM, which treated the injected instruction as authoritative.
findings.impact: DOCX is a standard enterprise document format. Body text injection is the most straightforward attack vector — the payload appears as regular document content. In document review, contract analysis, compliance checking, and summarisation pipelines, an attacker can embed instructions that redirect the AI's analysis, alter its conclusions, or force specific outputs.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via docx_comment_text_extraction
findings.remediation_brief: Strip document comments, headers, footers, and annotations before feeding document content to the LLM. Only extract and process the visible body text for AI analysis.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction placed in a DOCX document's comment annotations. Document comments are a secondary content channel that some parsers (python-docx, docx2txt) extract alongside body text. The pipeline included comment text in the LLM context, and the model treated the injected instruction as authoritative.
findings.impact: Comment-based injection targets document review and collaboration pipelines. Comments are a semi-hidden content channel — they appear in sidebars during editing but are often stripped or ignored in final renderings, making them a covert injection vector. Pipelines that extract and process all document content (including comments, headers, footers, and annotations) are vulnerable.

findings.title: AI Prompt Injection — {category} via zip_member_text_injection
findings.remediation_brief: Implement content scanning on all extracted archive members before LLM ingestion. Apply the same instruction-detection filtering to extracted text files as to directly uploaded documents. Limit the types of files that can be extracted and processed from archives.
findings.description: The AI pipeline followed an injected instruction placed in text files within a ZIP archive (document.txt, data.csv, notes.md). Pipelines that automatically extract and process archive contents are vulnerable when extracted text is passed to the LLM without sanitisation.
findings.impact: ZIP/archive injection targets document processing and data ingestion pipelines that automatically extract and process compressed archives. The injected payload is spread across multiple archive members (TXT, CSV, Markdown), maximising the chance of reaching the LLM through whichever extraction path the pipeline uses. This vector also enables payload delivery through legitimate-looking data files.

findings.title: Relay Established Successfully
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Operational success event. Ensure the session is deactivated cleanly after scanning completes.
findings.description: A pivot relay session was established between pivot-client and pivot-agent. Authentication, TLS handshake, and network profile activation all succeeded. Scanner traffic can now reach the target CIDR.

findings.title: Authentication Failed — Invalid HMAC Token
findings.remediation_brief: Verify that security.auth_token matches exactly on both agent and client configurations (including whitespace). For chained profiles, ensure upstream.auth_token matches the upstream relay's token.
findings.description: The AUTH message sent by a connecting client contained an HMAC-SHA256 digest that did not match the expected value for the provided nonce and shared secret. The connection was rejected.

findings.title: Replay Attack Detected — Nonce Already Used
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate the source IP of the replayed authentication attempt. Verify TLS is enforced end-to-end (no MitM). Rotate auth_token and regenerate TLS certificates if compromise is suspected.
findings.description: An AUTH message was received with a nonce that has been used in a previous authentication attempt within the current session. This is indicative of a replay attack — a captured AUTH message being retransmitted.

findings.title: TLS Handshake Failed
findings.remediation_brief: 1. Ensure ca.crt on the client was generated by the same CA that signed agent.crt. 2. Confirm security.tls.server_hostname in client config matches CN/SAN in agent.crt. 3. Check certificate expiry. 4. Verify TLS 1.2+ is supported on both sides.
findings.description: The TLS handshake between pivot-client and pivot-agent failed. Possible causes: certificate not trusted by the client's CA bundle, CN/SAN mismatch, expired certificate, or unsupported TLS version.

findings.title: Unauthorised Connection Attempt — IP Not in Allowlist
findings.remediation_brief: Review allowed_peers in the agent configuration. If the source IP is legitimate, add it to the allowlist. Investigate unexpected connection sources.
findings.description: A connection was received from a source IP that is not present in security.allowed_peers. The connection was rejected after TLS handshake but before authentication, minimising information leakage.

findings.title: iptables Rule Applied Successfully
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Verify rule cleanup occurs on session deactivation.
findings.description: iptables FORWARD and MASQUERADE rules were successfully installed on the relay device for a network profile. IP forwarding is active. Scanner traffic will be NATted to the relay's LAN IP.

findings.title: iptables Rule Cleanup Completed
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Verify with: sudo iptables -L FORWARD -n -v and sudo iptables -t nat -L POSTROUTING -n -v
findings.description: All iptables rules installed for a relay session were removed successfully. ip_forward was reset to its pre-session value if no other sessions are active. Relay state is fully clean.

findings.title: Relay Chain Established
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Operational success event. Verify end-to-end connectivity with a test scan before the full engagement.
findings.description: A multi-hop relay chain was successfully established. The current agent spawned an internal chain_connector (pivot-client) to a downstream relay and received network profile activation confirmation. All intermediate routes are active.

findings.title: Connection to Upstream Relay Failed
findings.remediation_brief: 1. Verify the upstream relay is running and reachable from the current relay device. 2. Check upstream.host and upstream.port in the profile configuration. 3. Verify auth_token, TLS certs, and network routing between relay nodes.
findings.description: A chained relay attempted to connect to its configured upstream relay (pivot-agent at upstream.host) but failed. The chain is broken and the target network is unreachable.

findings.title: Certificate Validation Failed — Agent Certificate Not Trusted
findings.remediation_brief: Verify cafile on the client points to the CA that signed the agent's certificate. Re-generate certificates with tools/pivot-gen-certs.sh if needed. Never set verify_hostname: false in production.
findings.description: The pivot-client rejected the agent's TLS certificate because it could not be validated against the configured CA bundle. This may indicate a certificate mismatch or a potential MitM attack.

findings.title: mTLS Client Certificate Required
findings.remediation_brief: Generate a client certificate with tools/pivot-gen-certs.sh and configure certfile/keyfile in the client's TLS configuration block.
findings.description: The agent is configured with require_client_cert: true (mutual TLS). Clients must present a valid certificate signed by the agent's CA in addition to HMAC token authentication.

findings.title: HMAC Verification Failed — Token Mismatch
findings.remediation_brief: Verify auth_token values match exactly on both sides. If mismatches persist after verifying configs, investigate for tampering or MitM. Rotate the shared secret.
findings.description: The HMAC-SHA256 digest computed from the client's nonce and the stored shared secret did not match the digest provided in the AUTH message. Authentication was denied. Constant-time comparison was used to prevent timing oracle attacks.

findings.title: iptables Rule Application Failed
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure pivot-agent is running as root or with CAP_NET_ADMIN + CAP_NET_RAW. Verify iptables is installed: which iptables. Check: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
findings.description: The agent could not install required iptables FORWARD or MASQUERADE rules. This prevents traffic forwarding to the target network. The relay session is non-functional.

findings.title: Route Installation Failed on Scanner
findings.remediation_brief: Run pivot-client with sudo. On Linux: verify ip command is available. On macOS: verify route command is available and sudo rights are granted.
findings.description: pivot-client failed to install the OS route for the target CIDR on the scanner machine. The scanner cannot reach the target network even though the relay session is active.

findings.title: Session Expired — Heartbeat Timeout
findings.remediation_brief: Ensure pivot-client is running and the network path between client and agent remains stable. Adjust heartbeat_interval and heartbeat_timeout in the config if the network is lossy.
findings.description: The relay session was closed because no HEARTBEAT message was received from the client within the configured heartbeat_timeout period. The client may have crashed or the network path was interrupted.

findings.title: Maximum Concurrent Sessions Reached
findings.remediation_brief: Increase session.max_sessions in the agent config if additional concurrent connections are needed. Verify that existing sessions are not stuck.
findings.description: A new connection was rejected because the agent has reached session.max_sessions. No additional relay clients can connect until an existing session is released.

findings.title: Protocol Message Too Large
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate the source of the oversized message. Ensure only authorised clients connect to the relay. Review for protocol anomalies.
findings.description: A received message exceeded the maximum permitted payload size (1 MB). The connection was closed. This may indicate a malformed client, a bug, or a potential memory exhaustion attempt.

findings.title: Malformed Protocol Message Received
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate the source of the malformed message. This may indicate a port scanner, an incompatible client version, or an active probe. Review allowed_peers configuration.
findings.description: A message was received that could not be parsed as valid JSON, was missing the required 'type' field, or had a zero-length payload. The connection was closed.

findings.title: sysctl ip_forward Activation Failed
findings.remediation_brief: Run pivot-agent as root. Manually verify: sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward. In some hardened environments, sysctl may be locked — consult system configuration.
findings.description: The agent could not set net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 via sysctl. Without IP forwarding enabled, traffic cannot be relayed between the VPN and LAN interfaces.

findings.title: Clean Session Deactivation Completed
findings.remediation_brief: No action required. Verify cleanup with: ip route show && iptables -L FORWARD -n -v
findings.description: The pivot-client sent a DEACTIVATE message and the agent responded with DEACTIVATE_RESPONSE. iptables rules, kernel routes, and ip_forward were all cleaned up. Session state is fully removed.

findings.title: Hardcoded Public DNS Resolvers Bypass Enterprise Controls
findings.owasp_web: A09:2021 Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
findings.remediation_brief: Modify device firmware to use only the DHCP-supplied DNS resolver. Implement DoH/DoT. Provide deployment-time toggle for hospital IT to constrain the resolver.
findings.description: Device sends DNS queries directly to public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1, etc.) instead of using the DHCP-supplied resolver, bypassing enterprise DNS filtering, sinkholing, anomaly detection and split-DNS.
findings.impact: Enterprise DNS controls are bypassed for the device's most security-relevant traffic. Security teams cannot detect or block the device contacting unexpected endpoints, cannot apply DNS-based egress restrictions, and cannot audit data-exfiltration patterns. Represents a HIPAA / SOC 2 logging control gap.

findings.title: Cleartext DNS Exposes External Service Topology
findings.remediation_brief: Implement DNS-over-HTTPS (RFC 8484) or DNS-over-TLS (RFC 7858) on the device.
findings.description: All DNS queries are sent over cleartext UDP/53. Any on-path observer can enumerate the full set of external services the device depends on.
findings.impact: An attacker who can passively observe device traffic learns the entire backend architecture without active probing — cloud-provider endpoints, push-notification dependencies, captive-portal probe destinations and SaaS services in use.

findings.title: Device Identity Leaked in TLS Client Certificate (mTLS)
findings.remediation_brief: Use opaque per-device identifier (UUID) as the Subject CN. Move human-readable serial / model into a custom certificate extension or SubjectAltName otherName.
findings.description: The device authenticates with a client X.509 certificate (mTLS). The certificate subject is sent in cleartext during the handshake and exposes identifying information (serial, model, vendor PKI topology).
findings.impact: Passive observers can extract the device's identity from the TLS handshake bytes without decrypting any application data. Privacy-relevant in clinical contexts where the presence of a particular medical device indicates the patient population being served.

findings.title: TLS ClientHello Offers Legacy CBC Cipher Suites
findings.remediation_brief: Remove CBC cipher suites from the device's TLS ClientHello offer list. Keep only AEAD: TLS 1.3 (0x1301/02/03) and TLS 1.2 ECDHE-AEAD (0xc02c/2b/30/2f).
findings.description: The device's TLS ClientHello offers legacy CBC-mode cipher suites alongside modern AEAD ciphers. While AEAD is typically negotiated, the CBC offer preserves a downgrade surface.
findings.impact: CBC suites are vulnerable to historical attacks (BEAST, Lucky13, POODLE-variants) when paired with TLS 1.0/1.1. In TLS 1.2 with correct implementation the practical exploit cost is high but the offer is unnecessary given AEAD alternatives are universally supported by every modern endpoint.

findings.title: DHCP Hostname Discloses Asset Identifier
findings.remediation_brief: Replace DHCP Host Name with an opaque per-device identifier (UUID or salted hash). The true serial should only travel inside the encrypted device-to-cloud channel.
findings.description: The device populates DHCP option 12 (Host Name) with an asset identifier (serial number, device tag) that is broadcast on every DHCP DISCOVER/REQUEST.
findings.impact: Any host on the broadcast domain can passively map the device's MAC and IP to the broadcast asset tag — vendor, model and serial are derivable without sending a single packet. Combined with mDNS reflection this is reflected across L3 boundaries.

findings.title: DNS Search-Suffix Appended to Fully-Qualified Hostnames
findings.remediation_brief: Patch device DNS client so hostnames with three or more labels (or trailing dot) bypass search-domain processing. Set 'ndots' threshold to 1.
findings.description: The device's DNS client appends the DHCP-supplied search domain to hostnames that are already fully-qualified. RFC 1535 and RFC 8767 require resolvers not to apply search-suffix processing to FQDNs.
findings.impact: An attacker controlling the search-suffix DNS zone can redirect the device's cloud traffic to attacker-controlled IPs. TLS server certificate validation usually catches the substitution, but the failure mode leaks connection metadata on every retry. If cert pinning is incorrectly implemented, the substitution succeeds.

findings.title: SMBv1 Traffic Observed (EternalBlue / NotPetya exposure)
findings.remediation_brief: Disable SMBv1 on every host. Confirm SMB2+ minimum on file servers. Block 445/tcp at segmentation boundary.
findings.description: SMBv1 protocol traffic observed between the device and one or more internal peers. SMBv1 is deprecated since 2014 and is the transport for EternalBlue (MS17-010) / WannaCry / NotPetya.
findings.impact: Active SMBv1 on a clinical network creates a worm propagation path. Disable per FDA Postmarket Cybersecurity Guidance and Joint Commission EHR-protection expectations.

findings.title: LLMNR / NBT-NS Name Resolution in Use (Responder Surface)
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLMNR (GPO: Turn Off Multicast Name Resolution = Enabled) and NBT-NS (Network adapter → WINS → Disable NetBIOS over TCP/IP). Block UDP/5355 and UDP/137 at every L3 boundary.
findings.description: LLMNR or NetBIOS Name Service broadcast-based name resolution is in use on the segment. These protocols are abused by Responder / Inveigh to poison name resolution and capture NTLMv2 hashes.
findings.impact: An attacker on the same broadcast domain runs `responder -I eth0` and captures hashes from any device that mistypes a hostname or uses a non-FQDN lookup. Hashes are crackable offline or relayed via ntlmrelayx for immediate authentication elsewhere (CVE-2019-1040 mitigations notwithstanding).

findings.title: SSDP / UPnP Broadcasts Expose Internal Services
findings.remediation_brief: Disable UPnP/SSDP on clinical-network hosts where not required. Block UDP/1900 at every L3 boundary.
findings.description: SSDP/UPnP discovery traffic observed on the segment. SSDP advertises every UPnP-aware device (smart TVs, consumer routers, printers, NAS, IoT) on the local broadcast domain.
findings.impact: SSDP discovery reveals consumer-IoT, printers, smart TVs, NAS and router admin interfaces to anyone on the LAN. In a clinical network this co-mingles consumer devices with medical equipment and facilitates lateral discovery.

findings.title: mDNS Activity Exposes Device Identity on Internal Segment
findings.remediation_brief: Disable mDNS on the device if not required. Audit network-side mDNS reflector config (Avahi `reflector=yes`, UniFi 'Multicast DNS') and disable cross-VLAN reflection.
findings.description: Device emits mDNS queries and/or responses on the local segment. mDNS exposes the device's hostname and services to any host on the multicast-reachable segment, and is reflected across L3 by mDNS-reflector-enabled gateways.
findings.impact: Device fingerprinting and asset enumeration without active probing. Reduces the cost of targeting a specific device for theft, social-engineering, or RF replay attack.

findings.title: LLDP Topology / Switch Firmware Disclosure
findings.remediation_brief: Disable LLDP on access ports facing devices (`no lldp transmit` / `no lldp receive`). Keep LLDP only on inter-switch trunks.
findings.description: LLDP TLVs observed on the segment leak switch identity, model and firmware. Information that downstream attackers can use to select vendor-specific CVEs.
findings.impact: An attacker passively learns the network gear vendor, model and firmware version without sending any probes. Combined with public CVE databases this is a free vulnerability-research head-start.

findings.title: ARP Anomalies (Duplicate IP-to-MAC Mappings)
findings.remediation_brief: Investigate each duplicate. Configure DAI (Dynamic ARP Inspection) on managed switches. Bind static IP↔MAC for critical clinical-device subnets.
findings.description: Duplicate ARP entries observed — one IP advertised by multiple MAC addresses. Possible legitimate HA pair, gratuitous ARP storm, or active ARP-spoofing / MitM.
findings.impact: If the duplicate is a MitM attack, the attacker is intercepting traffic between the device and another host. Even when legitimate (HA failover), the unannounced duplicate breaks deterministic L2 routing and may drop packets.

findings.title: Cleartext FTP Traffic Observed (credentials in plaintext)
findings.remediation_brief: Disable FTP. Use SFTP (SSH) or FTPS (FTP over TLS, explicit AUTH TLS). Block 21/tcp at segmentation boundary.
findings.description: FTP control-channel traffic observed in cleartext. FTP USER/PASS commands and file contents are passively captureable by any on-path observer.
findings.impact: Any L2 / SPAN / WiFi-sniffing attacker can capture FTP credentials and uploaded/downloaded file content. In a clinical setting this may include device firmware, calibration data, or PHI.

findings.title: Cleartext Telnet Traffic Observed
findings.remediation_brief: Replace Telnet with SSH. Block 23/tcp at every L3 boundary.
findings.description: Telnet traffic observed in cleartext. Telnet credentials and keystrokes are sent in plaintext and trivially captured by passive observers.
findings.impact: Full session capture — usernames, passwords and every keystroke are recoverable from a passive sniff. Common on legacy embedded and industrial-control devices.

findings.title: SNMPv1/v2c Community String in Cleartext
findings.remediation_brief: Migrate to SNMPv3 with authentication (SHA) + encryption (AES). Disable SNMPv1/v2c. Restrict SNMP source IPs at the device.
findings.description: SNMP community strings (passwords) observed in plaintext. Communities like 'public' / 'private' / vendor-default values grant MIB-table read access (or write if RW).
findings.impact: SNMP community strings are passwords. An attacker capturing them can read MIB data (interface stats, ARP tables, routing tables) and with a write community can reconfigure the device.

findings.title: HTTP Basic Authentication Observed in Cleartext
findings.remediation_brief: Wrap the affected service in TLS (HTTPS) or replace Basic Auth with token/cookie-based scheme over TLS. Block plain HTTP on authenticated admin endpoints.
findings.description: HTTP Basic Auth headers observed in cleartext. Authorization: Basic <base64> is one base64-decode step away from username:password.
findings.impact: Basic Auth credentials are base64-encoded usernames+passwords. Any passive observer can decode them in one step (`base64 -d`). Often reused across many systems.

findings.title: LDAP Bind Observed Without TLS
findings.remediation_brief: Enforce LDAPS (TCP/636) or LDAP+StartTLS. Block plain LDAP (389/tcp) at the firewall.
findings.description: LDAP bind request observed in cleartext. Without LDAPS or StartTLS, the bind DN and password are exposed.
findings.impact: An attacker capturing the bind can extract the LDAP credentials. Domain-bound accounts are reusable across the AD forest and may unlock additional services (Kerberos, file shares, mail, VPN).

findings.title: App Transport Security: arbitrary loads allowed
findings.remediation_brief: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads or scope to specific domains via NSExceptionDomains.
findings.description: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads=true disables ATS globally; non-HTTPS connections are permitted.
